Chapter 30: Backpropagation Math

Prerequisite

  • The Chain Rule: Knowing how to propagate derivatives through nested functions.
  • Matrix Calculus: Comfort with matrix-vector products and outer products.

1. Conceptual Hook

When we train a deep neural network, we adjust millions of weights to minimize a loss function. If we calculated the gradient of the loss with respect to each individual weight from scratch, we would need to run the entire network calculations over and over for every single weight. For modern networks, this would take years. The algorithm that allows us to calculate all these gradients in a single step is backpropagation.

Backpropagation is a highly efficient implementation of the chain rule. Instead of computing gradients independently, it uses dynamic programming. It runs a forward pass to calculate the activations of every neuron, and then runs a backward pass that caches and propagates error signals from the output layer to the input. By recycling these intermediate values, backpropagation reduces the computational complexity of gradient calculation from a disastrous quadratic scale to a linear scale, making deep learning practically viable.

2. Formal Definition

Consider an LLL-layer feedforward neural network. The feedforward equations for layer lll (where l=1,2,…,Ll = 1, 2, \dots, Ll=1,2,…,L) are: z(l)=W(l)a(l−1)+b(l)z^{(l)} = W^{(l)} a^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)}z(l)=W(l)a(l−1)+b(l) a(l)=σ(z(l))a^{(l)} = \sigma(z^{(l)})a(l)=σ(z(l)) where:

  • W(l)∈Rnl×nl−1W^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l \times n_{l-1}}W(l)∈Rnl​×nl−1​ is the weight matrix for layer lll.
  • b(l)∈Rnlb^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l}b(l)∈Rnl​ is the bias vector for layer lll.
  • a(l−1)∈Rnl−1a^{(l-1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{l-1}}a(l−1)∈Rnl−1​ is the activation vector from the previous layer (a(0)=xa^{(0)} = xa(0)=x, the input vector).
  • z(l)∈Rnlz^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l}z(l)∈Rnl​ is the pre-activation logit vector of layer lll.
  • σ\sigmaσ is the activation function (applied element-wise).

Let CCC be the scalar cost function (e.g. Mean Squared Error or Cross-Entropy) evaluating the network's output a(L)a^{(L)}a(L) against target label yyy.

We define the error signal vector for layer lll as the partial derivative of the cost with respect to the pre-activation logits: δ(l)=∂C∂z(l)∈Rnl\delta^{(l)} = \frac{\partial C}{\partial z^{(l)}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l}δ(l)=∂z(l)∂C​∈Rnl​

The Four Fundamental Equations of Backpropagation

  1. Error at the output layer LLL: δ(L)=∇a(L)C⊙σ′(z(L))\delta^{(L)} = \nabla_{a^{(L)}} C \odot \sigma'(z^{(L)})δ(L)=∇a(L)​C⊙σ′(z(L))
  2. Error at a hidden layer lll (w.r.t the next layer l+1l+1l+1): δ(l)=((W(l+1))Tδ(l+1))⊙σ′(z(l))\delta^{(l)} = \left( (W^{(l+1)})^T \delta^{(l+1)} \right) \odot \sigma'(z^{(l)})δ(l)=((W(l+1))Tδ(l+1))⊙σ′(z(l))
  3. Gradient of the cost w.r.t the bias b(l)b^{(l)}b(l): ∂C∂b(l)=δ(l)\frac{\partial C}{\partial b^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)}∂b(l)∂C​=δ(l)
  4. Gradient of the cost w.r.t the weight W(l)W^{(l)}W(l): ∂C∂W(l)=δ(l)(a(l−1))T\frac{\partial C}{\partial W^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} (a^{(l-1)})^T∂W(l)∂C​=δ(l)(a(l−1))T where ⊙\odot⊙ represents the Hadamard (element-wise) product.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Derivation of the Four Backpropagation Equations

We derive the fundamental equations of backpropagation using index notation and the multivariable chain rule.

Proof of Equation 1 (Output Error δ(L)\delta^{(L)}δ(L)): By definition, the iii-th component of the error vector δ(L)\delta^{(L)}δ(L) is: δi(L)=∂C∂zi(L)\delta_i^{(L)} = \frac{\partial C}{\partial z_i^{(L)}}δi(L)​=∂zi(L)​∂C​ Since the cost CCC depends directly on the activations a(L)a^{(L)}a(L), and each ak(L)a_k^{(L)}ak(L)​ depends on zk(L)z_k^{(L)}zk(L)​: δi(L)=∑k∂C∂ak(L)∂ak(L)∂zi(L)\delta_i^{(L)} = \sum_k \frac{\partial C}{\partial a_k^{(L)}} \frac{\partial a_k^{(L)}}{\partial z_i^{(L)}}δi(L)​=∑k​∂ak(L)​∂C​∂zi(L)​∂ak(L)​​ Because ak(L)=σ(zk(L))a_k^{(L)} = \sigma(z_k^{(L)})ak(L)​=σ(zk(L)​), the derivative ∂ak(L)∂zi(L)\frac{\partial a_k^{(L)}}{\partial z_i^{(L)}}∂zi(L)​∂ak(L)​​ is non-zero only when k=ik = ik=i. Thus, the summation collapses to: δi(L)=∂C∂ai(L)σ′(zi(L))\delta_i^{(L)} = \frac{\partial C}{\partial a_i^{(L)}} \sigma'(z_i^{(L)})δi(L)​=∂ai(L)​∂C​σ′(zi(L)​) Vectorizing this coordinate-wise equation yields: δ(L)=∇a(L)C⊙σ′(z(L))■\delta^{(L)} = \nabla_{a^{(L)}} C \odot \sigma'(z^{(L)}) \quad \blacksquareδ(L)=∇a(L)​C⊙σ′(z(L))■

Proof of Equation 2 (Hidden Layer Error δ(l)\delta^{(l)}δ(l)): We apply the chain rule to relate δ(l)\delta^{(l)}δ(l) to the error of the subsequent layer δ(l+1)\delta^{(l+1)}δ(l+1): δj(l)=∂C∂zj(l)=∑k∂C∂zk(l+1)∂zk(l+1)∂zj(l)=∑kδk(l+1)∂zk(l+1)∂zj(l)\delta_j^{(l)} = \frac{\partial C}{\partial z_j^{(l)}} = \sum_k \frac{\partial C}{\partial z_k^{(l+1)}} \frac{\partial z_k^{(l+1)}}{\partial z_j^{(l)}} = \sum_k \delta_k^{(l+1)} \frac{\partial z_k^{(l+1)}}{\partial z_j^{(l)}}δj(l)​=∂zj(l)​∂C​=∑k​∂zk(l+1)​∂C​∂zj(l)​∂zk(l+1)​​=∑k​δk(l+1)​∂zj(l)​∂zk(l+1)​​ Using the relation zk(l+1)=∑rWkr(l+1)ar(l)+bk(l+1)z_k^{(l+1)} = \sum_r W_{kr}^{(l+1)} a_r^{(l)} + b_k^{(l+1)}zk(l+1)​=∑r​Wkr(l+1)​ar(l)​+bk(l+1)​, we take the derivative w.r.t zj(l)z_j^{(l)}zj(l)​: ∂zk(l+1)∂zj(l)=∑rWkr(l+1)∂ar(l)∂zj(l)\frac{\partial z_k^{(l+1)}}{\partial z_j^{(l)}} = \sum_r W_{kr}^{(l+1)} \frac{\partial a_r^{(l)}}{\partial z_j^{(l)}}∂zj(l)​∂zk(l+1)​​=∑r​Wkr(l+1)​∂zj(l)​∂ar(l)​​ Since ar(l)=σ(zr(l))a_r^{(l)} = \sigma(z_r^{(l)})ar(l)​=σ(zr(l)​), ∂ar(l)∂zj(l)\frac{\partial a_r^{(l)}}{\partial z_j^{(l)}}∂zj(l)​∂ar(l)​​ is non-zero only when r=jr = jr=j: ∂zk(l+1)∂zj(l)=Wkj(l+1)σ′(zj(l))\frac{\partial z_k^{(l+1)}}{\partial z_j^{(l)}} = W_{kj}^{(l+1)} \sigma'(z_j^{(l)})∂zj(l)​∂zk(l+1)​​=Wkj(l+1)​σ′(zj(l)​) Substitute this back into the coordinate summation: δj(l)=∑kδk(l+1)Wkj(l+1)σ′(zj(l))=(∑kWkj(l+1)δk(l+1))σ′(zj(l))\delta_j^{(l)} = \sum_k \delta_k^{(l+1)} W_{kj}^{(l+1)} \sigma'(z_j^{(l)}) = \left( \sum_k W_{kj}^{(l+1)} \delta_k^{(l+1)} \right) \sigma'(z_j^{(l)})δj(l)​=∑k​δk(l+1)​Wkj(l+1)​σ′(zj(l)​)=(∑k​Wkj(l+1)​δk(l+1)​)σ′(zj(l)​) Notice that ∑kWkj(l+1)δk(l+1)\sum_k W_{kj}^{(l+1)} \delta_k^{(l+1)}∑k​Wkj(l+1)​δk(l+1)​ is the jjj-th component of the matrix-vector product (W(l+1))Tδ(l+1)(W^{(l+1)})^T \delta^{(l+1)}(W(l+1))Tδ(l+1). Vectorizing this expression yields: δ(l)=((W(l+1))Tδ(l+1))⊙σ′(z(l))■\delta^{(l)} = \left( (W^{(l+1)})^T \delta^{(l+1)} \right) \odot \sigma'(z^{(l)}) \quad \blacksquareδ(l)=((W(l+1))Tδ(l+1))⊙σ′(z(l))■

Proof of Equations 3 and 4 (Parameter Gradients): Using the chain rule to find the derivative of the cost with respect to individual weights and biases at layer lll: ∂C∂Wij(l)=∂C∂zi(l)∂zi(l)∂Wij(l)\frac{\partial C}{\partial W_{ij}^{(l)}} = \frac{\partial C}{\partial z_i^{(l)}} \frac{\partial z_i^{(l)}}{\partial W_{ij}^{(l)}}∂Wij(l)​∂C​=∂zi(l)​∂C​∂Wij(l)​∂zi(l)​​ Since zi(l)=∑rWir(l)ar(l−1)+bi(l)z_i^{(l)} = \sum_r W_{ir}^{(l)} a_r^{(l-1)} + b_i^{(l)}zi(l)​=∑r​Wir(l)​ar(l−1)​+bi(l)​, we have ∂zi(l)∂Wij(l)=aj(l−1)\frac{\partial z_i^{(l)}}{\partial W_{ij}^{(l)}} = a_j^{(l-1)}∂Wij(l)​∂zi(l)​​=aj(l−1)​. Substituting this: ∂C∂Wij(l)=δi(l)aj(l−1)\frac{\partial C}{\partial W_{ij}^{(l)}} = \delta_i^{(l)} a_j^{(l-1)}∂Wij(l)​∂C​=δi(l)​aj(l−1)​ This coordinate product is the definition of the outer product of δ(l)\delta^{(l)}δ(l) and a(l−1)a^{(l-1)}a(l−1), yielding: ∂C∂W(l)=δ(l)(a(l−1))T■\frac{\partial C}{\partial W^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} (a^{(l-1)})^T \quad \blacksquare∂W(l)∂C​=δ(l)(a(l−1))T■ For the bias gradient: ∂C∂bi(l)=∂C∂zi(l)∂zi(l)∂bi(l)\frac{\partial C}{\partial b_i^{(l)}} = \frac{\partial C}{\partial z_i^{(l)}} \frac{\partial z_i^{(l)}}{\partial b_i^{(l)}}∂bi(l)​∂C​=∂zi(l)​∂C​∂bi(l)​∂zi(l)​​ Since ∂zi(l)∂bi(l)=1\frac{\partial z_i^{(l)}}{\partial b_i^{(l)}} = 1∂bi(l)​∂zi(l)​​=1: ∂C∂bi(l)=δi(l)  ⟹  ∂C∂b(l)=δ(l)■\frac{\partial C}{\partial b_i^{(l)}} = \delta_i^{(l)} \implies \frac{\partial C}{\partial b^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} \quad \blacksquare∂bi(l)​∂C​=δi(l)​⟹∂b(l)∂C​=δ(l)■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Single-Neuron Network

Let a simple network be defined by: z=wx+b  ⟹  a=σ(z)z = wx + b \implies a = \sigma(z)z=wx+b⟹a=σ(z), with MSE loss C=12(a−y)2C = \frac{1}{2}(a - y)^2C=21​(a−y)2. Inputs: x=2x = 2x=2, target y=1y = 1y=1, current parameters: w=0.5,b=0w = 0.5, b = 0w=0.5,b=0. Learning rate: η=0.1\eta = 0.1η=0.1. Activation: Sigmoid σ(z)=11+e−z\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}σ(z)=1+e−z1​.

  1. Forward Pass:
    • z=(0.5)(2)+0=1.0z = (0.5)(2) + 0 = 1.0z=(0.5)(2)+0=1.0
    • a=σ(1.0)=11+e−1≈0.731a = \sigma(1.0) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-1}} \approx 0.731a=σ(1.0)=1+e−11​≈0.731
    • C=12(0.731−1)2≈0.036C = \frac{1}{2}(0.731 - 1)^2 \approx 0.036C=21​(0.731−1)2≈0.036
  2. Backward Pass:
    • ∇aC=∂C∂a=(a−y)=(0.731−1)=−0.269\nabla_a C = \frac{\partial C}{\partial a} = (a - y) = (0.731 - 1) = -0.269∇a​C=∂a∂C​=(a−y)=(0.731−1)=−0.269
    • σ′(z)=a(1−a)=(0.731)(1−0.731)≈0.196\sigma'(z) = a(1-a) = (0.731)(1 - 0.731) \approx 0.196σ′(z)=a(1−a)=(0.731)(1−0.731)≈0.196
    • Output error δ=∇aC⋅σ′(z)=(−0.269)(0.196)≈−0.0527\delta = \nabla_a C \cdot \sigma'(z) = (-0.269)(0.196) \approx -0.0527δ=∇a​C⋅σ′(z)=(−0.269)(0.196)≈−0.0527
  3. Compute Gradients:
    • ∂C∂w=δ⋅x=(−0.0527)(2)=−0.1054\frac{\partial C}{\partial w} = \delta \cdot x = (-0.0527)(2) = -0.1054∂w∂C​=δ⋅x=(−0.0527)(2)=−0.1054
    • ∂C∂b=δ=−0.0527\frac{\partial C}{\partial b} = \delta = -0.0527∂b∂C​=δ=−0.0527
  4. Perform Weight Update:
    • wnew=w−η∂C∂w=0.5−(0.1)(−0.1054)=0.51054w_{new} = w - \eta \frac{\partial C}{\partial w} = 0.5 - (0.1)(-0.1054) = 0.51054wnew​=w−η∂w∂C​=0.5−(0.1)(−0.1054)=0.51054
    • bnew=b−η∂C∂b=0−(0.1)(−0.0527)=0.00527b_{new} = b - \eta \frac{\partial C}{\partial b} = 0 - (0.1)(-0.0527) = 0.00527bnew​=b−η∂b∂C​=0−(0.1)(−0.0527)=0.00527

Example 2: Simple 3-Layer MLP Chain

Let an input a(0)=1a^{(0)} = 1a(0)=1 pass through w(1)=2  ⟹  a(1)  ⟹  w(2)=0.5  ⟹  a(2)w^{(1)} = 2 \implies a^{(1)} \implies w^{(2)} = 0.5 \implies a^{(2)}w(1)=2⟹a(1)⟹w(2)=0.5⟹a(2). Assume linear activations σ(z)=z  ⟹  σ′(z)=1\sigma(z) = z \implies \sigma'(z) = 1σ(z)=z⟹σ′(z)=1 for simplicity. Let b(1)=b(2)=0b^{(1)} = b^{(2)} = 0b(1)=b(2)=0. The cost function is C=12(a(2)−y)2C = \frac{1}{2}(a^{(2)} - y)^2C=21​(a(2)−y)2 with target y=3y = 3y=3.

  1. Forward Pass:
    • z(1)=w(1)a(0)=2(1)=2  ⟹  a(1)=2z^{(1)} = w^{(1)} a^{(0)} = 2(1) = 2 \implies a^{(1)} = 2z(1)=w(1)a(0)=2(1)=2⟹a(1)=2
    • z(2)=w(2)a(1)=(0.5)(2)=1  ⟹  a(2)=1z^{(2)} = w^{(2)} a^{(1)} = (0.5)(2) = 1 \implies a^{(2)} = 1z(2)=w(2)a(1)=(0.5)(2)=1⟹a(2)=1
    • C=12(1−3)2=2C = \frac{1}{2}(1 - 3)^2 = 2C=21​(1−3)2=2
  2. Backward Pass:
    • δ(2)=(a(2)−y)⋅1=(1−3)=−2\delta^{(2)} = (a^{(2)} - y) \cdot 1 = (1 - 3) = -2δ(2)=(a(2)−y)⋅1=(1−3)=−2
    • δ(1)=((w(2))Tδ(2))⋅1=(0.5)(−2)=−1\delta^{(1)} = \left( (w^{(2)})^T \delta^{(2)} \right) \cdot 1 = (0.5)(-2) = -1δ(1)=((w(2))Tδ(2))⋅1=(0.5)(−2)=−1
  3. Compute Gradients:
    • ∂C∂w(2)=δ(2)a(1)=(−2)(2)=−4\frac{\partial C}{\partial w^{(2)}} = \delta^{(2)} a^{(1)} = (-2)(2) = -4∂w(2)∂C​=δ(2)a(1)=(−2)(2)=−4
    • ∂C∂w(1)=δ(1)a(0)=(−1)(1)=−1\frac{\partial C}{\partial w^{(1)}} = \delta^{(1)} a^{(0)} = (-1)(1) = -1∂w(1)∂C​=δ(1)a(0)=(−1)(1)=−1

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Autograd Systems (PyTorch / TensorFlow): Modern deep learning frameworks build dynamic computation graphs during the forward pass. Calling .backward() executes reverse-mode automatic differentiation, computing the backpropagation equations automatically.
  2. Vanishing Gradients: If we use Sigmoid activations, their derivative σ′(z)\sigma'(z)σ′(z) peaks at 0.250.250.25. Multiplying these values recursively across many hidden layers causes the error signal δ(l)\delta^{(l)}δ(l) to vanish as it reaches early layers, halting training.
  3. Mini-Batch Gradient Aggregation: During standard training, we run backpropagation over a batch of BBB samples. The final weight gradient is the average of the individual sample gradients: ∂C∂W(l)=1B∑b=1Bδb(l)(ab(l−1))T\frac{\partial C}{\partial W^{(l)}} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \delta_b^{(l)} (a_b^{(l-1)})^T∂W(l)∂C​=B1​∑b=1B​δb(l)​(ab(l−1)​)T.
  4. Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT): In recurrent neural networks (RNNs), the model is unrolled across time steps. BPTT applies standard backpropagation backward through the temporal dependencies to compute gradients for shared weights.
  5. Integrated Gradients for Model Interpretability: To understand feature attribution, we integrate the gradients of a model's prediction with respect to input pixels (∂y∂x\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}∂x∂y​), which are computed by running backpropagation all the way back to the input layer.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating the dual-pass information flow of backpropagation:

  • Show a sequence of layers: Input Layer a(0)a^{(0)}a(0), Hidden Layer a(1)a^{(1)}a(1), and Output Layer a(2)a^{(2)}a(2) culminating in a Loss CCC.
  • Draw blue arrows pointing from left to right to illustrate the Forward Pass. Label them with equations showing activations propagating forward: z(l)=W(l)a(l−1)+b(l)→a(l)=σ(z(l))z^{(l)} = W^{(l)} a^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)} \to a^{(l)} = \sigma(z^{(l)})z(l)=W(l)a(l−1)+b(l)→a(l)=σ(z(l)).
  • Draw red arrows pointing from right to left to illustrate the Backward Pass. Show the output error signal δ(2)\delta^{(2)}δ(2) flowing backward.
  • Show how δ(2)\delta^{(2)}δ(2) is transformed by (W(2))T(W^{(2)})^T(W(2))T and scaled by σ′(z(1))\sigma'(z^{(1)})σ′(z(1)) to compute δ(1)\delta^{(1)}δ(1), visualizing how the error signal propagates recursively.
  • Draw vertical branches at each layer showing the local gradient computation: ∂C∂W(l)=δ(l)(a(l−1))T\frac{\partial C}{\partial W^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} (a^{(l-1)})^T∂W(l)∂C​=δ(l)(a(l−1))T, highlighting that gradients are computed locally by combining incoming activations and backward-flowing error signals.

title: Chain Rule
description: Composite functions, multivariable chain rule, limit definition proof, and backpropagation in deep networks.
content:
Chapter 31: Chain Rule

Prerequisite

  • Function Composition: Familiarity with nested functions of the form f(g(x))f(g(x))f(g(x)).
  • Partial Derivatives: Understanding rates of change along specific coordinate directions.

1. Conceptual Hook

In deep learning, we stack layers of neurons to form composite functions of extreme depth: y=fL(fL−1(…(f1(x))… ))y = f_L(f_{L-1}(\dots(f_1(x))\dots))y=fL​(fL−1​(…(f1​(x))…)). When a model makes a prediction, the input data flows forward through this sequence of nested functions. But when we want to train the network, how do we calculate the influence of a weight in the very first layer on the final error at the output? We cannot analyze them in isolation. We use the chain rule.

The chain rule is the mathematical gear system of calculus. It allows us to compute the derivative of a nested composite function by multiplying the rates of change (local derivatives) of its constituent parts. Just as a series of connected gears transfers rotational force from the first wheel to the last, the chain rule propagates sensitivity from the final loss function all the way back to the earliest weights in our network. It is the core algorithm that powers backpropagation.

2. Formal Definition

Single-Variable Chain Rule

Let g:R→Rg: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}g:R→R be differentiable at xxx, and f:R→Rf: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}f:R→R be differentiable at g(x)g(x)g(x). The composite function h(x)=(f∘g)(x)=f(g(x))h(x) = (f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))h(x)=(f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)) is differentiable at xxx, and its derivative is: h′(x)=f′(g(x))⋅g′(x)h'(x) = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)h′(x)=f′(g(x))⋅g′(x)

In Leibniz notation, if y=f(u)y = f(u)y=f(u) and u=g(x)u = g(x)u=g(x), then: dydx=dydu⋅dudx\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}dxdy​=dudy​⋅dxdu​

Multivariable Chain Rule (General Form)

Let g:Rn→Rmg: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^mg:Rn→Rm be differentiable at xxx, and f:Rm→Rpf: \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^pf:Rm→Rp be differentiable at g(x)g(x)g(x). The derivative of the composite function h=f∘g:Rn→Rph = f \circ g: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^ph=f∘g:Rn→Rp is given by the product of their Jacobian matrices: Dx(f∘g)=Dg(x)(f)⋅Dx(g)D_x(f \circ g) = D_{g(x)}(f) \cdot D_x(g)Dx​(f∘g)=Dg(x)​(f)⋅Dx​(g) where D(f)∈Rp×mD(f) \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times m}D(f)∈Rp×m and D(g)∈Rm×nD(g) \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}D(g)∈Rm×n represent the Jacobian matrices of first-order partial derivatives.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Rigorous Proof of the Single-Variable Chain Rule

A naive proof of the chain rule splits the difference quotient: ΔyΔx=ΔyΔuΔuΔx\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta u} \frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x}ΔxΔy​=ΔuΔy​ΔxΔu​, and takes the limit. However, this fails if Δu=0\Delta u = 0Δu=0 for values near xxx (causing division by zero). We present a rigorous proof that avoids this pitfall using the linear approximation error formulation.

Proof: Let y=f(u)y = f(u)y=f(u) and u=g(x)u = g(x)u=g(x). We assume ggg is differentiable at x0x_0x0​, and fff is differentiable at u0=g(x0)u_0 = g(x_0)u0​=g(x0​). Let Δx\Delta xΔx be an increment in xxx, and let Δu=g(x0+Δx)−g(x0)\Delta u = g(x_0 + \Delta x) - g(x_0)Δu=g(x0​+Δx)−g(x0​). By the differentiability of ggg at x0x_0x0​, ggg is continuous at x0x_0x0​, which implies: lim⁡Δx→0Δu=0\lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \Delta u = 0limΔx→0​Δu=0

Define the linear approximation error function E(k)E(k)E(k) for fff around u0u_0u0​ as: E(k)={f(u0+k)−f(u0)k−f′(u0)if k≠00if k=0E(k) = \begin{cases} \frac{f(u_0 + k) - f(u_0)}{k} - f'(u_0) & \text{if } k \neq 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } k = 0 \end{cases}E(k)={kf(u0​+k)−f(u0​)​−f′(u0​)0​if k=0if k=0​ Since fff is differentiable at u0u_0u0​, the limit of the difference quotient is exactly f′(u0)f'(u_0)f′(u0​), meaning: lim⁡k→0E(k)=0\lim_{k \to 0} E(k) = 0limk→0​E(k)=0 By construction, E(k)E(k)E(k) is continuous at k=0k=0k=0. Multiplying the error definition by kkk, we obtain an equation valid for all values of kkk (including k=0k=0k=0): f(u0+k)−f(u0)=[f′(u0)+E(k)]kf(u_0 + k) - f(u_0) = \left[ f'(u_0) + E(k) \right] kf(u0​+k)−f(u0​)=[f′(u0​)+E(k)]k

Now, substitute k=Δuk = \Delta uk=Δu: f(g(x0+Δx))−f(g(x0))=[f′(g(x0))+E(Δu)]Δuf(g(x_0 + \Delta x)) - f(g(x_0)) = \left[ f'(g(x_0)) + E(\Delta u) \right] \Delta uf(g(x0​+Δx))−f(g(x0​))=[f′(g(x0​))+E(Δu)]Δu Divide both sides by the non-zero increment Δx\Delta xΔx: f(g(x0+Δx))−f(g(x0))Δx=[f′(g(x0))+E(Δu)]ΔuΔx\frac{f(g(x_0 + \Delta x)) - f(g(x_0))}{\Delta x} = \left[ f'(g(x_0)) + E(\Delta u) \right] \frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x}Δxf(g(x0​+Δx))−f(g(x0​))​=[f′(g(x0​))+E(Δu)]ΔxΔu​

Take the limit as Δx→0\Delta x \to 0Δx→0 of both sides. Using the limit product rule: (f∘g)′(x0)=lim⁡Δx→0[f′(g(x0))+E(Δu)]⋅lim⁡Δx→0g(x0+Δx)−g(x0)Δx(f \circ g)'(x_0) = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \left[ f'(g(x_0)) + E(\Delta u) \right] \cdot \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{g(x_0 + \Delta x) - g(x_0)}{\Delta x}(f∘g)′(x0​)=limΔx→0​[f′(g(x0​))+E(Δu)]⋅limΔx→0​Δxg(x0​+Δx)−g(x0​)​ Since E(k)E(k)E(k) is continuous at 000, and lim⁡Δx→0Δu=0\lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \Delta u = 0limΔx→0​Δu=0: lim⁡Δx→0E(Δu)=E(0)=0\lim_{\Delta x \to 0} E(\Delta u) = E(0) = 0limΔx→0​E(Δu)=E(0)=0 Evaluating the second limit yields the derivative g′(x0)g'(x_0)g′(x0​): (f∘g)′(x0)=[f′(g(x0))+0]⋅g′(x0)=f′(g(x0))⋅g′(x0)■(f \circ g)'(x_0) = \left[ f'(g(x_0)) + 0 \right] \cdot g'(x_0) = f'(g(x_0)) \cdot g'(x_0) \quad \blacksquare(f∘g)′(x0​)=[f′(g(x0​))+0]⋅g′(x0​)=f′(g(x0​))⋅g′(x0​)■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Nested Single-Variable Derivative

Differentiate h(x)=sin⁡(x2)h(x) = \sin(x^2)h(x)=sin(x2) using the chain rule.

  1. Identify the nested functions: y=f(u)=sin⁡(u)whereu=g(x)=x2y = f(u) = \sin(u) \quad \text{where} \quad u = g(x) = x^2y=f(u)=sin(u)whereu=g(x)=x2
  2. Calculate the individual derivatives: dydu=cos⁡(u)=cos⁡(x2)\frac{dy}{du} = \cos(u) = \cos(x^2)dudy​=cos(u)=cos(x2) dudx=2x\frac{du}{dx} = 2xdxdu​=2x
  3. Multiply the derivatives: dydx=dydu⋅dudx=cos⁡(x2)⋅2x=2xcos⁡(x2)\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx} = \cos(x^2) \cdot 2x = 2x\cos(x^2)dxdy​=dudy​⋅dxdu​=cos(x2)⋅2x=2xcos(x2)

Example 2: Multivariable Chain Rule

Let z=f(x,y)=x2+3xyz = f(x, y) = x^2 + 3xyz=f(x,y)=x2+3xy, where x(t)=sin⁡(t)x(t) = \sin(t)x(t)=sin(t) and y(t)=ety(t) = e^ty(t)=et. Find the derivative dzdt\frac{dz}{dt}dtdz​ at t=0t = 0t=0.

  1. Compute the partial derivatives of zzz: ∂z∂x=2x+3y,∂z∂y=3x\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 2x + 3y, \quad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = 3x∂x∂z​=2x+3y,∂y∂z​=3x
  2. Compute the derivatives w.r.t ttt: dxdt=cos⁡(t),dydt=et\frac{dx}{dt} = \cos(t), \quad \frac{dy}{dt} = e^tdtdx​=cos(t),dtdy​=et
  3. Evaluate variables at t=0t = 0t=0: x(0)=sin⁡(0)=0,y(0)=e0=1x(0) = \sin(0) = 0, \quad y(0) = e^0 = 1x(0)=sin(0)=0,y(0)=e0=1 ∂z∂x=2(0)+3(1)=3,∂z∂y=3(0)=0\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 2(0) + 3(1) = 3, \quad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = 3(0) = 0∂x∂z​=2(0)+3(1)=3,∂y∂z​=3(0)=0 dxdt=cos⁡(0)=1,dydt=e0=1\frac{dx}{dt} = \cos(0) = 1, \quad \frac{dy}{dt} = e^0 = 1dtdx​=cos(0)=1,dtdy​=e0=1
  4. Apply the multivariable chain rule: dzdt=∂z∂xdxdt+∂z∂ydydt=(3)(1)+(0)(1)=3\frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \frac{dy}{dt} = (3)(1) + (0)(1) = 3dtdz​=∂x∂z​dtdx​+∂y∂z​dtdy​=(3)(1)+(0)(1)=3

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Backpropagation: Neural networks update weights using gradient descent. The gradient of the loss with respect to early weights is computed by chaining the partial derivatives backwards layer-by-layer: ∂L∂w(1)=∂L∂a(L)∂a(L)∂a(L−1)…∂a(2)∂w(1)\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w^{(1)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{(L)}} \frac{\partial a^{(L)}}{\partial a^{(L-1)}} \dots \frac{\partial a^{(2)}}{\partial w^{(1)}}∂w(1)∂L​=∂a(L)∂L​∂a(L−1)∂a(L)​…∂w(1)∂a(2)​.
  2. Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT): In Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), the model is unrolled over time steps. The chain rule calculates how an error at step TTT propagates through recurrent state transitions to affect weights at step t=1t=1t=1.
  3. Residual Networks (ResNets): ResNets add shortcut links to layers: y=x+f(x)y = x + f(x)y=x+f(x). Chaining derivatives through this link yields ∂y∂x=1+f′(x)\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = 1 + f'(x)∂x∂y​=1+f′(x). The addition of the "111" term prevents gradients from vanishing during backpropagation.
  4. Reinforcement Learning (Policy Gradients): In policy gradient optimization, the reward depends on actions, which depend on network policy outputs. The chain rule calculates the gradient of the expected reward with respect to policy parameters.
  5. Differentiable Rendering: In 3D computer vision, the pixel loss is propagated backward through the rendering equations using the chain rule to optimize 3D shape and texture parameters directly from 2D photos.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating the flow of derivatives in a computational graph:

  • Show an input variable xxx pointing to an intermediate node u=g(x)u = g(x)u=g(x) with an arrow labeled dudx\frac{du}{dx}dxdu​ (local derivative).
  • Show the intermediate node uuu pointing to the output node y=f(u)y = f(u)y=f(u) with an arrow labeled dydu\frac{dy}{du}dudy​.
  • Draw a path under these nodes showing the forward pass (values flowing left to right) and a second path showing the backward pass (gradients flowing right to left).
  • Illustrate how the total derivative dydx\frac{dy}{dx}dxdy​ is computed by multiplying the labels along the path: dydu⋅dudx\frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}dudy​⋅dxdu​, visualizing the chain rule as a sequential multiplier of sensitivities.

Chapter 32: Critical Points

Prerequisite

  • Gradient Vector: Understanding that ∇f(x)=0\nabla f(x) = \mathbf{0}∇f(x)=0 represents a flat local slope.
  • Hessian Matrix: Knowing how second-order derivatives define local curvature.

1. Conceptual Hook

When training a machine learning model, our goal is to find the parameter settings that produce the lowest possible error on our task. We do this by adjusting weights to slide down the loss landscape. But how do we know when we have reached the bottom? How do we identify the potential endpoints of our optimization process? We look for critical points.

A critical point is any coordinate in the parameter space where the gradient of the function is exactly zero: ∇f(x)=0\nabla f(x) = \mathbf{0}∇f(x)=0. At these locations, the local surface is temporarily flat, meaning that small steps in any direction yield no immediate change in the output. These points represent the mathematical junctions of optimization: they are the candidates for local minima (the valleys we want), local maxima (the peaks we avoid), and saddle points (deceptive flat zones). Identifying and classifying these points is essential to understanding whether our models have successfully converged.

2. Formal Definition

Let f:U→Rf: U \to \mathbb{R}f:U→R be a scalar-valued function defined on an open set U⊆RnU \subseteq \mathbb{R}^nU⊆Rn. A point x∗∈Ux^* \in Ux∗∈U is defined as a critical point (or stationary point) of fff if:

  1. The gradient of fff at x∗x^*x∗ is the zero vector: ∇f(x∗)=0\nabla f(x^*) = \mathbf{0}∇f(x∗)=0 which implies that all first-order partial derivatives vanish simultaneously: ∂f∂xi(x∗)=0∀i=1,2,…,n\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(x^*) = 0 \quad \forall i = 1, 2, \dots, n∂xi​∂f​(x∗)=0∀i=1,2,…,n
  2. Or if the function fff is not differentiable at x∗x^*x∗.

Classification via the Hessian

If fff is twice-differentiable at a critical point x∗x^*x∗ where ∇f(x∗)=0\nabla f(x^*) = \mathbf{0}∇f(x∗)=0, we can classify the point using the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix Hf(x∗)H_f(x^*)Hf​(x∗):

  • Local Minimum: Hf(x∗)≻0H_f(x^*) \succ 0Hf​(x∗)≻0 (positive definite, all eigenvalues λi>0\lambda_i > 0λi​>0).
  • Local Maximum: Hf(x∗)≺0H_f(x^*) \prec 0Hf​(x∗)≺0 (negative definite, all eigenvalues λi<0\lambda_i < 0λi​<0).
  • Saddle Point: Hf(x∗)H_f(x^*)Hf​(x∗) is indefinite (has both positive and negative eigenvalues).

3. Illustrative Derivation

Derivation of the Lagrange Multiplier Method

In machine learning, we often optimize objectives under constraints (for example, keeping weight vectors unit norm, or bounding margins in SVMs). We derive how critical points are identified in constrained systems using the Method of Lagrange Multipliers.

Suppose we want to find the critical points of a function f(x)f(x)f(x) subject to an equality constraint g(x)=cg(x) = cg(x)=c, where f,g:Rn→Rf, g: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}f,g:Rn→R are differentiable.

Proof:

  1. Geometric Tangency Condition: At a constrained optimum x∗x^*x∗, the contour curve of f(x)f(x)f(x) must be tangent to the constraint curve g(x)=cg(x) = cg(x)=c. If they were not tangent, they would cross, meaning we could move along the constraint curve to increase or decrease f(x)f(x)f(x).

  2. Collinearity of Gradients: Since the contours are tangent at x∗x^*x∗, their normal vectors must point in the same (or exact opposite) direction. The gradient vector is always orthogonal to its contour lines. Therefore, the gradient of the objective ∇f(x∗)\nabla f(x^*)∇f(x∗) and the gradient of the constraint ∇g(x∗)\nabla g(x^*)∇g(x∗) must be collinear: ∇f(x∗)=λ∇g(x∗)\nabla f(x^*) = \lambda \nabla g(x^*)∇f(x∗)=λ∇g(x∗) where λ∈R\lambda \in \mathbb{R}λ∈R is the scaling factor, known as the Lagrange multiplier.

  3. The Lagrangian Function: We can unify this collinearity condition and the constraint equation into a single unconstrained function called the Lagrangian, L:Rn×R→R\mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}L:Rn×R→R: L(x,λ)=f(x)−λ(g(x)−c)\mathcal{L}(x, \lambda) = f(x) - \lambda(g(x) - c)L(x,λ)=f(x)−λ(g(x)−c)

  4. Finding Critical Points of L\mathcal{L}L: We find the critical points of this unconstrained function by setting its gradient with respect to both xxx and λ\lambdaλ to zero:

    • Gradient w.r.t xxx: ∇xL(x,λ)=∇f(x)−λ∇g(x)=0  ⟹  ∇f(x)=λ∇g(x)\nabla_x \mathcal{L}(x, \lambda) = \nabla f(x) - \lambda \nabla g(x) = \mathbf{0} \implies \nabla f(x) = \lambda \nabla g(x)∇x​L(x,λ)=∇f(x)−λ∇g(x)=0⟹∇f(x)=λ∇g(x)
    • Partial derivative w.r.t λ\lambdaλ: ∂L∂λ=−(g(x)−c)=0  ⟹  g(x)=c\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \lambda} = -(g(x) - c) = 0 \implies g(x) = c∂λ∂L​=−(g(x)−c)=0⟹g(x)=c Solving this system of equations yields the critical points of the constrained system. ■\blacksquare■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Unconstrained Local Minimum

Find and classify the critical points of the function f(x,y)=x2+2y2−4x−8y+6f(x, y) = x^2 + 2y^2 - 4x - 8y + 6f(x,y)=x2+2y2−4x−8y+6.

  1. Find the Gradient: ∇f(x,y)=[2x−44y−8]\nabla f(x, y) = \begin{bmatrix} 2x - 4 \\ 4y - 8 \end{bmatrix}∇f(x,y)=[2x−44y−8​]
  2. Set the Gradient to zero: 2x−4=0  ⟹  x=22x - 4 = 0 \implies x = 22x−4=0⟹x=2 4y−8=0  ⟹  y=24y - 8 = 0 \implies y = 24y−8=0⟹y=2 The only critical point is x∗=(2,2)x^* = (2, 2)x∗=(2,2).
  3. Compute the Hessian: Hf(x,y)=(∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2)=(2004)H_f(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y} \\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \partial x} & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}Hf​(x,y)=(∂x2∂2f​∂y∂x∂2f​​∂x∂y∂2f​∂y2∂2f​​)=(20​04​)
  4. Evaluate at x∗x^*x∗: Hf(2,2)=(2004)H_f(2, 2) = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}Hf​(2,2)=(20​04​). The eigenvalues are λ1=2\lambda_1 = 2λ1​=2 and λ2=4\lambda_2 = 4λ2​=4. Since both eigenvalues are strictly positive, the Hessian is positive definite, confirming (2,2)(2, 2)(2,2) is a strict local minimum.

Example 2: Constrained Minimization

Minimize the objective function f(x,y)=x2+y2f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2f(x,y)=x2+y2 subject to the equality constraint x+y=2x + y = 2x+y=2.

  1. Formulate the Lagrangian: L(x,y,λ)=x2+y2−λ(x+y−2)\mathcal{L}(x, y, \lambda) = x^2 + y^2 - \lambda(x + y - 2)L(x,y,λ)=x2+y2−λ(x+y−2)
  2. Find the partial derivatives and set to zero: ∂L∂x=2x−λ=0  ⟹  x=λ2\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = 2x - \lambda = 0 \implies x = \frac{\lambda}{2}∂x∂L​=2x−λ=0⟹x=2λ​ ∂L∂y=2y−λ=0  ⟹  y=λ2\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y} = 2y - \lambda = 0 \implies y = \frac{\lambda}{2}∂y∂L​=2y−λ=0⟹y=2λ​ ∂L∂λ=−(x+y−2)=0  ⟹  x+y=2\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \lambda} = -(x + y - 2) = 0 \implies x + y = 2∂λ∂L​=−(x+y−2)=0⟹x+y=2
  3. Solve the system: Substitute xxx and yyy expressions into the constraint: λ2+λ2=2  ⟹  λ=2\frac{\lambda}{2} + \frac{\lambda}{2} = 2 \implies \lambda = 22λ​+2λ​=2⟹λ=2   ⟹  x=1,y=1\implies x = 1, \quad y = 1⟹x=1,y=1 The constrained critical point is at (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1) with a minimum value of f(1,1)=2f(1, 1) = 2f(1,1)=2.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. SGD Convergence Limits: First-order optimizers (like SGD) iteratively update network parameters to find coordinates where the gradient of the loss function vanishes: ∇L(θ)≈0\nabla L(\theta) \approx \mathbf{0}∇L(θ)≈0, indicating convergence at a critical point.
  2. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Solution: In linear regression, we solve for parameters by setting the gradient of the sum of squared residuals to zero: ∇w∥y−Xw∥22=0\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\|_2^2 = \mathbf{0}∇w​∥y−Xw∥22​=0. This leads to the normal equations: XTXw=XTy\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}XTXw=XTy.
  3. Saddle Point Bottlenecks: In deep learning, the vast majority of high-dimensional critical points are saddle points rather than local minima. Optimizers like Adam introduce momentum to "roll through" these flat regions where standard gradient descent stalls.
  4. Support Vector Machines (SVMs): Setting up the optimal separating hyperplane under margin constraints requires solving a dual Lagrangian objective. The support vectors correspond to the critical points of this constrained quadratic program.
  5. Principal Component Analysis (PCA): Finding principal components involves maximizing variance subject to weight vector orthnormal constraints. The eigenvectors of the covariance matrix are the critical points of this constrained Lagrangian formulation.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating the three types of critical points:

  • Show three side-by-side 3D plots:
    1. Local Minimum: A smooth bowl shape. Draw a flat tangent plane touching the very bottom. Label the gradient as ∇f=0\nabla f = \mathbf{0}∇f=0 and indicate the curvature is positive upwards in all directions (H≻0H \succ 0H≻0).
    2. Local Maximum: A smooth dome shape. Draw a flat tangent plane touching the peak. Label the gradient as ∇f=0\nabla f = \mathbf{0}∇f=0 and indicate the curvature is negative downwards in all directions (H≺0H \prec 0H≺0).
    3. Saddle Point: A classic horse-saddle shape. Draw a flat tangent plane touching the center. Label the gradient as ∇f=0\nabla f = \mathbf{0}∇f=0. Draw a green line curving upwards along one axis (positive eigenvalue) and a red line curving downwards along the other axis (negative eigenvalue).
  • Use this visualization to emphasize that a zero gradient alone is not enough to identify a minimum; we must check the second-order curvature.

Chapter 33: Derivatives

Prerequisite

  • Functions: Understanding y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x) as a mapping from inputs to outputs.
  • Limits: Concept of analyzing a function's behavior as inputs approach a point.

1. Conceptual Hook

In machine learning, training a model is like navigating a thick fog down a mountain. You cannot see the bottom (the optimal parameters that minimize error), but you can feel the slope of the ground beneath your feet. To make progress, you take a step in the direction that slopes downward. The mathematical tool that measures this local slope is the derivative.

A derivative is the measurement of sensitivity. It tells us exactly how much a function's output changes in response to a tiny, microscopic change in its input. If the function is our model's loss (error) and the input is a neural network weight, the derivative tells us whether to increase or decrease that weight to reduce the error. The derivative is the fundamental compass of optimization, driving every update step in gradient descent.

2. Formal Definition

For a real-valued function f:R→Rf: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}f:R→R, the derivative at a point xxx in the interior of its domain is defined as the limit of the difference quotient, provided the limit exists: f′(x)=dfdx=lim⁡h→0f(x+h)−f(x)hf'(x) = \frac{df}{dx} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}f′(x)=dxdf​=limh→0​hf(x+h)−f(x)​

If this limit exists at xxx, we say the function fff is differentiable at xxx. For fff to be differentiable on an open interval (a,b)(a, b)(a,b), the limit must exist for all points in the interval.

Differentiability vs. Continuity

If a function is differentiable at xxx, it is guaranteed to be continuous at xxx. However, the converse is not true. A function can be continuous but non-differentiable at a point. A classic example is the absolute value function f(x)=∣x∣f(x) = |x|f(x)=∣x∣, which is continuous everywhere but has a sharp "corner" at x=0x = 0x=0, where the left-hand limit (−lim⁡h→0−hh=−1-\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{-h}{h} = -1−limh→0​h−h​=−1) and right-hand limit (111) of the difference quotient do not match.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Derivation of the Sigmoid Activation Derivative

In neural networks, we require the derivatives of activation functions to backpropagate errors. We derive the derivative of the Sigmoid function, σ(x)=11+e−x\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}σ(x)=1+e−x1​, demonstrating how it can be expressed elegantly in terms of itself.

Proof: Using the quotient rule (uv)′=u′v−uv′v2\left( \frac{u}{v} \right)' = \frac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}(vu​)′=v2u′v−uv′​ (or the chain rule on u(x)−1u(x)^{-1}u(x)−1): Let u(x)=1u(x) = 1u(x)=1 and v(x)=1+e−xv(x) = 1 + e^{-x}v(x)=1+e−x. σ′(x)=ddx((1+e−x)−1)\sigma'(x) = \frac{d}{dx} \left( (1 + e^{-x})^{-1} \right)σ′(x)=dxd​((1+e−x)−1) Applying the chain rule: σ′(x)=−1⋅(1+e−x)−2⋅ddx(1+e−x)\sigma'(x) = -1 \cdot (1 + e^{-x})^{-2} \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(1 + e^{-x})σ′(x)=−1⋅(1+e−x)−2⋅dxd​(1+e−x) Since ddx(1+e−x)=−e−x\frac{d}{dx}(1 + e^{-x}) = -e^{-x}dxd​(1+e−x)=−e−x: σ′(x)=−(1+e−x)−2⋅(−e−x)\sigma'(x) = -(1 + e^{-x})^{-2} \cdot (-e^{-x})σ′(x)=−(1+e−x)−2⋅(−e−x) σ′(x)=e−x(1+e−x)2\sigma'(x) = \frac{e^{-x}}{(1 + e^{-x})^2}σ′(x)=(1+e−x)2e−x​

Now, let us manipulate this fraction to express it in terms of σ(x)\sigma(x)σ(x): σ′(x)=11+e−x⋅e−x1+e−x\sigma'(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}} \cdot \frac{e^{-x}}{1 + e^{-x}}σ′(x)=1+e−x1​⋅1+e−xe−x​ Notice that e−x1+e−x=(1+e−x)−11+e−x=1−11+e−x\frac{e^{-x}}{1 + e^{-x}} = \frac{(1 + e^{-x}) - 1}{1 + e^{-x}} = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}1+e−xe−x​=1+e−x(1+e−x)−1​=1−1+e−x1​. Substitute σ(x)=11+e−x\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}σ(x)=1+e−x1​ back into the expression: σ′(x)=σ(x)⋅(1−σ(x))■\sigma'(x) = \sigma(x) \cdot (1 - \sigma(x)) \quad \blacksquareσ′(x)=σ(x)⋅(1−σ(x))■ This simple form makes the Sigmoid function highly computationally efficient in neural network backpropagation, as we do not need to compute expensive exponential functions twice.

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Limit Definition Walkthrough

Find the derivative of f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2 using the formal limit definition.

  1. Set up the limit: f′(x)=lim⁡h→0(x+h)2−x2hf'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(x+h)^2 - x^2}{h}f′(x)=limh→0​h(x+h)2−x2​
  2. Expand the numerator: f′(x)=lim⁡h→0x2+2xh+h2−x2hf'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - x^2}{h}f′(x)=limh→0​hx2+2xh+h2−x2​ f′(x)=lim⁡h→02xh+h2hf'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{2xh + h^2}{h}f′(x)=limh→0​h2xh+h2​
  3. Factor out and divide by hhh: f′(x)=lim⁡h→0(2x+h)f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} (2x + h)f′(x)=limh→0​(2x+h)
  4. Evaluate the limit as h→0h \to 0h→0: f′(x)=2xf'(x) = 2xf′(x)=2x

Example 2: The ReLU Activation Function

The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is defined as f(x)=max⁡(0,x)f(x) = \max(0, x)f(x)=max(0,x).

  1. Differentiate for x>0x > 0x>0: For positive inputs, f(x)=x  ⟹  f′(x)=1f(x) = x \implies f'(x) = 1f(x)=x⟹f′(x)=1.
  2. Differentiate for x<0x < 0x<0: For negative inputs, f(x)=0  ⟹  f′(x)=0f(x) = 0 \implies f'(x) = 0f(x)=0⟹f′(x)=0.
  3. Analyze at x=0x = 0x=0: The function has a sharp corner at the origin. The left-side slope is 000 and the right-side slope is 111. The derivative is undefined at x=0x=0x=0. In practice, deep learning libraries assign an arbitrary value (often 000 or 0.50.50.5) or use a subgradient, where the subdifferential interval at x=0x=0x=0 is [0,1][0, 1][0,1]. f′(x)={1if x>00if x<0[0,1]if x=0f'(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } x < 0 \\ [0, 1] & \text{if } x = 0 \end{cases}f′(x)=⎩⎨⎧​10[0,1]​if x>0if x<0if x=0​

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Gradient Descent Optimization: Model parameters θ\thetaθ are updated iteratively using the negative of the derivative of the cost function: θnew=θold−ηf′(θold)\theta_{new} = \theta_{old} - \eta f'(\theta_{old})θnew​=θold​−ηf′(θold​), where η\etaη is the learning rate.
  2. Backpropagation: Neural networks calculate the sensitivity of the final loss to weights in early layers by multiplying local derivatives layer-by-layer using the chain rule.
  3. Vanishing Gradients: If an activation function's derivative is always small (for example, the Sigmoid derivative peaks at 0.250.250.25), multiplying these derivatives over many layers causes the gradient to vanish, halting learning in deep architectures.
  4. Regularization Derivatives: L2 regularization adds a penalty λ2w2\frac{\lambda}{2} w^22λ​w2 to the loss. Its derivative with respect to weight is λw\lambda wλw, which is subtracted during update steps, performing weight decay.
  5. Adversarial Attacks (FGSM): Adversarial attacks (like Fast Gradient Sign Method) find malicious perturbations by taking the derivative of the loss function with respect to the input pixels, shifting the image in the direction that maximizes error.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating the limit definition of the derivative:

  • Show a curve representing a function y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x).
  • Plot a point (x,f(x))(x, f(x))(x,f(x)) and a neighboring point (x+h,f(x+h))(x+h, f(x+h))(x+h,f(x+h)) on the curve.
  • Draw a secant line passing through both points. Label the slope of this line as the difference quotient: f(x+h)−f(x)h\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}hf(x+h)−f(x)​.
  • Draw a series of arrows showing the interval hhh shrinking towards 000. Show how the secant line rotates as the second point slides down the curve.
  • Show the final tangent line touching the curve at exactly (x,f(x))(x, f(x))(x,f(x)), and label its slope as the derivative f′(x)f'(x)f′(x), visualizing the transition from average rate of change to instantaneous slope.

Chapter 34: Gradient

Prerequisite

  • Partial Derivatives: Understanding rates of change along individual coordinate axes.
  • Vector Norms: Knowing how to compute the L2L_2L2​ length of a vector.

1. Conceptual Hook

In machine learning, training a model is a journey across an unknown, high-dimensional loss landscape. We start at a random point (random weights) with high error. To find the bottom of the error valley, we cannot search the entire space. We must make decisions locally based on the slope of the hill we are standing on. The mathematical compass that points us in the direction of the steepest slope is the gradient.

The gradient is a vector that gathers all first-order partial derivatives of a scalar function. While a single partial derivative tells us the slope in only one axis-aligned direction, the gradient combines them to point in the direction of steepest ascent—the path that increases the function's output the fastest. By taking a step in the exact opposite direction (the negative gradient), we perform gradient descent, sliding down the error hill toward a minimum. It is the fundamental signal that drives learning in neural networks.

2. Formal Definition

Let f:U→Rf: U \to \mathbb{R}f:U→R be a differentiable scalar-valued function defined on an open set U⊆RnU \subseteq \mathbb{R}^nU⊆Rn. The gradient of fff at a point x∈Ux \in Ux∈U, denoted ∇f(x)\nabla f(x)∇f(x) or grad f(x)\text{grad } f(x)grad f(x), is the column vector of its partial derivatives: ∇f(x)=[∂f∂x1(x)∂f∂x2(x)⋮∂f∂xn(x)]\nabla f(x) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(x) \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}(x) \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}(x) \end{bmatrix}∇f(x)=​∂x1​∂f​(x)∂x2​∂f​(x)⋮∂xn​∂f​(x)​​

The Directional Derivative

The rate of change of fff in the direction of a unit vector v∈Rnv \in \mathbb{R}^nv∈Rn (∥v∥2=1\|v\|_2 = 1∥v∥2​=1) is the directional derivative, denoted Dvf(x)D_v f(x)Dv​f(x): Dvf(x)=lim⁡h→0f(x+hv)−f(x)hD_v f(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + hv) - f(x)}{h}Dv​f(x)=limh→0​hf(x+hv)−f(x)​ If fff is differentiable, the directional derivative can be computed directly as the inner product of the gradient and the direction vector: Dvf(x)=∇f(x)TvD_v f(x) = \nabla f(x)^T vDv​f(x)=∇f(x)Tv

3. Illustrative Derivation

Proof that the Gradient Points in the Direction of Steepest Ascent

We prove that the directional derivative is maximized when the direction vector vvv points in the same direction as the gradient vector ∇f(x)\nabla f(x)∇f(x), establishing that the gradient points along the path of steepest ascent.

Proof: Let v∈Rnv \in \mathbb{R}^nv∈Rn be a unit vector (∥v∥2=1\|v\|_2 = 1∥v∥2​=1). The directional derivative of fff in the direction of vvv is: Dvf(x)=∇f(x)TvD_v f(x) = \nabla f(x)^T vDv​f(x)=∇f(x)Tv Using the geometric definition of the inner product: ∇f(x)Tv=∥∇f(x)∥2∥v∥2cos⁡(θ)\nabla f(x)^T v = \|\nabla f(x)\|_2 \|v\|_2 \cos(\theta)∇f(x)Tv=∥∇f(x)∥2​∥v∥2​cos(θ) where θ\thetaθ is the angle of separation between the vectors ∇f(x)\nabla f(x)∇f(x) and vvv.

Since vvv is a unit vector (∣v∥2=1|v\|_2 = 1∣v∥2​=1): Dvf(x)=∥∇f(x)∥2cos⁡(θ)D_v f(x) = \|\nabla f(x)\|_2 \cos(\theta)Dv​f(x)=∥∇f(x)∥2​cos(θ)

To find the direction vvv that maximizes the rate of change Dvf(x)D_v f(x)Dv​f(x), we must maximize this expression. Since the norm ∥∇f(x)∥2\|\nabla f(x)\|_2∥∇f(x)∥2​ is fixed at the point xxx, the maximum value depends entirely on cos⁡(θ)\cos(\theta)cos(θ):

  • The maximum value of cos⁡(θ)\cos(\theta)cos(θ) is 111, which occurs when θ=0\theta = 0θ=0.
  • An angle of θ=0\theta = 0θ=0 implies that vvv is collinear and points in the exact same direction as ∇f(x)\nabla f(x)∇f(x): v=∇f(x)∥∇f(x)∥2(assuming ∇f(x)≠0)v = \frac{\nabla f(x)}{\|\nabla f(x)\|_2} \quad (\text{assuming } \nabla f(x) \neq \mathbf{0})v=∥∇f(x)∥2​∇f(x)​(assuming ∇f(x)=0)
  • The maximum rate of change (steepest ascent rate) is the magnitude of the gradient: max⁡vDvf(x)=∥∇f(x)∥2\max_v D_v f(x) = \|\nabla f(x)\|_2maxv​Dv​f(x)=∥∇f(x)∥2​

Conversely, to minimize the rate of change (steepest descent), we choose θ=π  ⟹  cos⁡(θ)=−1\theta = \pi \implies \cos(\theta) = -1θ=π⟹cos(θ)=−1: v=−∇f(x)∥∇f(x)∥2v = -\frac{\nabla f(x)}{\|\nabla f(x)\|_2}v=−∥∇f(x)∥2​∇f(x)​ which yields the minimum rate of change: −∥∇f(x)∥2-\|\nabla f(x)\|_2−∥∇f(x)∥2​. This mathematically justifies the gradient descent update direction. ■\blacksquare■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Basic Gradient Evaluation

Evaluate the gradient of the function f(x,y)=100−2x2−y2f(x, y) = 100 - 2x^2 - y^2f(x,y)=100−2x2−y2 at the point (3,10)(3, 10)(3,10).

  1. Compute the partial derivatives: ∂f∂x=−4x\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = -4x∂x∂f​=−4x ∂f∂y=−2y\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = -2y∂y∂f​=−2y
  2. Construct the gradient vector: ∇f(x,y)=[−4x−2y]\nabla f(x, y) = \begin{bmatrix} -4x \\ -2y \end{bmatrix}∇f(x,y)=[−4x−2y​]
  3. Evaluate at (3,10)(3, 10)(3,10): ∇f(3,10)=[−4(3)−2(10)]=[−12−20]\nabla f(3, 10) = \begin{bmatrix} -4(3) \\ -2(10) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -12 \\ -20 \end{bmatrix}∇f(3,10)=[−4(3)−2(10)​]=[−12−20​] To increase the function value the fastest at (3,10)(3, 10)(3,10), one should move in the direction [−12,−20]T[-12, -20]^T[−12,−20]T. To decrease it fastest, move along [12,20]T[12, 20]^T[12,20]T.

Example 2: Directional Derivative Calculation

Find the rate of change of f(x,y)=2x2y+3y2f(x, y) = 2x^2 y + 3y^2f(x,y)=2x2y+3y2 at the point (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) in the direction of the vector u=[34]u = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}u=[34​].

  1. Normalize the direction vector to unit length: ∥u∥2=32+42=5  ⟹  v=u∥u∥2=[0.60.8]\|u\|_2 = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5 \implies v = \frac{u}{\|u\|_2} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 \\ 0.8 \end{bmatrix}∥u∥2​=32+42​=5⟹v=∥u∥2​u​=[0.60.8​]
  2. Calculate the gradient vector: ∇f(x,y)=[∂(2x2y+3y2)∂x∂(2x2y+3y2)∂y]=[4xy2x2+6y]\nabla f(x, y) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial(2x^2y + 3y^2)}{\partial x} \\ \frac{\partial(2x^2y + 3y^2)}{\partial y} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4xy \\ 2x^2 + 6y \end{bmatrix}∇f(x,y)=[∂x∂(2x2y+3y2)​∂y∂(2x2y+3y2)​​]=[4xy2x2+6y​]
  3. Evaluate the gradient at (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2): ∇f(1,2)=[4(1)(2)2(1)2+6(2)]=[814]\nabla f(1, 2) = \begin{bmatrix} 4(1)(2) \\ 2(1)^2 + 6(2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 14 \end{bmatrix}∇f(1,2)=[4(1)(2)2(1)2+6(2)​]=[814​]
  4. Compute the directional derivative: Dvf(1,2)=∇f(1,2)Tv=[8,14][0.60.8]=(8)(0.6)+(14)(0.8)=4.8+11.2=16D_v f(1, 2) = \nabla f(1, 2)^T v = \begin{bmatrix} 8, & 14 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 \\ 0.8 \end{bmatrix} = (8)(0.6) + (14)(0.8) = 4.8 + 11.2 = 16Dv​f(1,2)=∇f(1,2)Tv=[8,​14​][0.60.8​]=(8)(0.6)+(14)(0.8)=4.8+11.2=16 The function value increases at a rate of 16 units per step in the direction of uuu.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD): Neural network parameter weights θ\thetaθ are updated by taking a step in the direction of the negative gradient of the loss function over a mini-batch of data: θ←θ−η∇θL\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}θ←θ−η∇θ​L.
  2. Backpropagation Output: The backward pass of a neural network calculates the gradient vector of the loss with respect to all trainable parameters (∇WL\nabla_W \mathcal{L}∇W​L, ∇bL\nabla_b \mathcal{L}∇b​L) to update the network layers.
  3. Saliency Maps for Interpretability: By computing the gradient of a classification score with respect to input pixels (∇xyclass\nabla_x y_{class}∇x​yclass​), we can visualize which parts of an image the model is most sensitive to when making a prediction.
  4. Wasserstein GAN Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP): To enforce the 1-Lipschitz constraint required for stable GAN training, a regularization penalty is added to restrict the norm of the critic's gradient with respect to interpolated inputs to 1: R=(∥∇x^D(x^)∥2−1)2\mathcal{R} = (\|\nabla_{\hat{x}} D(\hat{x})\|_2 - 1)^2R=(∥∇x^​D(x^)∥2​−1)2.
  5. Gradient Boosting (GBMs): In algorithms like XGBoost, successive decision trees are trained to predict the negative gradients of the loss function, acting as a functional gradient descent in the space of weak learners.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating the geometry of gradients:

  • Show a 3D mountain peak representing a function z=f(x,y)z = f(x, y)z=f(x,y) with concentric contour circles projected on the flat 2D plane below. Label the contours as "Level Sets" (lines of constant loss).
  • Plot a point on the hill.
  • Draw an arrow pointing straight up the hill along the path of steepest climb.
  • Draw the projection of this arrow on the 2D plane, representing the gradient vector ∇f\nabla f∇f.
  • Highlight that this gradient vector ∇f\nabla f∇f is strictly perpendicular (orthogonal) to the contour line passing through the point, visually demonstrating that moving along a contour line results in a rate of change of 0, while moving perpendicular to it (along the gradient) yields the maximum rate of change.

title: Hessian Matrix
description: Second-order partial derivatives, multivariable curvature, Taylor expansions, and the second derivative test.

Chapter 35: Hessian Matrix

Prerequisite

  • Partial Derivatives: Knowing how to compute first-order and second-order derivative variations.
  • Taylor Series: Familiarity with approximating functions using polynomial expansions.

1. Conceptual Hook

In machine learning optimization, the gradient tells us which direction is "downhill" so we can update our weights. However, the gradient does not tell us how the slope is changing. Is the valley widening out into a flat, stable plain, or is it narrowing into a steep, treacherous crevice? To capture this rate of change of the slope, we need a mathematical tool that measures local curvature: the Hessian matrix.

The Hessian matrix aggregates all second-order partial derivatives of a scalar-valued function. If the gradient represents the velocity of our optimization journey, the Hessian represents its acceleration. It measures the curvature of the loss landscape in every direction. By analyzing the eigenvalues of the Hessian, we can diagnose whether a critical point is a local minimum, a local maximum, or a saddle point. It is the core mathematical engine for advanced curvature-aware optimizers, Bayesian neural networks, and network pruning algorithms.

2. Formal Definition

Let f:U→Rf: U \to \mathbb{R}f:U→R be a twice-differentiable scalar-valued function defined on an open set U⊆RnU \subseteq \mathbb{R}^nU⊆Rn. The Hessian matrix of fff at a point a∈Ua \in Ua∈U, denoted Hf(a)H_f(a)Hf​(a) or ∇2f(a)\nabla^2 f(a)∇2f(a), is the square n×nn \times nn×n matrix of second-order partial derivatives: Hf(a)=(∂2f∂x12(a)∂2f∂x1∂x2(a)…∂2f∂x1∂xn(a)∂2f∂x2∂x1(a)∂2f∂x22(a)…∂2f∂x2∂xn(a)⋮⋮⋱⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1(a)∂2f∂xn∂x2(a)…∂2f∂xn2(a))H_f(a) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1^2}(a) & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1 \partial x_2}(a) & \dots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1 \partial x_n}(a) \\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_2 \partial x_1}(a) & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_2^2}(a) & \dots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_2 \partial x_n}(a) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n \partial x_1}(a) & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n \partial x_2}(a) & \dots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n^2}(a) \end{pmatrix}Hf​(a)=​∂x12​∂2f​(a)∂x2​∂x1​∂2f​(a)⋮∂xn​∂x1​∂2f​(a)​∂x1​∂x2​∂2f​(a)∂x22​∂2f​(a)⋮∂xn​∂x2​∂2f​(a)​……⋱…​∂x1​∂xn​∂2f​(a)∂x2​∂xn​∂2f​(a)⋮∂xn2​∂2f​(a)​​ where (Hf(a))ij=∂2f∂xi∂xj(a)(H_f(a))_{ij} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(a)(Hf​(a))ij​=∂xi​∂xj​∂2f​(a).

Symmetry and Clairaut's Theorem

If the second-order partial derivatives are continuous on UUU, then by Clairaut's Theorem, the mixed partial derivatives are symmetric: ∂2f∂xi∂xj=∂2f∂xj∂xi  ⟹  Hf(a)=Hf(a)T\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_j \partial x_i} \implies H_f(a) = H_f(a)^T∂xi​∂xj​∂2f​=∂xj​∂xi​∂2f​⟹Hf​(a)=Hf​(a)T The Hessian is therefore a real symmetric matrix, meaning its eigenvalues are always real and it can be orthogonally diagonalized.

Second-Order Taylor Approximation

The Hessian matrix represents the second-order term of the multivariable Taylor expansion of fff around a point aaa: f(a+h)≈f(a)+∇f(a)Th+12hTHf(a)hf(a + h) \approx f(a) + \nabla f(a)^T h + \frac{1}{2} h^T H_f(a) hf(a+h)≈f(a)+∇f(a)Th+21​hTHf​(a)h where ∇f(a)∈Rn\nabla f(a) \in \mathbb{R}^n∇f(a)∈Rn is the gradient vector.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Derivation of the Multivariable Second Derivative Test

We derive how the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix determine the classification of critical points.

Let a∈Ua \in Ua∈U be a critical point of the function fff, meaning the gradient vector vanishes: ∇f(a)=0\nabla f(a) = \mathbf{0}∇f(a)=0 Using the second-order Taylor expansion for a small perturbation vector h∈Rnh \in \mathbb{R}^nh∈Rn: f(a+h)−f(a)≈12hTHf(a)hf(a + h) - f(a) \approx \frac{1}{2} h^T H_f(a) hf(a+h)−f(a)≈21​hTHf​(a)h The difference f(a+h)−f(a)f(a+h) - f(a)f(a+h)−f(a) determines whether f(a)f(a)f(a) is a local minimum, local maximum, or saddle point. This difference is governed by the sign of the quadratic form hTHf(a)hh^T H_f(a) hhTHf​(a)h.

  1. Case 1: Positive Definite Hessian (Hf(a)≻0H_f(a) \succ 0Hf​(a)≻0): If the Hessian is positive definite, all of its eigenvalues are strictly positive: λi>0\lambda_i > 0λi​>0 for all iii. By definition of positive definiteness: hTHf(a)h>0∀h≠0h^T H_f(a) h > 0 \quad \forall h \neq \mathbf{0}hTHf​(a)h>0∀h=0 Substituting this into the Taylor approximation: f(a+h)−f(a)>0  ⟹  f(a+h)>f(a)f(a + h) - f(a) > 0 \implies f(a + h) > f(a)f(a+h)−f(a)>0⟹f(a+h)>f(a) Since any small step away from aaa increases the function value, aaa is a strict local minimum.

  2. Case 2: Negative Definite Hessian (Hf(a)≺0H_f(a) \prec 0Hf​(a)≺0): If the Hessian is negative definite, all of its eigenvalues are strictly negative: λi<0\lambda_i < 0λi​<0 for all iii. By definition: hTHf(a)h<0∀h≠0h^T H_f(a) h < 0 \quad \forall h \neq \mathbf{0}hTHf​(a)h<0∀h=0 Substituting this into the Taylor approximation: f(a+h)−f(a)<0  ⟹  f(a+h)<f(a)f(a + h) - f(a) < 0 \implies f(a + h) < f(a)f(a+h)−f(a)<0⟹f(a+h)<f(a) Since any small step away from aaa decreases the function value, aaa is a strict local maximum.

  3. Case 3: Indefinite Hessian: If the Hessian has both positive and negative eigenvalues, there exist some directions u∈Rnu \in \mathbb{R}^nu∈Rn where uTHf(a)u>0u^T H_f(a) u > 0uTHf​(a)u>0 and other directions v∈Rnv \in \mathbb{R}^nv∈Rn where vTHf(a)v<0v^T H_f(a) v < 0vTHf​(a)v<0. Thus, taking a step along uuu increases the function value, while taking a step along vvv decreases it. The point aaa is a saddle point. ■\blacksquare■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Local Minimum Classification

Let f(x,y)=x2+y2f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2f(x,y)=x2+y2. Classify the critical point at the origin (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0).

  1. Compute the Gradient: ∇f(x,y)=[2x2y]=[00]  ⟹  (x,y)=(0,0) is indeed a critical point.\nabla f(x, y) = \begin{bmatrix} 2x \\ 2y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \implies (x, y) = (0, 0) \text{ is indeed a critical point.}∇f(x,y)=[2x2y​]=[00​]⟹(x,y)=(0,0) is indeed a critical point.
  2. Compute the second-order partial derivatives: ∂2f∂x2=2,∂2f∂y2=2,∂2f∂x∂y=0\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} = 2, \quad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} = 2, \quad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y} = 0∂x2∂2f​=2,∂y2∂2f​=2,∂x∂y∂2f​=0
  3. Construct the Hessian: Hf(0,0)=(2002)H_f(0, 0) = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}Hf​(0,0)=(20​02​)
  4. Evaluate Eigenvalues: Since the matrix is diagonal, the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries: λ1=2,λ2=2\lambda_1 = 2, \lambda_2 = 2λ1​=2,λ2​=2. Since both eigenvalues are strictly positive (λi>0\lambda_i > 0λi​>0), the Hessian is positive definite, confirming the origin is a strict local minimum.

Example 2: Saddle Point Classification

Let f(x,y)=x2−y2f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2f(x,y)=x2−y2. Classify the critical point at the origin (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0).

  1. Compute the Gradient: ∇f(x,y)=[2x−2y]=[00]  ⟹  (0,0) is a critical point.\nabla f(x, y) = \begin{bmatrix} 2x \\ -2y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \implies (0, 0) \text{ is a critical point.}∇f(x,y)=[2x−2y​]=[00​]⟹(0,0) is a critical point.
  2. Compute the second-order partial derivatives: ∂2f∂x2=2,∂2f∂y2=−2,∂2f∂x∂y=0\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} = 2, \quad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} = -2, \quad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y} = 0∂x2∂2f​=2,∂y2∂2f​=−2,∂x∂y∂2f​=0
  3. Construct the Hessian: Hf(0,0)=(200−2)H_f(0, 0) = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}Hf​(0,0)=(20​0−2​)
  4. Evaluate Eigenvalues: The eigenvalues are λ1=2\lambda_1 = 2λ1​=2 and λ2=−2\lambda_2 = -2λ2​=−2. Since the eigenvalues have mixed signs, the Hessian is indefinite, confirming the origin is a saddle point.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Newton's Method in Optimization: Standard gradient descent updates weights using only first-order gradients. Newton's method incorporates curvature by multiplying the gradient by the inverse Hessian matrix: θt+1=θt−H−1∇L(θt)\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - H^{-1} \nabla L(\theta_t)θt+1​=θt​−H−1∇L(θt​), allowing quadratic convergence.
  2. Bayesian Neural Networks (Laplace Approximation): To model parameter uncertainty, the posterior weight distribution is approximated by a Gaussian centered at the MAP estimate, where the covariance matrix is the inverse Hessian of the log-posterior: Σ=H−1\Sigma = H^{-1}Σ=H−1.
  3. Weight Pruning (Optimal Brain Damage): To compress neural networks, we identify non-essential weights. The saliency of a weight wiw_iwi​ is approximated using the diagonal elements of the Hessian matrix: si=12Hiiwi2s_i = \frac{1}{2} H_{ii} w_i^2si​=21​Hii​wi2​. Weights with low saliency are pruned.
  4. Loss Landscape Generalization: The eigenvalues of the Hessian at a local minimum indicate the flatness of the basin. Minima with small eigenvalues ("flat minima") generalize better to test data than minima with large eigenvalues ("sharp minima"), which are prone to overfitting.
  5. Hessian-Free Optimization: For deep models, storing and inverting the O(d2)O(d^2)O(d2) Hessian is impossible. Hessian-free optimizers bypass this by using finite differences or automatic differentiation to compute only Hessian-vector products (HvHvHv), which require only O(d)O(d)O(d) memory.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating the relationship between Hessian eigenvalues and surface geometry:

  • Case 1: Positive Definite (H≻0H \succ 0H≻0): Draw a 3D parabolic bowl opening upwards. Label the eigenvalues as λ1,λ2>0\lambda_1, \lambda_2 > 0λ1​,λ2​>0 and the origin as a local minimum.
  • Case 2: Negative Definite (H≺0H \prec 0H≺0): Draw a 3D parabolic dome opening downwards. Label the eigenvalues as λ1,λ2<0\lambda_1, \lambda_2 < 0λ1​,λ2​<0 and the origin as a local maximum.
  • Case 3: Indefinite (HHH mixed signs): Draw a 3D saddle shape. Draw a green arrow curving upwards along the xxx-axis (λ1>0\lambda_1 > 0λ1​>0) and a red arrow curving downwards along the yyy-axis (λ2<0\lambda_2 < 0λ2​<0). Label the center as a saddle point.
  • Annotate the curvature of each graph to visually show how the Hessian defines the local shape of the optimization landscape.

description: Mastering the mathematical foundations of artificial intelligence.
content:
Chapter 29: The Language of Change: Introduction to Calculus

Roadmap Objective

  • To understand the mechanics of "Continuous Change" and evolution.
  • To outline the tools for finding the "Best Path" through a landscape.
  • To bridge the gap between "A Moving Car" and "Learning Weights."

1. Introduction to the Subject: The Language of Change

Calculus is the study of Dynamic Flux. While Linear Algebra described the rigid lines of the world, Calculus describes the "Flow" between them. It is the language of the infinitesimal shift—the tiny adjustment that leads to a monumental outcome.

Think about Mall Parking Logic. You enter the massive garage, and you aren't just a static point; you are part of a continuous movement. You are navigating spiral ramps, climbing between levels, and spinning your steering wheel. As you move, your altitude and orientation are constantly shifting. If the ramp is too steep, you accelerate; if the turn is too sharp, you brake. You are constantly "Adjusting" your state based on the "Slope" of the world around you. This is the heart of Calculus—measuring how things change right now so we can control where they end up later. In Machine Learning, we don't just want to know where our model is; we want to know exactly which way to "Turn the Wheel" to reach the exit gate—the point of lowest error.

2. What Topics We Will Learn: The Tools of the Flow

In the coming chapters, we will equip you with the "Microscope" required to see these tiny shifts. We will learn how to break a complex journey down into a series of predictable steps:

  • The Instantaneous Shift (Derivatives): we will start by learning how to measure the "Slope" of any point. We will move from looking at the whole ramp to looking at the single inch under your tires.
  • The Steepest Path (Gradients): We will expand our view to multi-dimensional landscapes. We will learn how to find the single direction that leads to the fastest descent (or the steepest climb).
  • The Ripple Effect (The Chain Rule): We will learn how a change in one part of a system (the engine) ripples through to the end result (the speed). This is the "Engine" of all Deep Learning.
  • The Matrix of Change (Jacobians and Hessians): We will look at how whole grids of variables change simultaneously. We will learn how to measure "Curvature" to see if the road ahead is a smooth valley or a sharp cliff.
  • The Accumulation (Integral Calculus): We will learn how to sum up all the tiny turns of the wheel to calculate the total distance traveled. We will learn how to "Recover" the state of the system from its rate of change.

3. How it is Useful for Machine Learning: The Engine of Learning

Calculus is the "Intelligence" in Artificial Intelligence. It is the mechanism that allows a model to actually "Learn" from its mistakes.

  • Optimization (Gradient Descent): Every time a model makes a guess, Calculus tells it: "You were off by X. To be better, shift your internal rules by Y units in THIS direction." Without Calculus, the model would just be guessing randomly forever.
  • Backpropagation: This is the most famous application of Calculus in the world. It uses the "Chain Rule" to trace an error from the final prediction all the way back through hundreds of layers of a neural network to find the specific "Weight" that caused the mistake.
  • Learning Rate Management: Calculus helps us decide how fast to move down the error ramp. Too fast, and we jump out of the garage; too slow, and we never find a spot. Calculus provides the "Speedometer" for the learning process.
  • Activation Function Design: We use Calculus to design the "Gates" of a neural network (like ReLU or Sigmoid). We ensure that these gates have the right "Slope" so that the learning signal can flow through the model without fading away.
  • Loss Surface Analysis: Calculus allows us to visualize the "Terrain" of our problem. It tells us if the "Valley" we found is a deep, stable one, or just a shallow "Puddle" that we should ignore.

The Core Philosophy: Calculus is the Mathematics of the Microscope. It allows us to zoom in on a complex, curvy world until it looks like a simple straight line. By mastering that "tiny straight line," we give the machine the power to navigate any landscape of data with surgical precision.

Chapter 36: Integral Calculus

Prerequisite

  • Differential Calculus: Knowing how to compute derivatives as local slopes.
  • Summation Notation: Familiarity with the ∑\sum∑ operator.

1. Conceptual Hook

In differential calculus, we isolate variables and evaluate local slopes to optimize parameters. However, in machine learning, we also need to aggregate continuous information globally. For example, how do we calculate the probability of a continuous variable falling within a range, find the expected reward of an agent in reinforcement learning, or calculate the Area Under the Curve (AUC) for model evaluation? To sum up these continuous variations, we use integral calculus.

Integral calculus is the mathematics of accumulation. It allows us to reconstruct total quantities from continuous rates of change. If a derivative tells us the instantaneous velocity of a process at a specific millisecond, the integral sums up those velocities over time to find the net distance traveled. It is the core mathematical framework behind continuous probability distributions, expectation formulas, and information entropy.

2. Formal Definition

The Riemann Integral

Let f:[a,b]→Rf: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}f:[a,b]→R be a bounded function. Let P={x0,x1,…,xn}P = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\}P={x0​,x1​,…,xn​} be a partition of the interval [a,b][a, b][a,b] such that: a=x0<x1<⋯<xn=ba = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = ba=x0​<x1​<⋯<xn​=b The width of the iii-th sub-interval is Δxi=xi−xi−1\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}Δxi​=xi​−xi−1​. Let xi∗∈[xi−1,xi]x_i^* \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]xi∗​∈[xi−1​,xi​] be an arbitrary sample point.

The Riemann integral of fff over [a,b][a, b][a,b] is defined as the limit of the Riemann sum as the mesh size of the partition ∥P∥=max⁡iΔxi\|P\| = \max_i \Delta x_i∥P∥=maxi​Δxi​ approaches zero: ∫abf(x) dx=lim⁡∥P∥→0∑i=1nf(xi∗)Δxi\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx = \lim_{\|P\| \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i^*) \Delta x_i∫ab​f(x)dx=lim∥P∥→0​∑i=1n​f(xi∗​)Δxi​ provided the limit exists and is independent of the choice of partition and sample points.

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

Let fff be continuous on [a,b][a, b][a,b].

  1. If F(x)=∫axf(t)dtF(x) = \int_a^x f(t) dtF(x)=∫ax​f(t)dt, then F′(x)=f(x)F'(x) = f(x)F′(x)=f(x) for all x∈(a,b)x \in (a, b)x∈(a,b).
  2. If FFF is any antiderivative of fff on [a,b][a, b][a,b] (meaning F′(x)=f(x)F'(x) = f(x)F′(x)=f(x)), then: ∫abf(x) dx=F(b)−F(a)\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx = F(b) - F(a)∫ab​f(x)dx=F(b)−F(a)

3. Illustrative Derivation

Derivation of the Integration by Parts Formula

In probability theory, we often integrate products of functions (for example, when deriving the expectation of a normal distribution ∫x⋅p(x)dx\int x \cdot p(x) dx∫x⋅p(x)dx). We derive the Integration by Parts formula directly from the product rule of differentiation.

Proof: Let u(x)u(x)u(x) and v(x)v(x)v(x) be differentiable functions. The product rule for differentiation states: ddx[u(x)v(x)]=u′(x)v(x)+u(x)v′(x)\frac{d}{dx} \left[ u(x)v(x) \right] = u'(x)v(x) + u(x)v'(x)dxd​[u(x)v(x)]=u′(x)v(x)+u(x)v′(x) Using alternative notation u′=dudxu' = \frac{du}{dx}u′=dxdu​ and v′=dvdxv' = \frac{dv}{dx}v′=dxdv​: ddx[u(x)v(x)]=v(x)dudx+u(x)dvdx\frac{d}{dx} \left[ u(x)v(x) \right] = v(x)\frac{du}{dx} + u(x)\frac{dv}{dx}dxd​[u(x)v(x)]=v(x)dxdu​+u(x)dxdv​

We integrate both sides of the equation with respect to xxx over the interval [a,b][a, b][a,b]: ∫abddx[u(x)v(x)]dx=∫abv(x)dudxdx+∫abu(x)dvdxdx\int_{a}^{b} \frac{d}{dx} \left[ u(x)v(x) \right] dx = \int_{a}^{b} v(x)\frac{du}{dx} dx + \int_{a}^{b} u(x)\frac{dv}{dx} dx∫ab​dxd​[u(x)v(x)]dx=∫ab​v(x)dxdu​dx+∫ab​u(x)dxdv​dx By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, the integral of the derivative on the left-hand side simplifies to the net change in the product function: ∫abddx[u(x)v(x)]dx=[u(x)v(x)]ab\int_{a}^{b} \frac{d}{dx} \left[ u(x)v(x) \right] dx = \left[ u(x)v(x) \right]_a^b∫ab​dxd​[u(x)v(x)]dx=[u(x)v(x)]ab​ Substitute this back: [u(x)v(x)]ab=∫abv(x)du+∫abu(x)dv\left[ u(x)v(x) \right]_a^b = \int_{a}^{b} v(x) du + \int_{a}^{b} u(x) dv[u(x)v(x)]ab​=∫ab​v(x)du+∫ab​u(x)dv Rearranging the terms to isolate the integral of u(x)dvu(x) dvu(x)dv: ∫abu(x)dv=[u(x)v(x)]ab−∫abv(x)du■\int_{a}^{b} u(x) dv = \left[ u(x)v(x) \right]_a^b - \int_{a}^{b} v(x) du \quad \blacksquare∫ab​u(x)dv=[u(x)v(x)]ab​−∫ab​v(x)du■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Definite Area Integration

Evaluate the definite integral of f(t)=3t2+2tf(t) = 3t^2 + 2tf(t)=3t2+2t over the interval [1,3][1, 3][1,3].

  1. Find the antiderivative F(t)F(t)F(t): F(t)=∫(3t2+2t)dt=t3+t2+CF(t) = \int (3t^2 + 2t) dt = t^3 + t^2 + CF(t)=∫(3t2+2t)dt=t3+t2+C
  2. Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: ∫13(3t2+2t)dt=[t3+t2]13\int_{1}^{3} (3t^2 + 2t) dt = \left[ t^3 + t^2 \right]_1^3∫13​(3t2+2t)dt=[t3+t2]13​
  3. Evaluate at the limits: F(3)=33+32=27+9=36F(3) = 3^3 + 3^2 = 27 + 9 = 36F(3)=33+32=27+9=36 F(1)=13+12=1+1=2F(1) = 1^3 + 1^2 = 1 + 1 = 2F(1)=13+12=1+1=2 ∫13(3t2+2t)dt=F(3)−F(1)=36−2=34\int_{1}^{3} (3t^2 + 2t) dt = F(3) - F(1) = 36 - 2 = 34∫13​(3t2+2t)dt=F(3)−F(1)=36−2=34

Example 2: Normalizing continuous probability distributions

A continuous random variable has a probability density function defined by p(x)=ce−xp(x) = c e^{-x}p(x)=ce−x for x≥0x \ge 0x≥0. Find the normalizing constant ccc such that p(x)p(x)p(x) is a valid PDF.

  1. Set up the normalization constraint: The total area under any probability density function must equal 1: ∫0∞ce−xdx=1\int_{0}^{\infty} c e^{-x} dx = 1∫0∞​ce−xdx=1
  2. Evaluate the improper integral: clim⁡b→∞∫0be−xdx=1c \lim_{b \to \infty} \int_{0}^{b} e^{-x} dx = 1climb→∞​∫0b​e−xdx=1 Find the antiderivative of e−xe^{-x}e−x, which is −e−x-e^{-x}−e−x: clim⁡b→∞[−e−x]0b=1c \lim_{b \to \infty} \left[ -e^{-x} \right]_0^b = 1climb→∞​[−e−x]0b​=1 clim⁡b→∞(−e−b−(−e0))=1c \lim_{b \to \infty} \left( -e^{-b} - (-e^0) \right) = 1climb→∞​(−e−b−(−e0))=1 Since lim⁡b→∞e−b=0\lim_{b \to \infty} e^{-b} = 0limb→∞​e−b=0: c(0+1)=1  ⟹  c=1c (0 + 1) = 1 \implies c = 1c(0+1)=1⟹c=1 The normalized PDF is p(x)=e−xp(x) = e^{-x}p(x)=e−x.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Continuous Probability Calculations: In Bayesian modeling, the probability of a continuous feature XXX falling within a range [a,b][a, b][a,b] is calculated by evaluating the definite integral of its density function: P(a≤X≤b)=∫abp(x)dxP(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b p(x) dxP(a≤X≤b)=∫ab​p(x)dx.
  2. Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC): The AUC-ROC score is a scalar metric used to evaluate binary classification models. It is computed by integrating the True Positive Rate (TPR) function with respect to the False Positive Rate (FPR): AUC=∫01TPR(FPR)d(FPR)AUC = \int_0^1 TPR(FPR) d(FPR)AUC=∫01​TPR(FPR)d(FPR).
  3. Expected Returns in Reinforcement Learning: The expected return of a policy trajectory τ\tauτ is calculated by integrating the product of the trajectory probability and its reward over all possible paths: Eτ∼π[R(τ)]=∫p(τ;π)R(τ)dτ\mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi}[R(\tau)] = \int p(\tau; \pi) R(\tau) d\tauEτ∼π​[R(τ)]=∫p(τ;π)R(τ)dτ.
  4. Differential Entropy: In information theory, the uncertainty of a continuous distribution is measured using differential entropy, which requires integrating the density function weighted by its log-density: H(X)=−∫−∞∞p(x)log⁡p(x)dxH(X) = -\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p(x) \log p(x) dxH(X)=−∫−∞∞​p(x)logp(x)dx.
  5. Monte Carlo Integration: Many integrals in Bayesian models (like the marginal likelihood denominator p(x)=∫p(x∣z)p(z)dzp(x) = \int p(x|z)p(z)dzp(x)=∫p(x∣z)p(z)dz) are analytically intractable. ML researchers approximate them using Monte Carlo integration, averaging random samples: ∫f(x)p(x)dx≈1N∑i=1Nf(xi)\int f(x)p(x)dx \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i)∫f(x)p(x)dx≈N1​∑i=1N​f(xi​).

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating the Riemann sum definition of integration:

  • Show a curved function graph y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x) over an interval [a,b][a, b][a,b].
  • Draw vertical lines partitioning the area under the curve into several narrow vertical rectangles of width Δx\Delta xΔx.
  • Highlight a single rectangle. Show its height is determined by the function value at a sample point f(xi∗)f(x_i^*)f(xi∗​), and its area is f(xi∗)Δxf(x_i^*) \Delta xf(xi∗​)Δx.
  • Show a second side-by-side graph where the partition is much finer (many more rectangles with a smaller width Δx\Delta xΔx). Illustrate how the jagged top edge of the rectangles matches the true curve much more closely.
  • Draw arrows demonstrating that as the partition width Δx\Delta xΔx shrinks to an infinitesimal differential dxdxdx, the sum of the rectangular areas converges to the exact area under the curve, visualizing the integral ∫abf(x)dx\int_a^b f(x) dx∫ab​f(x)dx.
