title: KL Divergence
description: Mastering the mathematical foundations of artificial intelligence.
content:
Chapter 80: KL Divergence

Prerequisite

  • Probability Distributions: Understanding that a discrete probability distribution PPP must satisfy ∑P(x)=1\sum P(x) = 1∑P(x)=1 and P(x)≥0P(x) \geq 0P(x)≥0.
  • Entropy: Familiarity with Shannon Entropy H(P)=−∑P(x)log⁡P(x)H(P) = -\sum P(x) \log P(x)H(P)=−∑P(x)logP(x) as a measure of average information or uncertainty.
  • Logarithmic Identities: Knowledge of log⁡(a/b)=log⁡a−log⁡b\log(a/b) = \log a - \log blog(a/b)=loga−logb and the properties of natural logarithms.

Analogy

Think of the IRCTC Counter Ticket system. You have a "True Intention"—exactly which train, class, and berth you want. This is the reality of your travel needs. Then, there is the Reservation Form you actually fill out at the counter.

KL Divergence is the measure of "Information Loss" or "Inefficiency" that happens when you use that physical form to represent your actual travel plans. If your form is perfectly filled out to match the available train logic, your "surprise" or "extra effort" at the counter is zero. But if your form (your model) assumes there are plenty of Side-Lower berths when the reality (the actual distribution) is that only Middle berths are left, you incur a penalty. KL Divergence quantifies how much "extra breath" you have to spend explaining yourself to the booking clerk because your form didn't perfectly match the reality of the railway database. It is not a distance—because explaining your travel plan to the clerk is not the same as the clerk explaining the database to you—it is a measure of divergence.

The Math Link

Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence, denoted as DKL(P∥Q)D_{KL}(P \parallel Q)DKL​(P∥Q), quantifies how much one probability distribution QQQ (the approximation) diverges from a second, reference probability distribution PPP (the ground truth).

For discrete probability distributions PPP and QQQ defined over the same probability space X\mathcal{X}X, the divergence is defined as:

DKL(P∥Q)=∑x∈XP(x)log⁡(P(x)Q(x))D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} P(x) \log \left( \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} \right)DKL​(P∥Q)=∑x∈X​P(x)log(Q(x)P(x)​)

Derivation and Components

We derive this by looking at the difference between Cross-Entropy and Entropy.

  1. Entropy of Truth (PPP): The minimum bits needed to encode the real situation. H(P)=−∑x∈XP(x)log⁡P(x)H(P) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} P(x) \log P(x)H(P)=−∑x∈X​P(x)logP(x)

  2. Cross-Entropy (P,QP, QP,Q): The bits needed if we use the "Form" (QQQ) to encode the "Truth" (PPP). H(P,Q)=−∑x∈XP(x)log⁡Q(x)H(P, Q) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} P(x) \log Q(x)H(P,Q)=−∑x∈X​P(x)logQ(x)

  3. The Divergence: The "extra" bits spent is the difference: DKL(P∥Q)=H(P,Q)−H(P)D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = H(P, Q) - H(P)DKL​(P∥Q)=H(P,Q)−H(P) DKL(P∥Q)=(−∑P(x)log⁡Q(x))−(−∑P(x)log⁡P(x))D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = \left( -\sum P(x) \log Q(x) \right) - \left( -\sum P(x) \log P(x) \right)DKL​(P∥Q)=(−∑P(x)logQ(x))−(−∑P(x)logP(x)) DKL(P∥Q)=∑P(x)(log⁡P(x)−log⁡Q(x))D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = \sum P(x) ( \log P(x) - \log Q(x) )DKL​(P∥Q)=∑P(x)(logP(x)−logQ(x)) DKL(P∥Q)=∑x∈XP(x)log⁡(P(x)Q(x))D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} P(x) \log \left( \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} \right)DKL​(P∥Q)=∑x∈X​P(x)log(Q(x)P(x)​)

Linking to the Analogy:

  • P(x)P(x)P(x): The True Intention (Actual probability of getting a seat).
  • Q(x)Q(x)Q(x): The Reservation Form (What you predicted/claimed on paper).
  • log⁡P(x)Q(x)\log \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}logQ(x)P(x)​: The Inaccuracy Penalty for each specific choice xxx on the form.

THE INTUITION KL Divergence is always non-negative (DKL≥0D_{KL} \geq 0DKL​≥0). It hits zero only if P=QP = QP=Q. Think of it as a "Surprise Index": how surprised will the booking clerk be when they compare your form to the actual ledger?

Let's Run the Numbers

Example 1: Filling the Form

You are filling a form for 3 types of coaches: Sleeper (SL), 3A, and 2A. The True Distribution (PPP) of available seats is [0.7,0.2,0.1][0.7, 0.2, 0.1][0.7,0.2,0.1]. Your Form (QQQ) assumes they are equally likely: [0.33,0.33,0.33][0.33, 0.33, 0.33][0.33,0.33,0.33].

Calculation: DKL(P∥Q)=0.7log⁡0.70.33+0.2log⁡0.20.33+0.1log⁡0.10.33D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = 0.7 \log \frac{0.7}{0.33} + 0.2 \log \frac{0.2}{0.33} + 0.1 \log \frac{0.1}{0.33}DKL​(P∥Q)=0.7log0.330.7​+0.2log0.330.2​+0.1log0.330.1​ DKL(P∥Q)=0.7(0.75)+0.2(−0.49)+0.1(−1.19)D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = 0.7(0.75) + 0.2(-0.49) + 0.1(-1.19)DKL​(P∥Q)=0.7(0.75)+0.2(−0.49)+0.1(−1.19) DKL(P∥Q)=0.525−0.098−0.119=0.308 natsD_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = 0.525 - 0.098 - 0.119 = 0.308 \text{ nats}DKL​(P∥Q)=0.525−0.098−0.119=0.308 nats

The Story: Because your form (QQQ) was too generic, you wasted 0.3080.3080.308 units of information efficiency. You over-prepared for 2A and 3A and under-prepared for the high-probability Sleeper class, leading to a mismatch at the counter.

Example 2: The 'Tatkal' Rush

In a Tatkal rush, timing is everything. The True Distribution (PPP) of tickets selling out within the first minute is [0.9 (Sold),0.1 (Available)][0.9 \text{ (Sold)}, 0.1 \text{ (Available)}][0.9 (Sold),0.1 (Available)]. Your Prediction (QQQ) is optimistic: [0.5 (Sold),0.5 (Available)][0.5 \text{ (Sold)}, 0.5 \text{ (Available)}][0.5 (Sold),0.5 (Available)].

Calculation: DKL(P∥Q)=0.9log⁡0.90.5+0.1log⁡0.10.5D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = 0.9 \log \frac{0.9}{0.5} + 0.1 \log \frac{0.1}{0.5}DKL​(P∥Q)=0.9log0.50.9​+0.1log0.50.1​ DKL(P∥Q)=0.9(0.587)+0.1(−1.609)D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = 0.9(0.587) + 0.1(-1.609)DKL​(P∥Q)=0.9(0.587)+0.1(−1.609) DKL(P∥Q)=0.528−0.161=0.367 natsD_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = 0.528 - 0.161 = 0.367 \text{ nats}DKL​(P∥Q)=0.528−0.161=0.367 nats

The Story: Your optimism (QQQ) diverged significantly from the brutal reality (PPP) of the Tatkal rush. The 0.3670.3670.367 value represents the "Information Shock" you face when the screen suddenly shows "Regret" despite your 50/50 prediction.

Example 3: The 'Waitlist' Uncertainty

A Waitlist (WL) ticket can either confirm (CNF) or stay WL. Reality (PPP): [0.1 (CNF),0.9 (WL)][0.1 \text{ (CNF)}, 0.9 \text{ (WL)}][0.1 (CNF),0.9 (WL)]. Your Guess (QQQ): [0.05 (CNF),0.95 (WL)][0.05 \text{ (CNF)}, 0.95 \text{ (WL)}][0.05 (CNF),0.95 (WL)].

Calculation: DKL(P∥Q)=0.1log⁡0.10.05+0.9log⁡0.90.95D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = 0.1 \log \frac{0.1}{0.05} + 0.9 \log \frac{0.9}{0.95}DKL​(P∥Q)=0.1log0.050.1​+0.9log0.950.9​ DKL(P∥Q)=0.1(0.693)+0.9(−0.054)D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = 0.1(0.693) + 0.9(-0.054)DKL​(P∥Q)=0.1(0.693)+0.9(−0.054) DKL(P∥Q)=0.0693−0.0486=0.0207 natsD_{KL}(P \parallel Q) = 0.0693 - 0.0486 = 0.0207 \text{ nats}DKL​(P∥Q)=0.0693−0.0486=0.0207 nats

The Story: In this case, your guess (QQQ) was very close to reality (PPP). The low KL Divergence of 0.02070.02070.0207 tells us that your "mental form" is almost perfectly aligned with the actual uncertainty of the railway waitlist. You won't be surprised.

Asymmetry is a Feature, Not a Bug: DKL(P∥Q)≠DKL(Q∥P)D_{KL}(P \parallel Q) \neq D_{KL}(Q \parallel P)DKL​(P∥Q)=DKL​(Q∥P). In ML, PPP is usually the fixed data distribution and QQQ is our trainable model. Swapping them changes the objective entirely: minimizing DKL(P∥Q)D_{KL}(P \parallel Q)DKL​(P∥Q) (forward KL) leads to mean-seeking behavior, while minimizing DKL(Q∥P)D_{KL}(Q \parallel P)DKL​(Q∥P) (reverse KL) leads to mode-seeking behavior, often seen in Variational Inference.

ML Applications

  1. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs): The loss function includes a KL term to force the learned latent distribution Q(z∣x)Q(z|x)Q(z∣x) to be close to a prior distribution P(z)P(z)P(z), typically a Standard Multivariate Gaussian N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0, I)N(0,I).
  2. t-SNE (t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding): This dimensionality reduction technique minimizes the KL Divergence between the joint probabilities of pairs of points in the high-dimensional space and their counterparts in the low-dimensional embedding.
  3. Knowledge Distillation: A "Student" model is trained to minimize the KL Divergence between its output probability distributions and the "soft targets" produced by a larger "Teacher" model.
  4. Reinforcement Learning (PPO): Proximal Policy Optimization uses a KL Divergence constraint to ensure that the updated policy πθ\pi_{\theta}πθ​ does not diverge too far from the old policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{old}}πθold​​, preventing catastrophic collapses in training stability.
  5. Language Modeling: When training with Cross-Entropy loss, we are implicitly minimizing the KL Divergence between the empirical distribution of the text corpus and the model's predicted token probabilities.

Debugging Tip: If you encounter NaN or Inf values while calculating KL Divergence, check your Q(x)Q(x)Q(x) values. If Q(x)=0Q(x) = 0Q(x)=0 for any xxx where P(x)>0P(x) > 0P(x)>0, the divergence goes to infinity. Always add a small epsilon ϵ≈1e−10\epsilon \approx 1e-10ϵ≈1e−10 to your denominator to ensure numerical stability.

title: Mutual Information
description: Mastering the mathematical foundations of artificial intelligence.
content:
Chapter 81: Mutual Information

Prerequisite

  • Entropy (HHH): A measure of the average uncertainty or "surprise" associated with a random variable.
  • Joint Probability Distribution: Understanding how two variables XXX and YYY behave simultaneously, denoted as P(X,Y)P(X, Y)P(X,Y).
  • Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence: A measure of how one probability distribution differs from a second, reference probability distribution.

Analogy

Think about the process of buying a new smartphone case. You are standing in the store with a primary goal: protecting your expensive device from a catastrophic shatter. You have two variables at play. Variable XXX is the "True Durability" of the phone—how it actually fares when it hits the pavement. Variable YYY is the "Case Design and Features"—the thickness of the silicone, the reinforced corners, and the brand's marketing claims.

Mutual Information is the measure of how much knowing the details of the Smartphone Case (YYY) actually reduces your uncertainty about the Phone's Survival (XXX).

If you pick a case at random without looking at it, your uncertainty about the phone's safety is at its maximum (High Entropy). However, if you see that the case has a 10-foot drop-test rating and military-grade carbon fiber, you suddenly know a lot more about your phone's likelihood of surviving a tumble. The "information" isn't just about the case; it’s about the relationship between the case and the phone. If the case and the phone's safety are completely independent—meaning a "protective" case is actually just a flimsy sticker—then the Mutual Information is zero. You’ve gained nothing. Mutual Information quantifies that "overlap" of knowledge where looking at the case tells you exactly what you need to know about the phone's fate.

The Math Link

Mathematically, Mutual Information I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y) quantifies the reduction in uncertainty of one random variable due to the knowledge of another. We define it as the KL Divergence between the joint distribution and the product of the marginal distributions.

For discrete random variables XXX and YYY defined over spaces X\mathcal{X}X and Y\mathcal{Y}Y:

I(X;Y)=∑x∈X∑y∈YP(x,y)log⁡(P(x,y)P(x)P(y))I(X; Y) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} P(x, y) \log \left( \frac{P(x, y)}{P(x)P(y)} \right)I(X;Y)=∑x∈X​∑y∈Y​P(x,y)log(P(x)P(y)P(x,y)​)

Derivation from Entropy

We can derive I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y) by looking at the difference between the total uncertainty of XXX and the remaining uncertainty of XXX given that YYY is known:

  1. Entropy of XXX: H(X)=−∑x∈XP(x)log⁡P(x)H(X) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} P(x) \log P(x)H(X)=−∑x∈X​P(x)logP(x)

  2. Conditional Entropy of XXX given YYY: H(X∣Y)=−∑x∈X,y∈YP(x,y)log⁡P(x∣y)H(X|Y) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}, y \in \mathcal{Y}} P(x, y) \log P(x|y)H(X∣Y)=−∑x∈X,y∈Y​P(x,y)logP(x∣y)

  3. The Relationship: I(X;Y)=H(X)−H(X∣Y)I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y)I(X;Y)=H(X)−H(X∣Y)

Linking the Symbols:

  • H(X)H(X)H(X): The total "danger" or uncertainty of your phone breaking before you even look at a case.
  • H(X∣Y)H(X|Y)H(X∣Y): The remaining "danger" after you have inspected the specs of the Smartphone Case.
  • I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y): The specific amount of "peace of mind" (information) provided by that case regarding the phone's safety.

THE INTUITION Think of Mutual Information as a "Reduction in Surprises." If I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y) is high, knowing YYY makes XXX predictable. If I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y) is low, YYY is just noise that tells you nothing about the outcome of XXX.

Let's Run the Numbers

Example 1: Finding the 'Drop-Proof' One

You are testing a new "Titan-Grip" case. Let XXX be the state of the phone (0: Broken, 1: Intact) and YYY be the Case Rating (0: Standard, 1: Rugged). Through testing, we find the following joint probabilities:

  • P(X=0,Y=0)=0.4P(X=0, Y=0) = 0.4P(X=0,Y=0)=0.4
  • P(X=1,Y=1)=0.5P(X=1, Y=1) = 0.5P(X=1,Y=1)=0.5
  • P(X=0,Y=1)=0.05P(X=0, Y=1) = 0.05P(X=0,Y=1)=0.05
  • P(X=1,Y=0)=0.05P(X=1, Y=0) = 0.05P(X=1,Y=0)=0.05

The Calculation:

  1. Marginal P(X):P(X=0)=0.45,P(X=1)=0.55P(X): P(X=0) = 0.45, P(X=1) = 0.55P(X):P(X=0)=0.45,P(X=1)=0.55
  2. Marginal P(Y):P(Y=0)=0.45,P(Y=1)=0.55P(Y): P(Y=0) = 0.45, P(Y=1) = 0.55P(Y):P(Y=0)=0.45,P(Y=1)=0.55
  3. I(X;Y)=0.4log⁡(0.40.45⋅0.45)+0.05log⁡(0.050.45⋅0.55)+0.05log⁡(0.050.55⋅0.45)+0.5log⁡(0.50.55⋅0.55)I(X; Y) = 0.4 \log(\frac{0.4}{0.45 \cdot 0.45}) + 0.05 \log(\frac{0.05}{0.45 \cdot 0.55}) + 0.05 \log(\frac{0.05}{0.55 \cdot 0.45}) + 0.5 \log(\frac{0.5}{0.55 \cdot 0.55})I(X;Y)=0.4log(0.45⋅0.450.4​)+0.05log(0.45⋅0.550.05​)+0.05log(0.55⋅0.450.05​)+0.5log(0.55⋅0.550.5​)
  4. I(X;Y)≈0.47 bitsI(X; Y) \approx 0.47 \text{ bits}I(X;Y)≈0.47 bits

The Story: Because the Mutual Information is high (relative to the max entropy of 1 bit), the "Rugged" label is a very strong predictor of whether your phone will survive. The case rating "shares" a lot of information with the physical reality of the drop.

Example 2: The Design vs. Utility

You find a "Designer" case that looks great but feels flimsy. Here, XXX is survival and YYY is "Beautiful Aesthetics." Suppose the joint distribution is P(x,y)=P(x)P(y)P(x, y) = P(x)P(y)P(x,y)=P(x)P(y) because the beauty of the case has zero physical impact on shock absorption.

  • P(X=1)=0.5,P(Y=1)=0.5P(X=1) = 0.5, P(Y=1) = 0.5P(X=1)=0.5,P(Y=1)=0.5
  • P(X=1,Y=1)=0.25P(X=1, Y=1) = 0.25P(X=1,Y=1)=0.25

The Calculation: I(X;Y)=∑P(x,y)log⁡(P(x)P(y)P(x)P(y))=∑P(x,y)log⁡(1)=0I(X; Y) = \sum P(x, y) \log \left( \frac{P(x)P(y)}{P(x)P(y)} \right) = \sum P(x, y) \log(1) = 0I(X;Y)=∑P(x,y)log(P(x)P(y)P(x)P(y)​)=∑P(x,y)log(1)=0

The Story: The math shows 000 bits of Mutual Information. This tells you that "Design" provides zero predictive power for "Utility." You might as well be guessing the phone's safety by flipping a coin; the case's appearance is irrelevant data.

Example 3: The Screen Guard

You add a tempered glass screen guard (YYY) to protect against screen-specific cracks (XXX). However, the guard is low quality and bubbles up.

  • P(X=Cracked)=0.2P(X=Cracked) = 0.2P(X=Cracked)=0.2
  • P(Y=Bubble)=0.8P(Y=Bubble) = 0.8P(Y=Bubble)=0.8
  • P(X=Cracked∣Y=Bubble)=0.19P(X=Cracked | Y=Bubble) = 0.19P(X=Cracked∣Y=Bubble)=0.19 (A very slight correlation)

The Calculation: H(X)=−(0.2log⁡0.2+0.8log⁡0.8)≈0.721H(X) = -(0.2 \log 0.2 + 0.8 \log 0.8) \approx 0.721H(X)=−(0.2log0.2+0.8log0.8)≈0.721 H(X∣Y)≈0.710H(X|Y) \approx 0.710H(X∣Y)≈0.710 I(X;Y)=0.721−0.710=0.011 bitsI(X; Y) = 0.721 - 0.710 = 0.011 \text{ bits}I(X;Y)=0.721−0.710=0.011 bits

The Story: The result is near zero. While the screen guard exists, it provides almost no "information" or protection against the crack. It’s an "uninformative feature"—the presence of the guard doesn't help you predict the screen's health.

Unlike Correlation, Mutual Information captures nonlinear relationships. While Pearson Correlation only cares about straight lines, MI is sensitive to any form of statistical dependence. However, MI is always non-negative (I(X;Y)≥0I(X; Y) \ge 0I(X;Y)≥0), meaning it can tell you how much variables relate, but not the direction (positive or negative) of that relationship.

ML Applications

  1. Feature Selection: In high-dimensional datasets, MI is used to rank features. We calculate the MI between each input feature and the target variable. Features with low MI are discarded as they provide negligible information for the model to learn the underlying mapping.
  2. Bayesian Network Learning: MI serves as a scoring function to determine the structure of a directed acyclic graph (DAG). It identifies which nodes (variables) should have edges between them based on their shared information content.
  3. Cross-Modal Learning: In models combining different data types (e.g., CLIP, which pairs images and text), MI is maximized between the image embedding and the text embedding to ensure the latent representations share the same semantic "meaning."
  4. Clustering Evaluation: Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) is a standard metric for comparing the results of a clustering algorithm against ground truth labels, especially when the number of clusters is unknown or labels are non-numeric.
  5. Decision Tree Construction: While Gini Impurity is common, Information Gain (which is essentially Mutual Information) is used in ID3 and C4.5 algorithms to determine the optimal split point by maximizing the reduction in entropy at each node.

Debugging Tip: If your Mutual Information values are coming out negative, check your log base and your probability sums. Mathematically, I(X;Y)I(X; Y)I(X;Y) can never be less than zero. If it is, you likely have a floating-point error or a leak in your joint probability table where ∑P(x,y)≠1\sum P(x,y) \neq 1∑P(x,y)=1.

title: Self-Information
description: Mastering the mathematical foundations of artificial intelligence.
content:
Chapter 82: Self-Information

Prerequisite

  • Probability Mass Functions (P(x)P(x)P(x)): Understanding how to assign probabilities to discrete outcomes within a sample space.
  • Logarithmic Identities: Comfort with the properties of logarithms, specifically log⁡(1/x)=−log⁡(x)\log(1/x) = -\log(x)log(1/x)=−log(x).
  • Expected Value: The foundational concept of what an outcome "costs" or "yields" on average.

Analogy

In the messy world of homeownership, a leaky roof is the ultimate test of your patience and your wallet. Self-information is the mathematical measure of your surprise—or the amount of "new news" you receive—when a specific event occurs regarding that leak.

Think of it this way: if you live in a rainforest and notice a drip, you aren't surprised. The "information content" of that drip is low because you already expected it; you’ve already come to terms with the dampness. However, if you live in a bone-dry desert and suddenly find a puddle in your hallway, that event carries massive self-information. It forces you to drop everything and re-evaluate your reality.

In this chapter, we quantify that feeling of "how much do I need to care about this?" The more unlikely the event, the more information it provides when it actually happens. We are measuring the degree to which an event disrupts your status quo.

The Math Link

To formalize this, we define Self-Information (also known as Surprisal) for a discrete random variable. Let X\mathcal{X}X be a discrete random variable with a probability mass function P(x)P(x)P(x) defined over a set of outcomes S\mathcal{S}S. For a specific outcome x∈Sx \in \mathcal{S}x∈S, the self-information I(x)I(x)I(x) is defined as:

I(x)=−log⁡b(P(x))I(x) = -\log_b(P(x))I(x)=−logb​(P(x))

Where:

  • P(x)P(x)P(x) is the probability of the event xxx occurring, such that 0≤P(x)≤10 \le P(x) \le 10≤P(x)≤1.
  • bbb is the base of the logarithm. In Information Theory, we typically use b=2b=2b=2 (measuring in bits) or b=eb=eb=e (measuring in nats).

The Derivation of Intuition: The measure I(x)I(x)I(x) must satisfy certain properties to align with our "leaky roof" logic:

  1. Monotonicity: If P(xi)>P(xj)P(x_i) > P(x_j)P(xi​)>P(xj​), then I(xi)<I(xj)I(x_i) < I(x_j)I(xi​)<I(xj​). A more likely leak should surprise you less.
  2. Additivity: For two independent leaks xxx and yyy, the information of both happening should be the sum of their individual informations: I(x,y)=−log⁡(P(x)⋅P(y))=−log⁡(P(x))+(−log⁡(P(y)))=I(x)+I(y)I(x, y) = -\log(P(x) \cdot P(y)) = -\log(P(x)) + (-\log(P(y))) = I(x) + I(y)I(x,y)=−log(P(x)⋅P(y))=−log(P(x))+(−log(P(y)))=I(x)+I(y)

In our analogy, if the probability of a leak P(x)P(x)P(x) is 1.01.01.0 (the roof is guaranteed to leak), the self-information is: I(x)=−log⁡(1.0)=0I(x) = -\log(1.0) = 0I(x)=−log(1.0)=0 You gained zero new information because you knew it was coming.

THE INTUITION Self-information isn't about the value of the data; it's about the unlikelihood. It represents the length of the "message" required to describe the event. Rare events (the massive structural failure) require a long, detailed explanation, whereas common events (the seasonal drip) can be summarized in a single, expected shrug.

Let's Run the Numbers

1. Finding the Source

You are inspecting the attic to find exactly where the water is coming through. There are 8 specific rafters where a leak could start. You assume each rafter is equally likely to be the culprit. You climb up and find the leak is at Rafter #4.

The Setup: Let xxx be the event that Rafter #4 is the source. Since there are 8 equally likely outcomes: P(x)=18P(x) = \frac{1}{8}P(x)=81​

The Calculation: I(x)=−log⁡2(18)I(x) = -\log_2\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)I(x)=−log2​(81​) I(x)=−(log⁡2(1)−log⁡2(8))I(x) = -(\log_2(1) - \log_2(8))I(x)=−(log2​(1)−log2​(8)) I(x)=−(0−3)=3 bitsI(x) = -(0 - 3) = 3 \text{ bits}I(x)=−(0−3)=3 bits

The Story: By finding the exact source among 8 equal possibilities, you have gained 3 bits of information. This is equivalent to having someone answer 3 "Yes/No" questions to narrow down the location (e.g., "Is it in the left half?", "Is it in the front section?", etc.). The math tells you exactly how much "searching effort" was resolved by that discovery.

2. The 'Bucket' Placement

You place a bucket under a known drip. Based on previous storms, there is a P(x)=0.8P(x) = 0.8P(x)=0.8 probability that the bucket will be full by morning. You wake up and find the bucket is indeed full.

The Setup: The event xxx (bucket is full) is highly probable.

The Calculation: I(x)=−log⁡2(0.8)I(x) = -\log_2(0.8)I(x)=−log2​(0.8) I(x)≈−(−0.322)I(x) \approx -(-0.322)I(x)≈−(−0.322) I(x)≈0.322 bitsI(x) \approx 0.322 \text{ bits}I(x)≈0.322 bits

The Story: Finding the bucket full tells you very little. You already expected this outcome, so the "news" of the full bucket carries low self-information. You don't need to change your plans or call a specialist; the high probability led to a low-impact realization.

3. The Plumber's Quote

A high-end specialist visits. He gives you a quote. Usually, quotes are high (P(high)=0.95P(\text{high}) = 0.95P(high)=0.95), but there is a slim P(cheap)=0.05P(\text{cheap}) = 0.05P(cheap)=0.05 chance he finds a simple fix and charges you the minimum. He hands you the bill, and it's the minimum charge.

The Setup: The event xxx (cheap fix) is a rare "black swan" event in the world of plumbing.

The Calculation: I(x)=−log⁡2(0.05)I(x) = -\log_2(0.05)I(x)=−log2​(0.05) I(x)≈−(−4.322)I(x) \approx -(-4.322)I(x)≈−(−4.322) I(x)≈4.322 bitsI(x) \approx 4.322 \text{ bits}I(x)≈4.322 bits

The Story: The self-information here is high. This "shock" to the system provides more information than the previous two scenarios combined. In ML terms, this is a high-signal event because it deviated so sharply from the expected distribution of your expenses.

Self-information only looks at a single outcome in isolation. Do not confuse it with Entropy, which is the average self-information across the entire probability distribution. If you only track the surprise of the "cheap quote" and ignore the "expensive quotes," you are looking at a single data point's contribution, not the system's overall uncertainty.

ML Applications

  1. Cross-Entropy Loss: In classification tasks, we minimize the negative log-likelihood of the ground truth class. This is essentially minimizing the self-information of the correct label under the predicted distribution.
  2. Anomaly Detection: By modeling the probability distribution of "normal" data, we can flag inputs with high self-information as potential outliers or security threats.
  3. Feature Selection: Features that provide high self-information relative to the target variable are often prioritized in decision tree splits (Information Gain).
  4. Natural Language Processing (NLP): In language modeling, "surprisal" is used to evaluate how unexpected a word is given its context, helping to refine word embeddings and next-token predictions.
  5. Active Learning: Algorithms can choose to label data points that have the highest self-information (the most "surprising" points), as these provide the most significant updates to the model's weights.

Debugging Tip: If your model's loss becomes NaN or Inf, check for P(x)=0P(x) = 0P(x)=0. The self-information of an impossible event is −log⁡(0)=∞-\log(0) = \infty−log(0)=∞. In implementation, always add a small epsilon (e.g., 1e−71e-71e−7) to your probabilities to prevent the "infinite surprise" that crashes your backpropagation.

title: Attention Mechanism Math
description: Scaled dot-product formulation, softmax gradient preservation proof, matrix shapes, and Transformer architectures.
content:
Chapter 10: Attention Mechanism Math

Prerequisite

  • Matrix Multiplication: Knowing how matrices represent compositions of linear maps.
  • Softmax Function: The math that turns scores into a probability distribution.

1. Conceptual Hook

In modern artificial intelligence, the Transformer architecture—which powers Large Language Models like GPT-4 and Gemini—rules supreme. The core engine driving this success is the attention mechanism.

Attention is a dynamic, differentiable selection engine. Instead of processing words in isolation or using fixed convolutional filters, attention allows words in a sentence to dynamically decide which neighboring words they should focus on to extract context. A word updates its meaning by taking a weighted average of neighbor representations, where the weights are calculated on the fly using vector dot products. It acts as a "soft" lookup table where queries are matched against keys to retrieve values, ensuring that the model can learn and route information flexibly.

2. Formal Definition

Let NNN be the number of query tokens and MMM be the number of key/value tokens. The input matrices are:

  • Queries (Q∈RN×dkQ \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d_k}Q∈RN×dk​): The representations searching for context.
  • Keys (K∈RM×dkK \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times d_k}K∈RM×dk​): The representations matching queries.
  • Values (V∈RM×dvV \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times d_v}V∈RM×dv​): The actual content to be aggregated.

The Scaled Dot-Product Attention is defined as: Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKTdk)V\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left( \frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) VAttention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QKT​)V

where the softmax function is applied row-wise to the attention score matrix: (softmax(QKTdk))ij=exp⁡(QiKjTdk)∑l=1Mexp⁡(QiKlTdk)\left( \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) \right)_{ij} = \frac{\exp\left( \frac{Q_i K_j^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)}{\sum_{l=1}^M \exp\left( \frac{Q_i K_l^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)}(softmax(dk​​QKT​))ij​=∑l=1M​exp(dk​​Qi​KlT​​)exp(dk​​Qi​KjT​​)​

The final output is a matrix of size RN×dv\mathbb{R}^{N \times d_v}RN×dv​ representing the context-weighted representations.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Derivation of the Variance Scaling Factor 1dk\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}dk​​1​

Why do we divide the queries and keys product by dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​? We prove that this factor preserves the variance of the inputs, preventing softmax gradient saturation.

Let q∈Rdkq \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}q∈Rdk​ and k∈Rdkk \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}k∈Rdk​ be a query and key vector. Assume that the components qiq_iqi​ and kjk_jkj​ are independent random variables with a mean of 0 and a variance of 1: E[qi]=E[kj]=0,Var(qi)=Var(kj)=1∀i,j\mathbb{E}[q_i] = \mathbb{E}[k_j] = 0, \quad \text{Var}(q_i) = \text{Var}(k_j) = 1 \quad \forall i, jE[qi​]=E[kj​]=0,Var(qi​)=Var(kj​)=1∀i,j Let the raw attention dot product be Z=qTk=∑i=1dkqikiZ = q^T k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_iZ=qTk=∑i=1dk​​qi​ki​.

  1. Calculate the Expected Value of ZZZ: E[Z]=E[∑i=1dkqiki]=∑i=1dkE[qiki]\mathbb{E}[Z] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i \right] = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} \mathbb{E}[q_i k_i]E[Z]=E[∑i=1dk​​qi​ki​]=∑i=1dk​​E[qi​ki​] Since qiq_iqi​ and kik_iki​ are independent: E[Z]=∑i=1dkE[qi]E[ki]=∑i=1dk(0)(0)=0\mathbb{E}[Z] = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} \mathbb{E}[q_i] \mathbb{E}[k_i] = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} (0)(0) = 0E[Z]=∑i=1dk​​E[qi​]E[ki​]=∑i=1dk​​(0)(0)=0

  2. Calculate the Variance of ZZZ: Since the terms qikiq_i k_iqi​ki​ are independent for different indices iii: Var(Z)=Var(∑i=1dkqiki)=∑i=1dkVar(qiki)\text{Var}(Z) = \text{Var}\left( \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i \right) = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} \text{Var}(q_i k_i)Var(Z)=Var(∑i=1dk​​qi​ki​)=∑i=1dk​​Var(qi​ki​) Recall that for independent variables XXX and YYY with E[X]=E[Y]=0\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[Y] = 0E[X]=E[Y]=0: Var(XY)=E[X2Y2]−(E[XY])2=E[X2]E[Y2]−(E[X]E[Y])2\text{Var}(XY) = \mathbb{E}[X^2 Y^2] - (\mathbb{E}[XY])^2 = \mathbb{E}[X^2]\mathbb{E}[Y^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y])^2Var(XY)=E[X2Y2]−(E[XY])2=E[X2]E[Y2]−(E[X]E[Y])2 Since Var(X)=E[X2]−(E[X])2  ⟹  E[X2]=1\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 \implies \mathbb{E}[X^2] = 1Var(X)=E[X2]−(E[X])2⟹E[X2]=1: Var(XY)=(1)(1)−(0)(0)=1\text{Var}(XY) = (1)(1) - (0)(0) = 1Var(XY)=(1)(1)−(0)(0)=1 Substituting this back into the variance summation: Var(Z)=∑i=1dk1=dk\text{Var}(Z) = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} 1 = d_kVar(Z)=∑i=1dk​​1=dk​

  3. Evaluate Softmax Impact: As the dimensionality dkd_kdk​ grows large, the variance of the dot product ZZZ grows linearly with dkd_kdk​. This means the dot products can take very large values in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions of flat plateaus where the gradients vanish: ∂softmax(x)i∂xj≈0for large ∣x∣\frac{\partial \text{softmax}(x)_i}{\partial x_j} \approx 0 \quad \text{for large } |x|∂xj​∂softmax(x)i​​≈0for large ∣x∣ This halts backpropagation training.

  4. Restore Variance to Unit Scale: We scale the dot product by the factor 1dk\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}dk​​1​: Var(Zdk)=1dkVar(Z)=dkdk=1■\text{Var}\left( \frac{Z}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) = \frac{1}{d_k} \text{Var}(Z) = \frac{d_k}{d_k} = 1 \quad \blacksquareVar(dk​​Z​)=dk​1​Var(Z)=dk​dk​​=1■ Dividing by dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ stabilizes the distribution of attention logits, ensuring gradients flow stably during backpropagation.

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Softmax Scaling Contrast

Suppose dk=100d_k = 100dk​=100 (so dk=10\sqrt{d_k} = 10dk​​=10). A query has raw dot products with two keys: Z=[50,20]Z = [50, 20]Z=[50,20].

  • Without Scaling: softmax([50,20])1=exp⁡(50)exp⁡(50)+exp⁡(20)≈1.0\text{softmax}([50, 20])_1 = \frac{\exp(50)}{\exp(50) + \exp(20)} \approx 1.0softmax([50,20])1​=exp(50)+exp(20)exp(50)​≈1.0 softmax([50,20])2=exp⁡(20)exp⁡(50)+exp⁡(20)≈0.0\text{softmax}([50, 20])_2 = \frac{\exp(20)}{\exp(50) + \exp(20)} \approx 0.0softmax([50,20])2​=exp(50)+exp(20)exp(20)​≈0.0 The model allocates 100% attention to the first token. The gradient for the second token is completely zeroed out.
  • With Scaling (Zdk=[5,2]\frac{Z}{\sqrt{d_k}} = [5, 2]dk​​Z​=[5,2]): softmax([5,2])1=exp⁡(5)exp⁡(5)+exp⁡(2)≈148.4148.4+7.4≈0.952\text{softmax}([5, 2])_1 = \frac{\exp(5)}{\exp(5) + \exp(2)} \approx \frac{148.4}{148.4 + 7.4} \approx 0.952softmax([5,2])1​=exp(5)+exp(2)exp(5)​≈148.4+7.4148.4​≈0.952 softmax([5,2])2=exp⁡(2)exp⁡(5)+exp⁡(2)≈7.4155.8≈0.048\text{softmax}([5, 2])_2 = \frac{\exp(2)}{\exp(5) + \exp(2)} \approx \frac{7.4}{155.8} \approx 0.048softmax([5,2])2​=exp(5)+exp(2)exp(2)​≈155.87.4​≈0.048 The smaller score maintains a non-zero probability (4.8%4.8\%4.8%), allowing gradients to flow back to both key representations.

Example 2: Simple Attention Forward Pass

Let dk=2,dv=2,N=2,M=2d_k = 2, d_v = 2, N=2, M=2dk​=2,dv​=2,N=2,M=2. Q=(1001),K=(1001),V=(10203040)Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad K = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad V = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 20 \\ 30 & 40 \end{pmatrix}Q=(10​01​),K=(10​01​),V=(1030​2040​)

  1. Compute QKTQK^TQKT: QKT=(1001)(1001)=(1001)QK^T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}QKT=(10​01​)(10​01​)=(10​01​)
  2. Scale by dk=2≈1.414\sqrt{d_k} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414dk​​=2​≈1.414: QKT2=(0.707000.707)\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{2}} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.707 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.707 \end{pmatrix}2​QKT​=(0.7070​00.707​)
  3. Apply Row-Wise Softmax:
    • Row 1: exp⁡(0.707)≈2.028\exp(0.707) \approx 2.028exp(0.707)≈2.028, exp⁡(0)=1\exp(0) = 1exp(0)=1. Sum =3.028= 3.028=3.028. Weights1=[2.0283.028,13.028]≈[0.67,0.33]\text{Weights}_{1} = \left[ \frac{2.028}{3.028}, \frac{1}{3.028} \right] \approx [0.67, 0.33]Weights1​=[3.0282.028​,3.0281​]≈[0.67,0.33]
    • Row 2: Similarly: Weights2=[0.33,0.67]\text{Weights}_{2} = [0.33, 0.67]Weights2​=[0.33,0.67] A=(0.670.330.330.67)A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.67 & 0.33 \\ 0.33 & 0.67 \end{pmatrix}A=(0.670.33​0.330.67​)
  4. Compute Output AVA VAV: Output=(0.670.330.330.67)(10203040)=(0.67(10)+0.33(30)0.67(20)+0.33(40)0.33(10)+0.67(30)0.33(20)+0.67(40))=(16.626.623.433.4)\text{Output} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.67 & 0.33 \\ 0.33 & 0.67 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 20 \\ 30 & 40 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.67(10) + 0.33(30) & 0.67(20) + 0.33(40) \\ 0.33(10) + 0.67(30) & 0.33(20) + 0.67(40) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 16.6 & 26.6 \\ 23.4 & 33.4 \end{pmatrix}Output=(0.670.33​0.330.67​)(1030​2040​)=(0.67(10)+0.33(30)0.33(10)+0.67(30)​0.67(20)+0.33(40)0.33(20)+0.67(40)​)=(16.623.4​26.633.4​)

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Multi-Head Attention (MHA): Instead of calculating attention once, transformers project queries, keys, and values hhh times into lower-dimensional subspaces, calculating attention in parallel. This allows the model to attend to multiple attributes simultaneously (e.g. grammar vs. coreference).
  2. Cross-Attention in Translation: In encoder-decoder translation networks, the decoder generates queries that attend to key-value pairs generated by the encoder, translating words in context.
  3. Vision Transformers (ViTs): In CV, images are divided into patches, flattened, and projected into embedding vectors. Self-attention dynamically connects remote patches of the image to analyze global structures.
  4. Graph Attention Networks (GATs): Nodes update their feature vectors by computing attention scores over neighboring nodes, weighting node aggregation based on topological importance.
  5. Multi-Modal Embeddings (CLIP): Text and image representations are aligned by calculating the dot product attention score between text token embeddings and image patch embeddings.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating the forward data flow of scaled dot-product attention:

  • Show Query (QQQ) and Key (KTK^TKT) matrices multiplying to generate a square N×NN \times NN×N matrix. Label this matrix "Raw Attention Scores."
  • Draw a step showing element-wise division of this matrix by the scalar dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​.
  • Draw a step showing a row-wise Softmax operation converting the scaled scores to "Attention Weights (summing to 1 per row)."
  • Show this weight matrix multiplying the Value (VVV) matrix to yield the final "Context-Weighted output."

title: Basis and Dimension
description: Linear independence, spanning sets, unique representations, and coordinate transformations.
content:
Chapter 11: Basis and Dimension

Prerequisite

  • Linear Independence: Knowing when a set of vectors contains no redundancies.
  • Vector Spaces & Span: Understanding closure and how linear combinations cover space.

1. Conceptual Hook

In machine learning, we often work with massive datasets containing thousands of features (e.g., pixel intensities in images or word occurrences in text). However, much of this raw data is highly redundant. To analyze and process this information efficiently, we must find the minimum set of independent features needed to represent our data without losing any information. This set is a basis, and the size of this set is the dimension of our representation space.

Think of a basis as the "leanest possible shopping list" of unique ingredients needed to cook every recipe in a cookbook. If you have two different brands of the exact same salt, your list is redundant. In ML, a basis represents the primary coordinate axes of our data space (such as principal components in PCA or latent factors in recommendation systems), while the dimension tells us the intrinsic complexity and capacity of our models.

2. Formal Definition

Let VVV be a vector space over a field F\mathbb{F}F. A set of vectors B={v1,v2,…,vn}⊂V\mathcal{B} = \{v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n\} \subset VB={v1​,v2​,…,vn​}⊂V is a basis of VVV if it satisfies two conditions:

  1. Linear Independence: The only linear combination of {vi}\{v_i\}{vi​} that equals the zero vector is the trivial one: ∑i=1ncivi=0  ⟹  c1=c2=⋯=cn=0\sum_{i=1}^n c_i v_i = 0 \implies c_1 = c_2 = \dots = c_n = 0∑i=1n​ci​vi​=0⟹c1​=c2​=⋯=cn​=0
  2. Spanning Property: Every vector in VVV can be written as a linear combination of vectors in B\mathcal{B}B: span(B)=V  ⟺  ∀x∈V,∃c1,…,cn∈Fs.t.x=∑i=1ncivi\text{span}(\mathcal{B}) = V \iff \forall x \in V, \exists c_1, \dots, c_n \in \mathbb{F} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad x = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i v_ispan(B)=V⟺∀x∈V,∃c1​,…,cn​∈Fs.t.x=∑i=1n​ci​vi​

The dimension of VVV, denoted dim⁡(V)\dim(V)dim(V), is the cardinality (number of elements) of its basis B\mathcal{B}B: dim⁡(V)=∣B∣=n\dim(V) = |\mathcal{B}| = ndim(V)=∣B∣=n

Uniqueness of Representation Theorem

Theorem: If B={v1,…,vn}\mathcal{B} = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}B={v1​,…,vn​} is a basis of VVV, then every vector x∈Vx \in Vx∈V can be expressed in the form x=∑i=1ncivix = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i v_ix=∑i=1n​ci​vi​ in exactly one way.

Proof: Suppose a vector xxx has two different representations under the basis B\mathcal{B}B: x=∑i=1naiviandx=∑i=1nbivix = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i \quad \text{and} \quad x = \sum_{i=1}^n b_i v_ix=∑i=1n​ai​vi​andx=∑i=1n​bi​vi​ Subtracting these two equations: x−x=∑i=1naivi−∑i=1nbivix - x = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i - \sum_{i=1}^n b_i v_ix−x=∑i=1n​ai​vi​−∑i=1n​bi​vi​ 0=∑i=1n(ai−bi)vi0 = \sum_{i=1}^n (a_i - b_i) v_i0=∑i=1n​(ai​−bi​)vi​ Since B\mathcal{B}B is a basis, its vectors are linearly independent. By definition of linear independence, the coefficients of this linear combination must all be zero: ai−bi=0∀i=1,…,n  ⟹  ai=bi∀i=1,…,na_i - b_i = 0 \quad \forall i=1, \dots, n \implies a_i = b_i \quad \forall i=1, \dots, nai​−bi​=0∀i=1,…,n⟹ai​=bi​∀i=1,…,n Thus, the coefficients are unique. ■\blacksquare■

3. Illustrative Derivation

Coordinate Transformations (Change of Basis)

In ML, we often transform data from a standard basis to a more informative one (e.g., projecting features onto principal components). Let us derive the change of basis transition matrix.

Let B={v1,…,vn}\mathcal{B} = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}B={v1​,…,vn​} and C={w1,…,wn}\mathcal{C} = \{w_1, \dots, w_n\}C={w1​,…,wn​} be two bases of an nnn-dimensional space VVV. Any vector x∈Vx \in Vx∈V can be represented in both bases: x=∑j=1n[x]Bjvjandx=∑i=1n[x]Ciwix = \sum_{j=1}^n [x]_\mathcal{B}^j v_j \quad \text{and} \quad x = \sum_{i=1}^n [x]_\mathcal{C}^i w_ix=∑j=1n​[x]Bj​vj​andx=∑i=1n​[x]Ci​wi​ where [x]B∈Fn[x]_\mathcal{B} \in \mathbb{F}^n[x]B​∈Fn and [x]C∈Fn[x]_\mathcal{C} \in \mathbb{F}^n[x]C​∈Fn are the coordinate vectors.

We can express each basis vector vjv_jvj​ of the basis B\mathcal{B}B as a linear combination of the basis vectors in C\mathcal{C}C: vj=∑i=1nPijwiv_j = \sum_{i=1}^n P_{ij} w_ivj​=∑i=1n​Pij​wi​ Substitute this representation of vjv_jvj​ back into the equation for xxx: x=∑j=1n[x]Bj(∑i=1nPijwi)=∑i=1n(∑j=1nPij[x]Bj)wix = \sum_{j=1}^n [x]_\mathcal{B}^j \left( \sum_{i=1}^n P_{ij} w_i \right) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \sum_{j=1}^n P_{ij} [x]_\mathcal{B}^j \right) w_ix=∑j=1n​[x]Bj​(∑i=1n​Pij​wi​)=∑i=1n​(∑j=1n​Pij​[x]Bj​)wi​ By uniqueness of coordinate representations under basis C\mathcal{C}C: [x]Ci=∑j=1nPij[x]Bj∀i=1,…,n[x]_\mathcal{C}^i = \sum_{j=1}^n P_{ij} [x]_\mathcal{B}^j \quad \forall i=1, \dots, n[x]Ci​=∑j=1n​Pij​[x]Bj​∀i=1,…,n In matrix form: [x]C=P[x]B[x]_\mathcal{C} = P [x]_\mathcal{B}[x]C​=P[x]B​ where P∈Fn×nP \in \mathbb{F}^{n \times n}P∈Fn×n is the transition matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the "old" basis vectors B\mathcal{B}B written in terms of the "new" basis C\mathcal{C}C: P=[ [v1]C[v2]C…[vn]C ]P = \Big[ \, [v_1]_\mathcal{C} \quad [v_2]_\mathcal{C} \quad \dots \quad [v_n]_\mathcal{C} \, \Big]P=[[v1​]C​[v2​]C​…[vn​]C​] Since B\mathcal{B}B and C\mathcal{C}C are bases, the transition matrix PPP is always invertible, and the reverse transformation is [x]B=P−1[x]C[x]_\mathcal{B} = P^{-1} [x]_\mathcal{C}[x]B​=P−1[x]C​.

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Coordinate Conversion

Let the standard basis of R2\mathbb{R}^2R2 be E={e1,e2}={[10],[01]}\mathcal{E} = \{e_1, e_2\} = \{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\}E={e1​,e2​}={[10​],[01​]}, and let a new basis be B={b1,b2}={[21],[12]}\mathcal{B} = \{b_1, b_2\} = \{\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\}B={b1​,b2​}={[21​],[12​]}. Find the coordinate vector [x]B[x]_\mathcal{B}[x]B​ for the standard vector x=[54]x = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}x=[54​].

  1. Set up the system x=c1b1+c2b2x = c_1 b_1 + c_2 b_2x=c1​b1​+c2​b2​: [54]=c1[21]+c2[12]  ⟹  (2112)[c1c2]=[54]\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \implies \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}[54​]=c1​[21​]+c2​[12​]⟹(21​12​)[c1​c2​​]=[54​]
  2. Solve using matrix inversion: The transition matrix from B\mathcal{B}B to E\mathcal{E}E is P=(2112)P = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}P=(21​12​). Its determinant is 2(2)−1(1)=32(2) - 1(1) = 32(2)−1(1)=3. P−1=13(2−1−12)P^{-1} = \frac{1}{3} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}P−1=31​(2−1​−12​) [x]B=P−1x=13(2−1−12)[54]=13[10−4−5+8]=[21][x]_\mathcal{B} = P^{-1} x = \frac{1}{3} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} 10 - 4 \\ -5 + 8 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[x]B​=P−1x=31​(2−1​−12​)[54​]=31​[10−4−5+8​]=[21​] This shows that the vector x=5e1+4e2x = 5e_1 + 4e_2x=5e1​+4e2​ is represented as 2b1+1b22b_1 + 1b_22b1​+1b2​ under the basis B\mathcal{B}B.

Example 2: Spanning Set Check

Verify whether the set A={a1,a2}={[110],[011]}\mathcal{A} = \{a_1, a_2\} = \{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\}A={a1​,a2​}={​110​​,​011​​} forms a basis for R3\mathbb{R}^3R3.

  1. Compare Dimension to Cardinality: The dimension of the vector space R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 is dim⁡(R3)=3\dim(\mathbb{R}^3) = 3dim(R3)=3. The number of vectors in A\mathcal{A}A is ∣A∣=2|\mathcal{A}| = 2∣A∣=2.
  2. Apply Dimension Theorem: Any spanning set of R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 must contain at least dim⁡(R3)=3\dim(\mathbb{R}^3) = 3dim(R3)=3 vectors. Since ∣A∣<3|\mathcal{A}| < 3∣A∣<3, the set cannot span R3\mathbb{R}^3R3. Specifically, any vector with a non-zero first coordinate and zero second coordinate (e.g., x=[1,0,0]Tx = [1, 0, 0]^Tx=[1,0,0]T) cannot be written as a linear combination of a1a_1a1​ and a2a_2a2​. Thus, A\mathcal{A}A is not a basis for R3\mathbb{R}^3R3.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Principal Component Analysis (PCA): PCA finds an orthogonal basis of the feature space aligned with the directions of maximum variance. Projecting data onto the first kkk eigenvectors of the covariance matrix reduces the dimension of the space from ddd to kkk, filtering out noise.
  2. Autoencoder Latent Dimension: The bottleneck layer in an autoencoder acts as a compressed, non-linear coordinate space. The dimension of this bottleneck dictates the compression ratio and capacity of the network to reconstruct complex inputs.
  3. Matrix Rank in Recommendation Systems: In collaborative filtering, the user-item rating matrix is assumed to have a low rank kkk. This rank kkk is the dimension of the latent factor space (e.g., movie genres or user preferences) that governs user ratings.
  4. Multicollinearity Diagnostics: If features in a dataset are not linearly independent (e.g., if one feature is a linear combination of others), the covariance matrix will not have full rank. This makes it impossible to compute its inverse, causing regression algorithms to fail.
  5. Kernel Methods in SVMs: Standard support vector machines fail when data is not linearly separable. By using the kernel trick, we implicitly map the data into a higher-dimensional space with a larger basis, allowing the model to construct a linear separating boundary.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here visualizing basis spans and dimension:

  • Show a 3D coordinate system (x,y,zx, y, zx,y,z).
  • Plot a 2D tilted plane passing through the origin. Label this plane as "Subspace WWW, dim⁡(W)=2\dim(W) = 2dim(W)=2."
  • Plot two linearly independent vectors b1b_1b1​ and b2b_2b2​ lying on this plane. Show that any point on the plane can be reached via a linear combination of b1b_1b1​ and b2b_2b2​, proving they form a basis for WWW.
  • Plot a third vector b3b_3b3​ that sticks out of the plane into the 3D space. Illustrate that to span the full 3D space R3\mathbb{R}^3R3, we must expand our basis to {b1,b2,b3}\{b_1, b_2, b_3\}{b1​,b2​,b3​}, increasing the dimension of our coordinate representation to 3.

title: Determinants
description: Axiomatic definitions of the determinant, Leibniz permutations, volume scaling, and Jacobian transformations.
content:
Chapter 12: Determinants

Prerequisite

  • Linear Transformations: Knowing how matrices map and distort coordinate spaces.
  • Permutations: Basic understanding of signs and ordering.

1. Conceptual Hook

In machine learning, we often transform data using high-dimensional matrices. But how do we know if a transformation stretches our dataset out, squeezes it down, or collapses it entirely? The mathematical metric that answers this is the determinant.

The determinant is a single scalar value that acts as the volume expansion factor of a matrix. It tells us how much the matrix scales the nnn-dimensional volume of any shape we transform. If the determinant is greater than 111, the space expands; if it is between 000 and 111, the space compresses; and if the determinant is exactly 000, the matrix squashes our data onto a lower-dimensional subspace, destroying information and making the transformation irreversible. In generative models like Normalizing Flows and VAEs, the determinant is the essential scaling factor that keeps probability density integration conserved.

2. Formal Definition

Axiomatically, the determinant is the unique function det⁡:Mn(F)→F\det: M_n(\mathbb{F}) \to \mathbb{F}det:Mn​(F)→F that satisfies three properties relative to the rows of a square matrix A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n:

  1. Multilinearity: The function is linear in each row vector individually.
  2. Alternating Property: If two rows of the matrix are interchanged, the sign of the determinant changes: det⁡(A)=−det⁡(Arow_swap)\det(A) = -\det(A_{row\_swap})det(A)=−det(Arow_swap​) This implies that if a matrix has two identical rows, its determinant is 000.
  3. Normalization: The determinant of the identity matrix is 111: det⁡(In)=1\det(I_n) = 1det(In​)=1

From these axioms, we derive the Leibniz formula for the determinant of an n×nn \times nn×n matrix AAA: det⁡(A)=∑σ∈Snsgn(σ)∏i=1nai,σ(i)\det(A) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \text{sgn}(\sigma) \prod_{i=1}^n a_{i, \sigma(i)}det(A)=∑σ∈Sn​​sgn(σ)∏i=1n​ai,σ(i)​ where SnS_nSn​ is the symmetric group of all permutations of {1,2,…,n}\{1, 2, \dots, n\}{1,2,…,n}, and sgn(σ)∈{+1,−1}\text{sgn}(\sigma) \in \{+1, -1\}sgn(σ)∈{+1,−1} is the signature of the permutation σ\sigmaσ (positive for an even number of swaps, negative for odd).

Core Properties

  • Multiplicative Property: det⁡(AB)=det⁡(A)det⁡(B)\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B)det(AB)=det(A)det(B).
  • Transpose: det⁡(AT)=det⁡(A)\det(A^T) = \det(A)det(AT)=det(A).
  • Scalar Multiplication: det⁡(c⋅A)=cndet⁡(A)\det(c \cdot A) = c^n \det(A)det(c⋅A)=cndet(A) for A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n and c∈Rc \in \mathbb{R}c∈R.
  • Invertibility Criterion: AAA is invertible if and only if det⁡(A)≠0\det(A) \neq 0det(A)=0.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Probability Density Preservation and the Jacobian Determinant

In generative machine learning, we often transform a simple probability distribution X∼fX(x)X \sim f_X(x)X∼fX​(x) (like a standard Gaussian) into a complex distribution Y=g(X)Y = g(X)Y=g(X) using a differentiable, invertible neural network layer. We prove why the Jacobian determinant is required to preserve probability density.

Let XXX and YYY be continuous random variables in Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd linked by Y=g(X)Y = g(X)Y=g(X), where ggg is a bijective and differentiable mapping. Let dydydy and dxdxdx represent corresponding tiny hyper-volumes in the two spaces. For probability density to be conserved, the probability mass in a region must remain identical before and after transformation: P(X∈dx)=P(Y∈dy)  ⟹  fX(x)∣dx∣=fY(y)∣dy∣P(X \in dx) = P(Y \in dy) \implies f_X(x) |dx| = f_Y(y) |dy|P(X∈dx)=P(Y∈dy)⟹fX​(x)∣dx∣=fY​(y)∣dy∣ fY(y)=fX(g−1(y))∣dx∣∣dy∣f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \frac{|dx|}{|dy|}fY​(y)=fX​(g−1(y))∣dy∣∣dx∣​

Under a local first-order Taylor expansion, the linear approximation of the mapping ggg near xxx is: dy=Jg(x)dxdy = J_g(x) dxdy=Jg​(x)dx where Jg(x)∈Rd×dJ_g(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}Jg​(x)∈Rd×d is the Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives: (Jg(x))ij=∂gi∂xj(J_g(x))_{ij} = \frac{\partial g_i}{\partial x_j}(Jg​(x))ij​=∂xj​∂gi​​ The matrix Jg(x)J_g(x)Jg​(x) acts as a local linear transformation mapping the hypercube dxdxdx to a parallelotope dydydy.

By the definition of the determinant, a linear operator scales any local volume by the absolute value of its determinant: Volume(dy)=∣det⁡(Jg(x))∣⋅Volume(dx)\text{Volume}(dy) = \left| \det(J_g(x)) \right| \cdot \text{Volume}(dx)Volume(dy)=∣det(Jg​(x))∣⋅Volume(dx) Thus, the volume ratio is: ∣dx∣∣dy∣=1∣det⁡(Jg(x))∣=∣det⁡(Jg−1(y))∣\frac{|dx|}{|dy|} = \frac{1}{\left| \det(J_g(x)) \right|} = \left| \det\left(J_{g^{-1}}(y)\right) \right|∣dy∣∣dx∣​=∣det(Jg​(x))∣1​=​det(Jg−1​(y))​ Substituting this back yields the Multivariate Change of Variables formula: fY(y)=fX(g−1(y))⋅∣det⁡(Jg−1(y))∣f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot \left| \det\left(J_{g^{-1}}(y)\right) \right|fY​(y)=fX​(g−1(y))⋅​det(Jg−1​(y))​ Without multiplying by the Jacobian determinant, the area under the probability density function would not integrate to 1, violating the fundamental axioms of probability. ■\blacksquare■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Cofactor Expansion of a 3×33 \times 33×3 Matrix

Calculate the determinant of the matrix: A=(103212011)A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}A=​120​011​321​​ Using cofactor expansion along the first row: det⁡(A)=a11C11+a12C12+a13C13\det(A) = a_{11} C_{11} + a_{12} C_{12} + a_{13} C_{13}det(A)=a11​C11​+a12​C12​+a13​C13​ det⁡(A)=1⋅(−1)1+1det⁡(1211)+0+3⋅(−1)1+3det⁡(2101)\det(A) = 1 \cdot (-1)^{1+1} \det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} + 0 + 3 \cdot (-1)^{1+3} \det\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}det(A)=1⋅(−1)1+1det(11​21​)+0+3⋅(−1)1+3det(20​11​)

  1. Compute the 2×22 \times 22×2 determinants: det⁡(1211)=(1)(1)−(2)(1)=−1\det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = (1)(1) - (2)(1) = -1det(11​21​)=(1)(1)−(2)(1)=−1 det⁡(2101)=(2)(1)−(1)(0)=2\det\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = (2)(1) - (1)(0) = 2det(20​11​)=(2)(1)−(1)(0)=2
  2. Substitute values back: det⁡(A)=1⋅(1)⋅(−1)+3⋅(1)⋅(2)=−1+6=5\det(A) = 1 \cdot (1) \cdot (-1) + 3 \cdot (1) \cdot (2) = -1 + 6 = 5det(A)=1⋅(1)⋅(−1)+3⋅(1)⋅(2)=−1+6=5 The matrix scales volumes by a factor of 5 and preserves orientation (since 5>05 > 05>0).

Example 2: Determinant of an Upper Triangular Matrix

Verify that the determinant of an upper triangular matrix UUU is the product of its diagonal elements: U=(d1ab0d2c00d3)U = \begin{pmatrix} d_1 & a & b \\ 0 & d_2 & c \\ 0 & 0 & d_3 \end{pmatrix}U=​d1​00​ad2​0​bcd3​​​ Expanding along the first column: det⁡(U)=d1⋅(−1)1+1det⁡(d2c0d3)−0+0\det(U) = d_1 \cdot (-1)^{1+1} \det\begin{pmatrix} d_2 & c \\ 0 & d_3 \end{pmatrix} - 0 + 0det(U)=d1​⋅(−1)1+1det(d2​0​cd3​​)−0+0 det⁡(U)=d1(d2d3−c(0))=d1d2d3\det(U) = d_1 \left( d_2 d_3 - c(0) \right) = d_1 d_2 d_3det(U)=d1​(d2​d3​−c(0))=d1​d2​d3​ This property is crucial in generative models. Models are designed with triangular Jacobian matrices (e.g., Masked Autoregressive Flows) because their determinants can be computed in O(n)O(n)O(n) time by multiplying the diagonal, bypassing the expensive O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) general calculation.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Normalizing Flows: Generative models like RealNVP compute the likelihood of complex data by passing it through invertible layers. To make training tractible, the layers are structured to have triangular Jacobians, allowing fast computation of the log-determinant term: log⁡∣det⁡J∣\log |\det J|log∣detJ∣.
  2. Multivariate Gaussian Classifiers: The probability density function of a multivariate Gaussian involves the covariance matrix determinant: f(x)∝1(2π)d∣det⁡(Σ)∣f(x) \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^d |\det(\Sigma)|}}f(x)∝(2π)d∣det(Σ)∣​1​. This term scales the normalizer based on the volume of the covariance dispersion.
  3. Hessian Curvature in Optimizers: The determinant of the Hessian matrix HHH (matrix of second partial derivatives) indicates the local curvature of the loss surface. A negative determinant in 2D indicates a saddle point, while a zero determinant indicates a flat plateau.
  4. Information Theory and Entropy: For a continuous multivariate Gaussian distribution, the differential entropy is directly proportional to the log of the determinant of its covariance matrix: H(X)=d2(1+log⁡(2π))+12log⁡(det⁡(Σ))H(X) = \frac{d}{2}(1 + \log(2\pi)) + \frac{1}{2}\log(\det(\Sigma))H(X)=2d​(1+log(2π))+21​log(det(Σ)).
  5. Matrix Singularity Diagnostics: In linear models, we check if det⁡(XTX)≈0\det(X^T X) \approx 0det(XTX)≈0 to detect multicollinearity. If it is close to zero, numerical instability will cause linear regression weights to explode.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating determinants as area-scaling factors in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2:

  • Show a unit square formed by basis vectors e1=[1,0]Te_1 = [1, 0]^Te1​=[1,0]T and e2=[0,1]Te_2 = [0, 1]^Te2​=[0,1]T. The area of this square is exactly 111.
  • Apply the matrix A=(2101.5)A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1.5 \end{pmatrix}A=(20​11.5​) to transform the basis vectors to a1=[2,0]Ta_1 = [2, 0]^Ta1​=[2,0]T and a2=[1,1.5]Ta_2 = [1, 1.5]^Ta2​=[1,1.5]T, forming a parallelogram.
  • Compute the area of this parallelogram: Base×Height=2×1.5=3\text{Base} \times \text{Height} = 2 \times 1.5 = 3Base×Height=2×1.5=3. This matches det⁡(A)=2(1.5)−1(0)=3\det(A) = 2(1.5) - 1(0) = 3det(A)=2(1.5)−1(0)=3, showing the area scales by exactly the determinant.
  • Show a flipped parallelogram with negative determinant (A=(021.50),det⁡(A)=−3A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 1.5 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \det(A) = -3A=(01.5​20​),det(A)=−3), demonstrating how a negative determinant denotes a swap in relative orientation (clockwise vs. counterclockwise).

title: Dot Product
description: Algebraic definition, law of cosines derivation, projections, and similarity measurements in machine learning.
content:
Chapter 13: Dot Product

Prerequisite

  • Vectors: Understanding components and coordinate systems.
  • Vector Norms: Knowing how to calculate the L2L_2L2​ Euclidean length of a vector.

1. Conceptual Hook

In machine learning, we often need to measure how closely aligned two objects are. For instance, how similar is a user's movie preference vector to a movie's genre vector? Or how much attention should a word vector in a sentence pay to another word vector? The fundamental mathematical operation that measures this alignment is the dot product.

The dot product is the ultimate similarity engine. It takes two equal-length vectors, multiplies their corresponding components, and adds them up to produce a single number. Geometrically, it projects one vector onto another and multiplies their lengths. If the vectors point in the same direction, their dot product is large and positive; if they are perpendicular, the product is zero (orthogonal); and if they point in opposite directions, the product is negative. It is the core mathematical building block of neural network layers, similarity search, and self-attention maps.

2. Formal Definition

Let u,v∈Rnu, v \in \mathbb{R}^nu,v∈Rn be two vectors in an nnn-dimensional real vector space. The dot product (or standard inner product), denoted u⋅vu \cdot vu⋅v or uTvu^T vuTv, is defined algebraically as: uTv=∑i=1nuivi=u1v1+u2v2+⋯+unvnu^T v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 + \dots + u_n v_nuTv=∑i=1n​ui​vi​=u1​v1​+u2​v2​+⋯+un​vn​

Geometrically, for vectors in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn, the dot product is defined as: uTv=∥u∥2∥v∥2cos⁡(θ)u^T v = \|u\|_2 \|v\|_2 \cos(\theta)uTv=∥u∥2​∥v∥2​cos(θ) where ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_2∥⋅∥2​ is the Euclidean norm, and θ\thetaθ is the angle of separation between the two vectors (0≤θ≤π0 \le \theta \le \pi0≤θ≤π).

Key Properties

For any vectors u,v,w∈Rnu, v, w \in \mathbb{R}^nu,v,w∈Rn and scalar c∈Rc \in \mathbb{R}c∈R:

  1. Commutativity: uTv=vTuu^T v = v^T uuTv=vTu
  2. Distributivity: uT(v+w)=uTv+uTwu^T (v + w) = u^T v + u^T wuT(v+w)=uTv+uTw
  3. Homogeneity: (c⋅u)Tv=c⋅(uTv)(c \cdot u)^T v = c \cdot (u^T v)(c⋅u)Tv=c⋅(uTv)
  4. Positive-Definiteness: uTu≥0u^T u \ge 0uTu≥0, and uTu=0  ⟺  u=0u^T u = 0 \iff u = 0uTu=0⟺u=0. Note that uTu=∥u∥22u^T u = \|u\|_2^2uTu=∥u∥22​.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Deriving the Geometric Dot Product Formula

We derive the equivalence between the algebraic and geometric definitions of the dot product using the Law of Cosines.

Consider the triangle in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn formed by vectors uuu, vvv, and their difference vector u−vu - vu−v. The lengths of the sides of this triangle are ∥u∥2\|u\|_2∥u∥2​, ∥v∥2\|v\|_2∥v∥2​, and ∥u−v∥2\|u - v\|_2∥u−v∥2​. By the Law of Cosines: ∥u−v∥22=∥u∥22+∥v∥22−2∥u∥2∥v∥2cos⁡(θ)\|u - v\|_2^2 = \|u\|_2^2 + \|v\|_2^2 - 2 \|u\|_2 \|v\|_2 \cos(\theta)∥u−v∥22​=∥u∥22​+∥v∥22​−2∥u∥2​∥v∥2​cos(θ)

Let us expand the left-hand side ∥u−v∥22\|u - v\|_2^2∥u−v∥22​ using the algebraic properties of the inner product: ∥u−v∥22=(u−v)T(u−v)\|u - v\|_2^2 = (u - v)^T (u - v)∥u−v∥22​=(u−v)T(u−v) Using the distributive and commutative properties: (u−v)T(u−v)=uTu−uTv−vTu+vTv(u - v)^T (u - v) = u^T u - u^T v - v^T u + v^T v(u−v)T(u−v)=uTu−uTv−vTu+vTv (u−v)T(u−v)=uTu−2uTv+vTv(u - v)^T (u - v) = u^T u - 2 u^T v + v^T v(u−v)T(u−v)=uTu−2uTv+vTv Substituting the norm definitions (xTx=∥x∥22x^T x = \|x\|_2^2xTx=∥x∥22​): ∥u−v∥22=∥u∥22−2uTv+∥v∥22\|u - v\|_2^2 = \|u\|_2^2 - 2 u^T v + \|v\|_2^2∥u−v∥22​=∥u∥22​−2uTv+∥v∥22​

Now, equate this expanded expression to our Law of Cosines equation: ∥u∥22−2uTv+∥v∥22=∥u∥22+∥v∥22−2∥u∥2∥v∥2cos⁡(θ)\|u\|_2^2 - 2 u^T v + \|v\|_2^2 = \|u\|_2^2 + \|v\|_2^2 - 2 \|u\|_2 \|v\|_2 \cos(\theta)∥u∥22​−2uTv+∥v∥22​=∥u∥22​+∥v∥22​−2∥u∥2​∥v∥2​cos(θ)

Subtract ∥u∥22+∥v∥22\|u\|_2^2 + \|v\|_2^2∥u∥22​+∥v∥22​ from both sides of the equation: −2uTv=−2∥u∥2∥v∥2cos⁡(θ)-2 u^T v = -2 \|u\|_2 \|v\|_2 \cos(\theta)−2uTv=−2∥u∥2​∥v∥2​cos(θ)

Divide both sides by −2-2−2: uTv=∥u∥2∥v∥2cos⁡(θ)u^T v = \|u\|_2 \|v\|_2 \cos(\theta)uTv=∥u∥2​∥v∥2​cos(θ) This completes the proof, establishing the link between algebraic components and spatial angles. ■\blacksquare■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Basic Dot Product Calculation

Let u=[123]u = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}u=​123​​ and v=[4−12]v = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}v=​4−12​​ in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3.

  1. Apply the algebraic definition: uTv=(1)(4)+(2)(−1)+(3)(2)u^T v = (1)(4) + (2)(-1) + (3)(2)uTv=(1)(4)+(2)(−1)+(3)(2) uTv=4−2+6=8u^T v = 4 - 2 + 6 = 8uTv=4−2+6=8 The positive result indicates that the vectors generally point in a similar direction (the angle between them is acute).

Example 2: Determining Angle of Separation

Find the angle θ\thetaθ between u=[10]u = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}u=[10​] and v=[13]v = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ \sqrt{3} \end{bmatrix}v=[13​​].

  1. Compute the dot product: uTv=(1)(1)+(0)(3)=1u^T v = (1)(1) + (0)(\sqrt{3}) = 1uTv=(1)(1)+(0)(3​)=1
  2. Compute the Euclidean norms: ∥u∥2=12+02=1\|u\|_2 = \sqrt{1^2 + 0^2} = 1∥u∥2​=12+02​=1 ∥v∥2=12+(3)2=1+3=2\|v\|_2 = \sqrt{1^2 + (\sqrt{3})^2} = \sqrt{1 + 3} = 2∥v∥2​=12+(3​)2​=1+3​=2
  3. Solve for cos⁡(θ)\cos(\theta)cos(θ): cos⁡(θ)=uTv∥u∥2∥v∥2=11⋅2=0.5\cos(\theta) = \frac{u^T v}{\|u\|_2 \|v\|_2} = \frac{1}{1 \cdot 2} = 0.5cos(θ)=∥u∥2​∥v∥2​uTv​=1⋅21​=0.5
  4. Find θ\thetaθ: θ=arccos⁡(0.5)=60∘(or π3 radians)\theta = \arccos(0.5) = 60^\circ \quad \left(\text{or } \frac{\pi}{3} \text{ radians}\right)θ=arccos(0.5)=60∘(or 3π​ radians) This geometric analysis calculates the exact angular separation of the two vectors.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Neural Network Activation: In a fully connected neuron, the output before activation is calculated as the dot product of the input feature vector xxx and the parameter weight vector www, plus a bias: y=wTx+by = w^T x + by=wTx+b. The dot product measures how closely the input matches the neuron's learned weights.
  2. Cosine Similarity in NLP: In vector search and natural language processing, semantic similarity between text embeddings is measured by the cosine of the angle between them: Sim(u,v)=uTv∥u∥2∥v∥2\text{Sim}(u, v) = \frac{u^T v}{\|u\|_2 \|v\|_2}Sim(u,v)=∥u∥2​∥v∥2​uTv​.
  3. Attention Maps in Transformers: Scaled dot-product attention computes the relationship between token representations by taking the dot product of Query and Key vectors, scaled by the feature dimension: Score(Qi,Kj)=QiTKjdk\text{Score}(Q_i, K_j) = \frac{Q_i^T K_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}Score(Qi​,Kj​)=dk​​QiT​Kj​​.
  4. Support Vector Machines (SVM): The decision boundary of a linear SVM is a hyperplane defined by the set of feature points where the dot product with the normal weight vector equals the bias: wTx+b=0w^T x + b = 0wTx+b=0.
  5. Kernel Trick: Dual formulations of ML models (like kernel SVMs or Kernel PCA) compute predictions using inner products in high-dimensional feature spaces, calculated implicitly via a kernel function: K(u,v)=ϕ(u)Tϕ(v)K(u, v) = \phi(u)^T \phi(v)K(u,v)=ϕ(u)Tϕ(v).

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating the dot product as a projection:

  • Show two vectors uuu and vvv drawn from the origin with an angle θ\thetaθ between them.
  • Draw a dashed perpendicular line from the tip of uuu down to the span of vvv. Label the distance from the origin to the foot of this perpendicular as the projection length of uuu onto vvv: ∥u∥2cos⁡(θ)\|u\|_2 \cos(\theta)∥u∥2​cos(θ).
  • Illustrate that the dot product is the product of this projection length and the length of vvv (∥v∥2\|v\|_2∥v∥2​).
  • Draw three side-by-side scenarios:
    1. Acute Angle (θ<90∘\theta < 90^\circθ<90∘): Projection points in the direction of vvv, resulting in a positive dot product.
    2. Right Angle (θ=90∘\theta = 90^\circθ=90∘): Projection length is zero, resulting in a zero dot product (orthogonality).
    3. Obtuse Angle (θ>90∘\theta > 90^\circθ>90∘): Projection points in the opposite direction of vvv, resulting in a negative dot product.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
description: Spectral theory, coordinate-free linear operators, characteristic polynomials, real symmetric matrices, and the Spectral Theorem.
content:
Chapter 14: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

Prerequisite

  • Linear Transformations: Matrix representations of linear maps T:V→VT: V \to VT:V→V on a vector space VVV.
  • Determinants and Kernels: Comprehending the operator null space ker⁡(T)\ker(T)ker(T) and how singular operators have vanishing determinants.
  • Inner Product Spaces: Familiarity with the standard inner product ⟨u,v⟩=uTv\langle u, v \rangle = u^T v⟨u,v⟩=uTv in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn and orthogonal projections.

1. Conceptual Hook

Think of eigenvalues and eigenvectors as the natural resonance axes of a physical system, like a drumhead or a guitar string.

When you strike a drumhead, the resulting vibrations appear chaotic. The surface deforms, waves propagate in all directions, and the shape changes dynamically. However, any complex vibration is actually a superposition of standing waves—modes of vibration where the drumhead moves purely up and down without traveling or warping sideways.

The eigenvectors are these fundamental standing wave patterns (the natural shapes of resonance). The transformation (striking the drum) only scales the amplitude of these patterns; it does not alter their spatial shape. The eigenvalues represent the resonant frequencies (the scaling factor of the amplitude).

In machine learning, instead of physical vibrations, we "strike" high-dimensional datasets with covariance matrices or graph Laplacians. The eigenvectors reveal the stable, non-warping modes of the data, while the eigenvalues tell us the energy or variance concentrated in those directions.

2. Formal Definition

Let VVV be a vector space over a field FFF (typically R\mathbb{R}R or C\mathbb{C}C). A linear operator is a map T:V→VT: V \to VT:V→V.

Coordinate-Free Definition

A non-zero vector v∈V∖{0}v \in V \setminus \{0\}v∈V∖{0} is an eigenvector of TTT if there exists a scalar λ∈F\lambda \in Fλ∈F (the eigenvalue) such that: T(v)=λvT(v) = \lambda vT(v)=λv This definition is coordinate-free; it does not depend on choosing a basis for VVV.

Matrix Representation and the Characteristic Equation

If VVV is finite-dimensional (d=dim⁡Vd = \dim Vd=dimV), we represent TTT as a square matrix A∈Fd×d\mathbf{A} \in F^{d \times d}A∈Fd×d under a chosen basis. The operator equation becomes: Av=λv  ⟺  (A−λI)v=0\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v} \iff (\mathbf{A} - \lambda \mathbf{I})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}Av=λv⟺(A−λI)v=0 For a non-zero vector v\mathbf{v}v to exist in the null space of (A−λI)(\mathbf{A} - \lambda \mathbf{I})(A−λI), the matrix operator must be singular. Thus, the eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial: p(λ)=det⁡(A−λI)=0p(\lambda) = \det(\mathbf{A} - \lambda \mathbf{I}) = 0p(λ)=det(A−λI)=0

The Spectral Theorem for Real Symmetric Matrices

Let A∈Rd×d\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}A∈Rd×d be a symmetric matrix (A=AT\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}^TA=AT). The Spectral Theorem guarantees that:

  1. All eigenvalues of A\mathbf{A}A are real: λi∈R\lambda_i \in \mathbb{R}λi​∈R.
  2. Eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
  3. A\mathbf{A}A is orthogonally diagonalizable: A=QΛQT=∑i=1dλiqiqiT\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{\Lambda} \mathbf{Q}^T = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \lambda_i \mathbf{q}_i \mathbf{q}_i^TA=QΛQT=∑i=1d​λi​qi​qiT​ where Q\mathbf{Q}Q is an orthogonal matrix (QTQ=I\mathbf{Q}^T \mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}QTQ=I) whose columns qi\mathbf{q}_iqi​ are the orthonormal eigenvectors of A\mathbf{A}A.

Gotcha: If a matrix is non-symmetric, it might not have a complete set of ddd linearly independent eigenvectors (known as a deficient matrix). In such cases, diagonalization fails. For real symmetric matrices, completeness and orthogonality are mathematically guaranteed.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Proof: Properties of Symmetric Matrix Spectra

We prove that (1) all eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are real, and (2) eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.

Proof: Let A∈Rd×d\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}A∈Rd×d be a symmetric matrix (A=AT\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}^TA=AT).

  1. Prove eigenvalues are real (λi∈R\lambda_i \in \mathbb{R}λi​∈R): Suppose λ∈C\lambda \in \mathbb{C}λ∈C is an eigenvalue of A\mathbf{A}A with eigenvector v∈Cd∖{0}\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{C}^d \setminus \{\mathbf{0}\}v∈Cd∖{0}: Av=λv\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}Av=λv Taking the conjugate transpose (Hermitian conjugate, denoted by H^HH) of both sides: (Av)H=(λv)H  ⟹  vHAH=λˉvH(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v})^H = (\lambda \mathbf{v})^H \implies \mathbf{v}^H \mathbf{A}^H = \bar{\lambda} \mathbf{v}^H(Av)H=(λv)H⟹vHAH=λˉvH Since A\mathbf{A}A is real and symmetric, AH=A‾T=AT=A\mathbf{A}^H = \overline{\mathbf{A}}^T = \mathbf{A}^T = \mathbf{A}AH=AT=AT=A. Thus: vHA=λˉvH\mathbf{v}^H \mathbf{A} = \bar{\lambda} \mathbf{v}^HvHA=λˉvH Post-multiply both sides of this equation by v\mathbf{v}v: vHAv=λˉvHv(Equation 1)\mathbf{v}^H \mathbf{A} \mathbf{v} = \bar{\lambda} \mathbf{v}^H \mathbf{v} \quad \text{(Equation 1)}vHAv=λˉvHv(Equation 1) Now, pre-multiply our original eigenvector equation Av=λv\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}Av=λv by vH\mathbf{v}^HvH: vHAv=λvHv(Equation 2)\mathbf{v}^H \mathbf{A} \mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}^H \mathbf{v} \quad \text{(Equation 2)}vHAv=λvHv(Equation 2) Equating Equation 1 and Equation 2 yields: λvHv=λˉvHv  ⟹  (λ−λˉ)vHv=0\lambda \mathbf{v}^H \mathbf{v} = \bar{\lambda} \mathbf{v}^H \mathbf{v} \implies (\lambda - \bar{\lambda}) \mathbf{v}^H \mathbf{v} = 0λvHv=λˉvHv⟹(λ−λˉ)vHv=0 Since v\mathbf{v}v is a non-zero vector, its inner product is strictly positive: vHv=∑i=1d∣vi∣2>0\mathbf{v}^H \mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^d |v_i|^2 > 0vHv=∑i=1d​∣vi​∣2>0. Thus: λ−λˉ=0  ⟹  λ=λˉ\lambda - \bar{\lambda} = 0 \implies \lambda = \bar{\lambda}λ−λˉ=0⟹λ=λˉ Since the eigenvalue equals its complex conjugate, λ\lambdaλ must be a real number (λ∈R\lambda \in \mathbb{R}λ∈R).

  2. Prove distinct eigenvectors are orthogonal (v1Tv2=0\mathbf{v}_1^T \mathbf{v}_2 = 0v1T​v2​=0): Let Av1=λ1v1\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_1 = \lambda_1 \mathbf{v}_1Av1​=λ1​v1​ and Av2=λ2v2\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_2 = \lambda_2 \mathbf{v}_2Av2​=λ2​v2​ with λ1≠λ2\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2λ1​=λ2​. Consider the inner product product expansion: λ1v1Tv2=(Av1)Tv2=v1TATv2\lambda_1 \mathbf{v}_1^T \mathbf{v}_2 = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_1)^T \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1^T \mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{v}_2λ1​v1T​v2​=(Av1​)Tv2​=v1T​ATv2​ Since A\mathbf{A}A is symmetric (AT=A\mathbf{A}^T = \mathbf{A}AT=A): λ1v1Tv2=v1TAv2=v1T(λ2v2)=λ2v1Tv2\lambda_1 \mathbf{v}_1^T \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1^T (\lambda_2 \mathbf{v}_2) = \lambda_2 \mathbf{v}_1^T \mathbf{v}_2λ1​v1T​v2​=v1T​Av2​=v1T​(λ2​v2​)=λ2​v1T​v2​ Rearranging terms: (λ1−λ2)v1Tv2=0(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2) \mathbf{v}_1^T \mathbf{v}_2 = 0(λ1​−λ2​)v1T​v2​=0 Since the eigenvalues are distinct (λ1−λ2≠0\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 \neq 0λ1​−λ2​=0), we conclude: v1Tv2=0■\mathbf{v}_1^T \mathbf{v}_2 = 0 \quad \blacksquarev1T​v2​=0■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Spectral Decomposition of a Symmetric Matrix

We decompose the symmetric matrix A=[3223]\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}A=[32​23​].

  1. Solve the Characteristic Equation: det⁡(A−λI)=det⁡[3−λ223−λ]=(3−λ)2−4=0\det(\mathbf{A} - \lambda \mathbf{I}) = \det \begin{bmatrix} 3-\lambda & 2 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{bmatrix} = (3-\lambda)^2 - 4 = 0det(A−λI)=det[3−λ2​23−λ​]=(3−λ)2−4=0 λ2−6λ+5=0  ⟹  (λ−5)(λ−1)=0\lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 5 = 0 \implies (\lambda - 5)(\lambda - 1) = 0λ2−6λ+5=0⟹(λ−5)(λ−1)=0 The eigenvalues are λ1=5\lambda_1 = 5λ1​=5 and λ2=1\lambda_2 = 1λ2​=1.
  2. Determine orthonormal eigenvectors:
    • For λ1=5\lambda_1 = 5λ1​=5: [−222−2][x1x2]=[00]  ⟹  x1=x2  ⟹  q1=12[11]\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \implies x_1 = x_2 \implies \mathbf{q}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[−22​2−2​][x1​x2​​]=[00​]⟹x1​=x2​⟹q1​=2​1​[11​]
    • For λ2=1\lambda_2 = 1λ2​=1: [2222][x1x2]=[00]  ⟹  x1=−x2  ⟹  q2=12[−11]\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \implies x_1 = -x_2 \implies \mathbf{q}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[22​22​][x1​x2​​]=[00​]⟹x1​=−x2​⟹q2​=2​1​[−11​] Note that q1Tq2=0\mathbf{q}_1^T \mathbf{q}_2 = 0q1T​q2​=0 (orthogonal).
  3. Reconstruct using the Spectral Theorem: Q=12[1−111],Λ=[5001]\mathbf{Q} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{\Lambda} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}Q=2​1​[11​−11​],Λ=[50​01​] QΛQT=12[1−111][5001][11−11]=12[5−151][11−11]=[3223]=A\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T = \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -1 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{A}QΛQT=21​[11​−11​][50​01​][1−1​11​]=21​[55​−11​][1−1​11​]=[32​23​]=A

Example 2: Eigenspectrum of a Non-Symmetric Matrix

We find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors for the non-symmetric matrix B=[01−23]\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}B=[0−2​13​].

  1. Solve the Characteristic Equation: det⁡(B−λI)=det⁡[−λ1−23−λ]=−λ(3−λ)+2=λ2−3λ+2=0  ⟹  (λ−2)(λ−1)=0\det(\mathbf{B} - \lambda \mathbf{I}) = \det \begin{bmatrix} -\lambda & 1 \\ -2 & 3-\lambda \end{bmatrix} = -\lambda(3-\lambda) + 2 = \lambda^2 - 3\lambda + 2 = 0 \implies (\lambda - 2)(\lambda - 1) = 0det(B−λI)=det[−λ−2​13−λ​]=−λ(3−λ)+2=λ2−3λ+2=0⟹(λ−2)(λ−1)=0 The eigenvalues are λ1=2\lambda_1 = 2λ1​=2 and λ2=1\lambda_2 = 1λ2​=1.
  2. Determine eigenvectors:
    • For λ1=2\lambda_1 = 2λ1​=2: [−21−21]v1=0  ⟹  v1=[12]\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{0} \implies \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}[−2−2​11​]v1​=0⟹v1​=[12​]
    • For λ2=1\lambda_2 = 1λ2​=1: [−11−22]v2=0  ⟹  v2=[11]\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{0} \implies \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[−1−2​12​]v2​=0⟹v2​=[11​] Note: The eigenvectors v1\mathbf{v}_1v1​ and v2\mathbf{v}_2v2​ are not orthogonal (v1Tv2=1⋅1+2⋅1=3≠0\mathbf{v}_1^T \mathbf{v}_2 = 1\cdot1 + 2\cdot1 = 3 \neq 0v1T​v2​=1⋅1+2⋅1=3=0), because B\mathbf{B}B is not symmetric.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Principal Component Analysis (PCA): Finding eigenvectors of the symmetric covariance matrix Σ=1nXTX\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}Σ=n1​XTX. The eigenvectors represent directions of maximum variance (principal components), used for dimension reduction.
  2. Spectral Graph Theory and GNNs: The normalized Graph Laplacian Lsym=I−D−1/2AD−1/2\mathbf{L}_{sym} = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{D}^{-1/2} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}Lsym​=I−D−1/2AD−1/2 is symmetric. Its eigenvectors define the graph Fourier basis, enabling graph convolutions.
  3. Google PageRank: Modeling internet browsing as a Markov chain. The PageRank score is the stationary distribution vector, which is the dominant eigenvector (eigenvalue λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1) of the hyperlink transition matrix.
  4. Deep Landscape Hessian Spectrum: Checking the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix ∇2L(θ)\nabla^2 L(\boldsymbol{\theta})∇2L(θ) to analyze loss landscape curvature. A large condition number λmax/λmin\lambda_{max} / \lambda_{min}λmax​/λmin​ indicates steep ravines.
  5. Kernel PCA and Spectral Clustering: Decomposing affinity and kernel matrices using eigenvectors to perform non-linear dimensionality reduction and cluster data.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating eigenvector scaling under transformation:

  • Draw two 2D grids side-by-side:
    1. Original Space: Draw a unit circle centered at the origin, with two coordinate arrows v1\mathbf{v}_1v1​ and v2\mathbf{v}_2v2​ pointing along different directions.
    2. Transformed Space: Draw an ellipse representing the grid after transformation by a matrix.
  • Show that while most vectors on the unit circle have rotated and shifted, the arrows representing eigenvectors v1\mathbf{v}_1v1​ and v2\mathbf{v}_2v2​ still point in their original directions, only stretched in length by their corresponding eigenvalues λ1\lambda_1λ1​ and λ2\lambda_2λ2​.
  • Add a caption explaining that eigenvectors are the invariant directions of a linear transformation that do not rotate during mapping, undergoing only scaling by a factor equal to their eigenvalue.
