content:
Chapter 23: Positive Definite Matrices

Prerequisite

  • Symmetric Matrices: Familiarity with matrices where A=ATA = A^TA=AT.
  • Eigenvalues: Understanding scaling factors along characteristic directions.

1. Conceptual Hook

In machine learning optimization, we are constantly navigating high-dimensional loss landscapes to find the lowest point. But how do we know if we have landed in a stable valley, a peak, or a treacherous saddle point? The mathematical structure that guarantees stability is the positive definite matrix.

A symmetric matrix is positive definite if it defines a quadratic energy function that remains strictly positive in all non-zero directions. Geometrically, it represents a perfect, upward-opening bowl. This shape ensures that optimization algorithms like Gradient Descent can safely converge to a unique, stable global minimum. From multivariate Gaussian distributions and Gaussian Process regression to support vector machine kernels and Hessian curvature, positive definiteness is the mathematical backbone of model stability and optimization.

2. Formal Definition

Let A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n be a real symmetric matrix (A=ATA = A^TA=AT).

  • Positive Definite (A≻0A \succ 0A≻0): AAA is positive definite if the scalar result of its quadratic form is strictly positive for every non-zero vector x∈Rnx \in \mathbb{R}^nx∈Rn: xTAx>0∀x∈Rn∖{0}x^T A x > 0 \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{\mathbf{0}\}xTAx>0∀x∈Rn∖{0}
  • Positive Semi-Definite (A⪰0A \succeq 0A⪰0): AAA is positive semi-definite if the quadratic form is non-negative for all vectors: xTAx≥0∀x∈Rnx^T A x \ge 0 \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^nxTAx≥0∀x∈Rn

Equivalent Characterizations

For a real symmetric matrix AAA, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. Positive Definiteness: A≻0A \succ 0A≻0.
  2. Positive Eigenvalues: All eigenvalues λi\lambda_iλi​ of AAA are strictly positive: λi>0∀i=1,…,n\lambda_i > 0 \quad \forall i=1, \dots, nλi​>0∀i=1,…,n
  3. Sylvester's Criterion: All principal minors of AAA (the determinants of its top-left submatrices) are strictly positive.
  4. Cholesky Decomposition: AAA can be decomposed uniquely as: A=LLTA = L L^TA=LLT where LLL is a lower triangular matrix with strictly positive diagonal entries.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Equivalence of Positive Definiteness and Positive Eigenvalues

We prove that a symmetric matrix A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n is positive definite if and only if all of its eigenvalues are strictly positive.

Proof: Since AAA is symmetric, by the Spectral Theorem, there exists an orthogonal matrix Q∈Rn×nQ \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}Q∈Rn×n (QTQ=InQ^T Q = I_nQTQ=In​) of eigenvectors such that: A=QΛQTA = Q \Lambda Q^TA=QΛQT where Λ=diag(λ1,λ2,…,λn)\Lambda = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_n)Λ=diag(λ1​,λ2​,…,λn​) is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues.

Let us evaluate the quadratic form xTAxx^T A xxTAx for any non-zero vector x∈Rnx \in \mathbb{R}^nx∈Rn: xTAx=xT(QΛQT)x=(QTx)TΛ(QTx)x^T A x = x^T (Q \Lambda Q^T) x = (Q^T x)^T \Lambda (Q^T x)xTAx=xT(QΛQT)x=(QTx)TΛ(QTx) Let y=QTxy = Q^T xy=QTx. Since QTQ^TQT is invertible (orthogonal), if x≠0x \neq 0x=0, then y≠0y \neq 0y=0. Expanding the diagonal product: xTAx=yTΛy=∑i=1nλiyi2x^T A x = y^T \Lambda y = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i y_i^2xTAx=yTΛy=∑i=1n​λi​yi2​

  1. Forward Direction (λi>0  ⟹  A≻0\lambda_i > 0 \implies A \succ 0λi​>0⟹A≻0): Assume λi>0\lambda_i > 0λi​>0 for all i=1,…,ni=1, \dots, ni=1,…,n. Since y≠0y \neq 0y=0, there exists at least one component yj≠0y_j \neq 0yj​=0, meaning yj2>0y_j^2 > 0yj2​>0. Since all other terms yi2≥0y_i^2 \ge 0yi2​≥0 and λi>0\lambda_i > 0λi​>0: ∑i=1nλiyi2>0  ⟹  xTAx>0\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i y_i^2 > 0 \implies x^T A x > 0∑i=1n​λi​yi2​>0⟹xTAx>0 Thus, AAA is positive definite.

  2. Reverse Direction (A≻0  ⟹  λi>0A \succ 0 \implies \lambda_i > 0A≻0⟹λi​>0): Assume AAA is positive definite (xTAx>0x^T A x > 0xTAx>0 for all x≠0x \neq 0x=0). Let qiq_iqi​ be the iii-th eigenvector of AAA corresponding to eigenvalue λi\lambda_iλi​. Since qiq_iqi​ is a basis vector, qi≠0q_i \neq 0qi​=0. Evaluate the quadratic form using x=qix = q_ix=qi​: qiTAqi=qiT(λiqi)=λi(qiTqi)=λi∥qi∥22q_i^T A q_i = q_i^T (\lambda_i q_i) = \lambda_i (q_i^T q_i) = \lambda_i \|q_i\|_2^2qiT​Aqi​=qiT​(λi​qi​)=λi​(qiT​qi​)=λi​∥qi​∥22​ By positive definiteness, qiTAqi>0q_i^T A q_i > 0qiT​Aqi​>0. Since ∥qi∥22>0\|q_i\|_2^2 > 0∥qi​∥22​>0: λi∥qi∥22>0  ⟹  λi>0\lambda_i \|q_i\|_2^2 > 0 \implies \lambda_i > 0λi​∥qi​∥22​>0⟹λi​>0 This holds for all eigenvalues λi\lambda_iλi​. Thus, all eigenvalues are strictly positive. ■\blacksquare■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: A Positive Definite Matrix

Let A=(2112)A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}A=(21​12​). Check if A≻0A \succ 0A≻0.

  1. Calculate Eigenvalues: det⁡(A−λI)=det⁡(2−λ112−λ)=(2−λ)2−1=λ2−4λ+3=0\det(A - \lambda I) = \det\begin{pmatrix} 2 - \lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 2 - \lambda \end{pmatrix} = (2 - \lambda)^2 - 1 = \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3 = 0det(A−λI)=det(2−λ1​12−λ​)=(2−λ)2−1=λ2−4λ+3=0 (λ−3)(λ−1)=0  ⟹  λ1=3,λ2=1(\lambda - 3)(\lambda - 1) = 0 \implies \lambda_1 = 3, \quad \lambda_2 = 1(λ−3)(λ−1)=0⟹λ1​=3,λ2​=1 Since both eigenvalues are strictly positive (3>03 > 03>0 and 1>01 > 01>0), AAA is positive definite.
  2. Check Cholesky Decomposition: We seek L=(l110l21l22)L = \begin{pmatrix} l_{11} & 0 \\ l_{21} & l_{22} \end{pmatrix}L=(l11​l21​​0l22​​) such that LLT=AL L^T = ALLT=A: (l110l21l22)(l11l210l22)=(l112l11l21l11l21l212+l222)=(2112)\begin{pmatrix} l_{11} & 0 \\ l_{21} & l_{22} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} l_{11} & l_{21} \\ 0 & l_{22} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} l_{11}^2 & l_{11} l_{21} \\ l_{11} l_{21} & l_{21}^2 + l_{22}^2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}(l11​l21​​0l22​​)(l11​0​l21​l22​​)=(l112​l11​l21​​l11​l21​l212​+l222​​)=(21​12​)
    • l112=2  ⟹  l11=2l_{11}^2 = 2 \implies l_{11} = \sqrt{2}l112​=2⟹l11​=2​
    • l11l21=1  ⟹  l21=12l_{11} l_{21} = 1 \implies l_{21} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}l11​l21​=1⟹l21​=2​1​
    • l212+l222=2  ⟹  12+l222=2  ⟹  l222=32  ⟹  l22=32l_{21}^2 + l_{22}^2 = 2 \implies \frac{1}{2} + l_{22}^2 = 2 \implies l_{22}^2 = \frac{3}{2} \implies l_{22} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}l212​+l222​=2⟹21​+l222​=2⟹l222​=23​⟹l22​=23​​ Since a unique lower-triangular LLL with positive diagonal elements exists, A≻0A \succ 0A≻0.

Example 2: An Indefinite Matrix

Let B=(1221)B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}B=(12​21​).

  1. Calculate Eigenvalues: det⁡(B−λI)=(1−λ)2−4=λ2−2λ−3=0  ⟹  (λ−3)(λ+1)=0  ⟹  λ1=3,λ2=−1\det(B - \lambda I) = (1 - \lambda)^2 - 4 = \lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 3 = 0 \implies (\lambda - 3)(\lambda + 1) = 0 \implies \lambda_1 = 3, \quad \lambda_2 = -1det(B−λI)=(1−λ)2−4=λ2−2λ−3=0⟹(λ−3)(λ+1)=0⟹λ1​=3,λ2​=−1 Since one eigenvalue is negative, BBB is indefinite.
  2. Verify using a test vector: Let x=[1−1]x = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}x=[1−1​]. The quadratic form is: xTBx=[1,−1](1221)[1−1]=[1,−1][1(1)+2(−1)2(1)+1(−1)]=[1,−1][−11]=−2x^T B x = \begin{bmatrix} 1, & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1, & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1(1) + 2(-1) \\ 2(1) + 1(-1) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1, & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = -2xTBx=[1,​−1​](12​21​)[1−1​]=[1,​−1​][1(1)+2(−1)2(1)+1(−1)​]=[1,​−1​][−11​]=−2 Since the quadratic form yields a negative value, BBB is not positive definite.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Covariance Matrices: By definition, empirical covariance matrices Σ=1nXTX\Sigma = \frac{1}{n} X^T XΣ=n1​XTX are always positive semi-definite (A⪰0A \succeq 0A⪰0). If features are linearly independent, Σ≻0\Sigma \succ 0Σ≻0. This ensures that the variance of any linear combination of features is strictly non-negative: Var(wTx)=wTΣw≥0\text{Var}(w^T x) = w^T \Sigma w \ge 0Var(wTx)=wTΣw≥0.
  2. Optimization Stability (The Hessian): In multivariate optimization, a critical point x∗x^*x∗ is a local minimum if the gradient ∇f(x∗)=0\nabla f(x^*) = 0∇f(x∗)=0 and the Hessian matrix H(x∗)=∇2f(x∗)H(x^*) = \nabla^2 f(x^*)H(x∗)=∇2f(x∗) is positive definite (H(x∗)≻0H(x^*) \succ 0H(x∗)≻0). This guarantees the landscape curves upwards in all directions.
  3. Kernel Methods (SVMs): By Mercer's Theorem, a function k(x,y)k(x, y)k(x,y) is a valid kernel if and only if the Gram matrix Kij=k(xi,xj)K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)Kij​=k(xi​,xj​) is positive semi-definite for any set of input vectors. This ensures that the kernel corresponds to a dot product in a valid Hilbert space.
  4. Gaussian Process Regression: GPs define distributions over functions, parameterized by a kernel covariance matrix KKK. This matrix must be positive definite to ensure the multivariate Gaussian probability density function is mathematically defined.
  5. Cholesky Sampling: To sample from a multivariate normal distribution N(μ,Σ)\mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)N(μ,Σ), we compute the Cholesky factorization Σ=LLT\Sigma = L L^TΣ=LLT. We then draw standard normal samples z∼N(0,I)z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)z∼N(0,I) and transform them: x=μ+Lzx = \mu + Lzx=μ+Lz. Cholesky decomposition requires Σ≻0\Sigma \succ 0Σ≻0.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here showing the 3D graph of quadratic forms f(x,y)=[x,y]A[xy]f(x, y) = \begin{bmatrix} x, & y \end{bmatrix} A \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}f(x,y)=[x,​y​]A[xy​] to illustrate definiteness:

  • Positive Definite (A≻0A \succ 0A≻0): Show a 3D parabolic bowl opening upwards. The minimum is at the origin (0,0,0)(0, 0, 0)(0,0,0), and any step away from the center results in a positive height.
  • Negative Definite (A≺0A \prec 0A≺0): Show an inverted 3D parabolic dome opening downwards, where any step away from the origin results in a negative height.
  • Indefinite Matrix: Show a saddle point (hyperbolic paraboloid), where moving along one axis curves upwards (positive eigenvalues) while moving along another axis curves downwards (negative eigenvalues). Label the origin as the saddle point.

title: Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHS)
description: Infinite-dimensional function spaces, the Riesz representation theorem, and the Representer Theorem.

Chapter 26: Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHS)

Prerequisite

  • Hilbert Spaces: Inner product spaces that are complete (every Cauchy sequence converges).
  • Dual Spaces: The space of bounded linear functionals mapping functions to scalars.
  • Positive Definiteness: Generalizing positive semi-definite matrices to continuous kernels.

Analogy

Think of a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) as an infinite-dimensional sorting warehouse with a master blueprint.

Imagine you are trying to classify complex, tangled shapes (like handwriting or protein sequences) that are impossible to separate on a flat table. To solve this, you decide to project these shapes into a high-dimensional space where they can be separated by a flat sheet of glass.

Normally, working in an infinite-dimensional space would require infinite memory and computational power—an impossible warehouse to manage.

The kernel is the "master blueprint." Instead of physically placing each item in the infinite warehouse and measuring their coordinates, the blueprint allows you to calculate the exact distance and relationship between any two items as if they were sitting in the warehouse, using only their original, flat-table coordinates. The reproducing property is the warehouse retrieval clerk: it guarantees that evaluating the value of a function at any specific point is as simple as taking a single inner product with the kernel.

The Math Link

1. Evaluation Functionals and RKHS Definition

Let H\mathcal{H}H be a Hilbert space of real-valued functions defined on a non-empty set X\mathcal{X}X. For any x∈Xx \in \mathcal{X}x∈X, the evaluation functional δx:H→R\delta_x: \mathcal{H} \to \mathbb{R}δx​:H→R is the operator that evaluates a function f∈Hf \in \mathcal{H}f∈H at the point xxx: δx(f)=f(x)\delta_x(f) = f(x)δx​(f)=f(x) A Hilbert space H\mathcal{H}H is a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) if and only if the evaluation functional δx\delta_xδx​ is bounded (continuous) for all x∈Xx \in \mathcal{X}x∈X: ∃Mx>0s.t.∣δx(f)∣=∣f(x)∣≤Mx∥f∥H∀f∈H\exists M_x > 0 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad |\delta_x(f)| = |f(x)| \le M_x \|f\|_{\mathcal{H}} \quad \forall f \in \mathcal{H}∃Mx​>0s.t.∣δx​(f)∣=∣f(x)∣≤Mx​∥f∥H​∀f∈H

2. The Reproducing Kernel

By the Riesz Representation Theorem, since δx\delta_xδx​ is a bounded linear functional on the Hilbert space H\mathcal{H}H, there exists a unique representative element in H\mathcal{H}H, which we denote as Kx∈HK_x \in \mathcal{H}Kx​∈H, such that: δx(f)=⟨f,Kx⟩H∀f∈H\delta_x(f) = \langle f, K_x \rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \quad \forall f \in \mathcal{H}δx​(f)=⟨f,Kx​⟩H​∀f∈H Defining the bivariate function K:X×X→RK: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}K:X×X→R as K(x,y)=Kx(y)K(x, y) = K_x(y)K(x,y)=Kx​(y), we obtain the two defining properties of a reproducing kernel:

  1. Membership: K(⋅,x)∈HK(\cdot, x) \in \mathcal{H}K(⋅,x)∈H for all x∈Xx \in \mathcal{X}x∈X.
  2. Reproducing Property: For all x∈Xx \in \mathcal{X}x∈X and f∈Hf \in \mathcal{H}f∈H: ⟨f,K(⋅,x)⟩H=f(x)\langle f, K(\cdot, x) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}} = f(x)⟨f,K(⋅,x)⟩H​=f(x) In particular, for any x,y∈Xx, y \in \mathcal{X}x,y∈X: ⟨K(⋅,x),K(⋅,y)⟩H=K(x,y)\langle K(\cdot, x), K(\cdot, y) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}} = K(x, y)⟨K(⋅,x),K(⋅,y)⟩H​=K(x,y)

3. Mercer's Theorem

A symmetric function K:X×X→RK: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}K:X×X→R is a reproducing kernel if and only if it is positive definite, meaning for any n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N, any points x1,…,xn∈Xx_1, \dots, x_n \in \mathcal{X}x1​,…,xn​∈X, and any coefficients c1,…,cn∈Rc_1, \dots, c_n \in \mathbb{R}c1​,…,cn​∈R: ∑i=1n∑j=1ncicjK(xi,xj)≥0\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n c_i c_j K(x_i, x_j) \ge 0∑i=1n​∑j=1n​ci​cj​K(xi​,xj​)≥0 Mercer's Theorem states that if KKK is continuous and positive definite on a compact domain X\mathcal{X}X, it can be expanded as: K(x,y)=∑i=1∞λiϕi(x)ϕi(y)K(x, y) = \sum_{i=1}^\infty \lambda_i \phi_i(x) \phi_i(y)K(x,y)=∑i=1∞​λi​ϕi​(x)ϕi​(y) where {λi}i=1∞\{\lambda_i\}_{i=1}^\infty{λi​}i=1∞​ are non-negative eigenvalues and {ϕi}i=1∞\{\phi_i\}_{i=1}^\infty{ϕi​}i=1∞​ are orthonormal eigenfunctions. This establishes the implicit feature map Φ(x)=(λ1ϕ1(x),λ2ϕ2(x),… )T\Phi(x) = (\sqrt{\lambda_1}\phi_1(x), \sqrt{\lambda_2}\phi_2(x), \dots)^TΦ(x)=(λ1​​ϕ1​(x),λ2​​ϕ2​(x),…)T into the sequence space ℓ2\ell^2ℓ2, verifying the kernel trick: ⟨Φ(x),Φ(y)⟩ℓ2=K(x,y)\langle \Phi(x), \Phi(y) \rangle_{\ell^2} = K(x, y)⟨Φ(x),Φ(y)⟩ℓ2​=K(x,y)

Proof-Based Exercises

Exercise 1: Proof of the Representer Theorem

Theorem: Let X\mathcal{X}X be a set, KKK a positive definite kernel, and HK\mathcal{H}_KHK​ its corresponding RKHS. Given a training set {(xi,yi)}i=1n⊂X×R\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathcal{X} \times \mathbb{R}{(xi​,yi​)}i=1n​⊂X×R, a strictly increasing regularization function Ω:[0,∞)→R\Omega: [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}Ω:[0,∞)→R, and an arbitrary loss function L:Rn→RL: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}L:Rn→R, any minimizer of the regularized empirical risk: f∗=arg⁡min⁡f∈HKL(f(x1),…,f(xn))+Ω(∥f∥HK2)f^* = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal{H}_K} L(f(x_1), \dots, f(x_n)) + \Omega(\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}^2)f∗=argminf∈HK​​L(f(x1​),…,f(xn​))+Ω(∥f∥HK​2​) must admit a representation of the form: f∗(x)=∑i=1nαiK(x,xi)for some α1,…,αn∈Rf^*(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i K(x, x_i) \quad \text{for some } \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n \in \mathbb{R}f∗(x)=∑i=1n​αi​K(x,xi​)for some α1​,…,αn​∈R

Proof: This is a bit of a headache if you try using infinite expansions, but here is the trick: use the orthogonal decomposition of Hilbert spaces. Let U=span{K(⋅,x1),…,K(⋅,xn)}⊂HK\mathcal{U} = \text{span}\{K(\cdot, x_1), \dots, K(\cdot, x_n)\} \subset \mathcal{H}_KU=span{K(⋅,x1​),…,K(⋅,xn​)}⊂HK​ be the finite-dimensional subspace spanned by the kernel evaluations at the data points. We can decompose any function f∈HKf \in \mathcal{H}_Kf∈HK​ into a component in U\mathcal{U}U and a component orthogonal to it in U⊥\mathcal{U}^\perpU⊥: f=f∥+f⊥f = f_{\parallel} + f_{\perp}f=f∥​+f⊥​ where f∥∈Uf_{\parallel} \in \mathcal{U}f∥​∈U and f⊥∈U⊥f_{\perp} \in \mathcal{U}^\perpf⊥​∈U⊥. By the definition of U\mathcal{U}U, we have: ⟨f⊥,K(⋅,xi)⟩HK=0∀i=1,…,n\langle f_{\perp}, K(\cdot, x_i) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_K} = 0 \quad \forall i=1, \dots, n⟨f⊥​,K(⋅,xi​)⟩HK​​=0∀i=1,…,n Evaluate fff at any training point xix_ixi​ using the reproducing property: f(xi)=⟨f,K(⋅,xi)⟩HK=⟨f∥+f⊥,K(⋅,xi)⟩HK=⟨f∥,K(⋅,xi)⟩HK+⟨f⊥,K(⋅,xi)⟩HKf(x_i) = \langle f, K(\cdot, x_i) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_K} = \langle f_{\parallel} + f_{\perp}, K(\cdot, x_i) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_K} = \langle f_{\parallel}, K(\cdot, x_i) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_K} + \langle f_{\perp}, K(\cdot, x_i) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_K}f(xi​)=⟨f,K(⋅,xi​)⟩HK​​=⟨f∥​+f⊥​,K(⋅,xi​)⟩HK​​=⟨f∥​,K(⋅,xi​)⟩HK​​+⟨f⊥​,K(⋅,xi​)⟩HK​​ Since f⊥∈U⊥f_{\perp} \in \mathcal{U}^\perpf⊥​∈U⊥, the second term vanishes: f(xi)=⟨f∥,K(⋅,xi)⟩HK=f∥(xi)f(x_i) = \langle f_{\parallel}, K(\cdot, x_i) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_K} = f_{\parallel}(x_i)f(xi​)=⟨f∥​,K(⋅,xi​)⟩HK​​=f∥​(xi​) This proves that the predictions of fff and f∥f_{\parallel}f∥​ are identical at all training points, meaning: L(f(x1),…,f(xn))=L(f∥(x1),…,f∥(xn))L(f(x_1), \dots, f(x_n)) = L(f_{\parallel}(x_1), \dots, f_{\parallel}(x_n))L(f(x1​),…,f(xn​))=L(f∥​(x1​),…,f∥​(xn​)) Now examine the regularization term. By the Pythagorean theorem in Hilbert spaces, since f∥⊥f⊥f_{\parallel} \perp f_{\perp}f∥​⊥f⊥​: ∥f∥HK2=∥f∥+f⊥∥HK2=∥f∥∥HK2+∥f⊥∥HK2≥∥f∥∥HK2\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}^2 = \|f_{\parallel} + f_{\perp}\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}^2 = \|f_{\parallel}\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}^2 + \|f_{\perp}\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}^2 \ge \|f_{\parallel}\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}^2∥f∥HK​2​=∥f∥​+f⊥​∥HK​2​=∥f∥​∥HK​2​+∥f⊥​∥HK​2​≥∥f∥​∥HK​2​ Since Ω\OmegaΩ is strictly increasing: Ω(∥f∥HK2)≥Ω(∥f∥∥HK2)\Omega(\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}^2) \ge \Omega(\|f_{\parallel}\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}^2)Ω(∥f∥HK​2​)≥Ω(∥f∥​∥HK​2​) with equality holding if and only if ∥f⊥∥HK2=0  ⟺  f⊥=0\|f_{\perp}\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}^2 = 0 \iff f_{\perp} = 0∥f⊥​∥HK​2​=0⟺f⊥​=0. Thus, the objective function value for f∥f_{\parallel}f∥​ is always strictly less than or equal to that of fff. Any minimizer f∗f^*f∗ must satisfy f⊥=0f_{\perp} = 0f⊥​=0, meaning f∗∈Uf^* \in \mathcal{U}f∗∈U. Consequently, f∗f^*f∗ must lie in the span of {K(⋅,x1),…,K(⋅,xn)}\{K(\cdot, x_1), \dots, K(\cdot, x_n)\}{K(⋅,x1​),…,K(⋅,xn​)}: f∗(x)=∑i=1nαiK(x,xi)f^*(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i K(x, x_i)f∗(x)=∑i=1n​αi​K(x,xi​) This completes the proof. ■\blacksquare■

Let's Run the Numbers

Example: Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR)

Suppose we have a 1D training set {(x1,y1),(x2,y2)}={(1,2),(2,3)}\{(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)\} = \{(1, 2), (2, 3)\}{(x1​,y1​),(x2​,y2​)}={(1,2),(2,3)} and we use a linear kernel K(x,z)=xzK(x, z) = xzK(x,z)=xz. We want to find the optimal function f∗(x)f^*(x)f∗(x) that minimizes: ∑i=12(f(xi)−yi)2+λ∥f∥HK2with λ=1\sum_{i=1}^2 (f(x_i) - y_i)^2 + \lambda \|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}^2 \quad \text{with } \lambda = 1∑i=12​(f(xi​)−yi​)2+λ∥f∥HK​2​with λ=1

  1. Apply the Representer Theorem: The optimal function is f∗(x)=α1K(x,x1)+α2K(x,x2)=α1(x)+α2(2x)=(α1+2α2)xf^*(x) = \alpha_1 K(x, x_1) + \alpha_2 K(x, x_2) = \alpha_1 (x) + \alpha_2 (2x) = (\alpha_1 + 2\alpha_2)xf∗(x)=α1​K(x,x1​)+α2​K(x,x2​)=α1​(x)+α2​(2x)=(α1​+2α2​)x.

  2. Formulate the Kernel Matrix KKK: K=(K(x1,x1)K(x1,x2)K(x2,x1)K(x2,x2))=(1224)K = \begin{pmatrix} K(x_1, x_1) & K(x_1, x_2) \\ K(x_2, x_1) & K(x_2, x_2) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}K=(K(x1​,x1​)K(x2​,x1​)​K(x1​,x2​)K(x2​,x2​)​)=(12​24​)

  3. Solve for α\alphaα: The KRR objective in matrix form is (Kα−y)2+λαTKα(K\alpha - y)^2 + \lambda \alpha^T K \alpha(Kα−y)2+λαTKα. Differentiating and setting to zero yields the system: (K+λI)α=y(K + \lambda I)\alpha = y(K+λI)α=y (1+1224+1)(α1α2)=(23)  ⟹  (2225)(α1α2)=(23)\begin{pmatrix} 1+1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4+1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_1 \\ \alpha_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} \implies \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_1 \\ \alpha_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}(1+12​24+1​)(α1​α2​​)=(23​)⟹(22​25​)(α1​α2​​)=(23​) Solving this linear system: α2=13,α1=23\alpha_2 = \frac{1}{3}, \quad \alpha_1 = \frac{2}{3}α2​=31​,α1​=32​ The optimal function is: f∗(x)=(23+2(13))x=43xf^*(x) = \left(\frac{2}{3} + 2\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\right)x = \frac{4}{3}xf∗(x)=(32​+2(31​))x=34​x

ML Applications

  1. Kernel Support Vector Machines (SVM): SVMs classify non-linearly separable data by implicitly mapping them to an infinite-dimensional RKHS. By using kernels like the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel K(x,y)=exp⁡(−γ∥x−y∥2)K(x, y) = \exp(-\gamma \|x-y\|^2)K(x,y)=exp(−γ∥x−y∥2), SVMs construct a linear hyperplane classifier in the RKHS, which maps back to a non-linear decision boundary in the input space X\mathcal{X}X.
  2. Gaussian Processes (GP): GPs define a prior distribution over functions, where the covariance between any two function evaluations is determined by a positive definite kernel. Solving a GP regression problem is mathematically equivalent to Kernel Ridge Regression, with the RKHS norm acting as the log-prior in a Bayesian formulation.
  3. Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD): MMD is a kernel-based statistical test used to determine whether two probability distributions PPP and QQQ are different. It measures the distance between the mean embeddings of PPP and QQQ in the RKHS: MMD2(P,Q)=∥EX∼P[Φ(X)]−EY∼Q[Φ(Y)]∥HK2\text{MMD}^2(P, Q) = \|\mathbb{E}_{X \sim P}[\Phi(X)] - \mathbb{E}_{Y \sim Q}[\Phi(Y)]\|_{\mathcal{H}_K}^2MMD2(P,Q)=∥EX∼P​[Φ(X)]−EY∼Q​[Φ(Y)]∥HK​2​ MMD is widely used to train Generative Adversarial Networks (MMD-GANs) and to evaluate domain adaptation.
  4. Kernel PCA: Standard PCA only identifies linear principal components. Kernel PCA projects data into an RKHS first, then performs PCA on the mapped features. This allows the extraction of non-linear principal components, revealing complex topological manifolds in the data.

Gotcha: While RBF kernels are incredibly powerful, they assume the data is dense and smooth. If your input space is high-dimensional and sparse (e.g., text document vectors), the RBF kernel can suffer from the curse of dimensionality, where the distance between any two points approaches a constant, causing the kernel matrix to degenerate into the identity matrix III.

title: Scalars
description: Mathematical fields, scaling operations, and the role of scalars in machine learning.
content:
Chapter 24: Scalars

Prerequisite

  • Fields & Sets: Basic understanding of sets of numbers (e.g., real numbers R\mathbb{R}R).
  • Arithmetic Operations: Familiarity with standard algebraic rules (associativity, distributivity).

1. Conceptual Hook

In Machine Learning, we are surrounded by massive datasets represented as high-dimensional vectors, matrices, and tensors. Yet, the entire network's training and optimization are ultimately driven by the most fundamental unit of algebra: the scalar.

A scalar represents a singular, isolated magnitude that has no direction. It is the global dial of your machine learning algorithms. The final loss value L\mathcal{L}L of a model is a single scalar that sums up the network's overall error; the learning rate η\etaη is a scalar that determines how large of a step we take down the loss mountain; and the temperature TTT in LLMs is a scalar that controls the randomness of generated tokens. Every massive matrix transformation is scaled, regularized, and thresholded by these singular values.

2. Formal Definition

Mathematically, a scalar is an element of a field F\mathbb{F}F. A field is a set equipped with two binary operations, addition (+++) and multiplication (⋅\cdot⋅), that satisfies the field axioms:

  1. Closure: ∀a,b∈F\forall a, b \in \mathbb{F}∀a,b∈F, both a+b∈Fa + b \in \mathbb{F}a+b∈F and a⋅b∈Fa \cdot b \in \mathbb{F}a⋅b∈F.
  2. Associativity: ∀a,b,c∈F\forall a, b, c \in \mathbb{F}∀a,b,c∈F, a+(b+c)=(a+b)+ca + (b + c) = (a + b) + ca+(b+c)=(a+b)+c and a⋅(b⋅c)=(a⋅b)⋅ca \cdot (b \cdot c) = (a \cdot b) \cdot ca⋅(b⋅c)=(a⋅b)⋅c.
  3. Commutativity: ∀a,b∈F\forall a, b \in \mathbb{F}∀a,b∈F, a+b=b+aa + b = b + aa+b=b+a and a⋅b=b⋅aa \cdot b = b \cdot aa⋅b=b⋅a.
  4. Identity Elements:
    • Exist an additive identity 0∈F0 \in \mathbb{F}0∈F such that a+0=aa + 0 = aa+0=a for all a∈Fa \in \mathbb{F}a∈F.
    • Exist a multiplicative identity 1∈F1 \in \mathbb{F}1∈F (1≠01 \neq 01=0) such that a⋅1=aa \cdot 1 = aa⋅1=a for all a∈Fa \in \mathbb{F}a∈F.
  5. Inverse Elements:
    • ∀a∈F\forall a \in \mathbb{F}∀a∈F, there exists −a∈F-a \in \mathbb{F}−a∈F such that a+(−a)=0a + (-a) = 0a+(−a)=0.
    • ∀a∈F∖{0}\forall a \in \mathbb{F} \setminus \{0\}∀a∈F∖{0}, there exists a−1∈Fa^{-1} \in \mathbb{F}a−1∈F such that a⋅a−1=1a \cdot a^{-1} = 1a⋅a−1=1.
  6. Distributivity: ∀a,b,c∈F\forall a, b, c \in \mathbb{F}∀a,b,c∈F, a⋅(b+c)=a⋅b+a⋅ca \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b + a \cdot ca⋅(b+c)=a⋅b+a⋅c.

In machine learning, the field is almost always the field of real numbers R\mathbb{R}R or, in spectral and complex-wave analysis, the field of complex numbers C\mathbb{C}C.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Linearity of the Scaling Operator

Let VVV be a vector space over the field F\mathbb{F}F. For a fixed scalar c∈Fc \in \mathbb{F}c∈F, define the scaling map Tc:V→VT_c: V \to VTc​:V→V as: Tc(v)=c⋅v∀v∈VT_c(v) = c \cdot v \quad \forall v \in VTc​(v)=c⋅v∀v∈V We prove that TcT_cTc​ is a linear operator on VVV.

Proof: A map is a linear operator if it preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication. Let u,v∈Vu, v \in Vu,v∈V and a∈Fa \in \mathbb{F}a∈F.

  1. Additivity: Tc(u+v)=c⋅(u+v)T_c(u + v) = c \cdot (u + v)Tc​(u+v)=c⋅(u+v) Using the vector space axiom of distributivity of scalar multiplication over vector addition: c⋅(u+v)=c⋅u+c⋅v=Tc(u)+Tc(v)c \cdot (u + v) = c \cdot u + c \cdot v = T_c(u) + T_c(v)c⋅(u+v)=c⋅u+c⋅v=Tc​(u)+Tc​(v)
  2. Homogeneity: Tc(a⋅v)=c⋅(a⋅v)T_c(a \cdot v) = c \cdot (a \cdot v)Tc​(a⋅v)=c⋅(a⋅v) Using the vector space axiom of compatibility of scalar multiplication: c⋅(a⋅v)=(c⋅a)⋅vc \cdot (a \cdot v) = (c \cdot a) \cdot vc⋅(a⋅v)=(c⋅a)⋅v Since the field F\mathbb{F}F is commutative under multiplication (c⋅a=a⋅cc \cdot a = a \cdot cc⋅a=a⋅c): (c⋅a)⋅v=(a⋅c)⋅v(c \cdot a) \cdot v = (a \cdot c) \cdot v(c⋅a)⋅v=(a⋅c)⋅v Using compatibility again: (a⋅c)⋅v=a⋅(c⋅v)=a⋅Tc(v)(a \cdot c) \cdot v = a \cdot (c \cdot v) = a \cdot T_c(v)(a⋅c)⋅v=a⋅(c⋅v)=a⋅Tc​(v) Thus, TcT_cTc​ is a linear operator. ■\blacksquare■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Scaling and Vector Norms

Let c=3c = 3c=3 be a scalar in R\mathbb{R}R, and let v=[12]v = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}v=[12​] be a vector in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2.

  1. Compute Tc(v)T_c(v)Tc​(v): Tc(v)=3⋅[12]=[3⋅13⋅2]=[36]T_c(v) = 3 \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \cdot 1 \\ 3 \cdot 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}Tc​(v)=3⋅[12​]=[3⋅13⋅2​]=[36​]
  2. Compute the Euclidean Norms: ∥v∥2=12+22=5≈2.236\|v\|_2 = \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.236∥v∥2​=12+22​=5​≈2.236 ∥Tc(v)∥2=32+62=45=35≈6.708\|T_c(v)\|_2 = \sqrt{3^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5} \approx 6.708∥Tc​(v)∥2​=32+62​=45​=35​≈6.708 This verifies that scaling a vector by a scalar scales its norm by the absolute value of the scalar: ∥cv∥=∣c∣∥v∥\|cv\| = |c|\|v\|∥cv∥=∣c∣∥v∥.

Example 2: Scalar Broadcasting vs. Matrix Addition

In coding libraries (NumPy, PyTorch), adding a scalar to a matrix triggers broadcasting, which is different from matrix addition in standard linear algebra. Let scalar c=5c = 5c=5 and matrix A=(1234)A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}A=(13​24​).

  • Mathematical Matrix-Scalar Addition (Standard): Not defined, because dimensions do not match.
  • Broadcasting Addition (Code): A+c→(1234)+(5555)=(6789)A + c \to \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 5 \\ 5 & 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 7 \\ 8 & 9 \end{pmatrix}A+c→(13​24​)+(55​55​)=(68​79​)
  • Mathematical Shift (Identity Matrix Scaling): To shift the diagonal elements mathematically: A+cI2=(1234)+5(1001)=(6239)A + cI_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} + 5 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ 3 & 9 \end{pmatrix}A+cI2​=(13​24​)+5(10​01​)=(63​29​)

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Learning Rate (η\etaη): In Gradient Descent, the scalar η\etaη scales the gradient vector before updating the parameters (θnew=θold−η∇L\theta_{new} = \theta_{old} - \eta \nabla Lθnew​=θold​−η∇L). This controls the optimization step size.
  2. Softmax Temperature (TTT): A scalar T>0T > 0T>0 divides the raw logits (zzz) in classification/generation tasks: pi=exp⁡(zi/T)/∑jexp⁡(zj/T)p_i = \exp(z_i/T) / \sum_j \exp(z_j/T)pi​=exp(zi​/T)/∑j​exp(zj​/T). Adjusting this scalar controls the entropy and randomness of the output distribution.
  3. Regularization Parameter (λ\lambdaλ): In Ridge or LASSO regression, the scalar λ\lambdaλ dictates the penalty magnitude placed on the model's weights, trading off training accuracy for generalization stability.
  4. Objective Loss Value (LLL): A loss function maps high-dimensional network predictions and ground truth labels to a single scalar L∈RL \in \mathbb{R}L∈R, which acts as the starting point for backpropagation.
  5. Perceptron Bias (bbb): The scalar bias bbb is added to the weighted sum of features (wTx+bw^T x + bwTx+b) to shift the activation function's decision boundary away from the origin.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here showing a 2D coordinate grid with a vector vvv starting from the origin.

  • Show three vectors plotted on the same line:
    1. The original vector v=[1,2]Tv = [1, 2]^Tv=[1,2]T (plotted in blue).
    2. A scaled vector 2v2v2v (plotted in green, showing extension).
    3. A scaled vector −0.5v-0.5v−0.5v (plotted in red, pointing in the opposite direction and shrunk to half its length).
  • Add a dashed line along the span of vvv to emphasize that scalar multiplication changes only the length and orientation, never pushing the vector off its one-dimensional subspace.

title: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
description: Decomposing general linear maps, spectral properties of A^T A, and the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem.
content:
Chapter 25: SVD

Prerequisite

  • Inner Product Spaces: Understanding orthobases, adjoint operators, and projections.
  • Spectral Theorem: Knowing that symmetric real matrices are orthogonally diagonalizable.
  • Matrix Properties: Familiarity with positive semi-definite (PSD) matrices.

Analogy

Think of Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) as the ultimate multi-dimensional camera rig.

Suppose you have a complex 3D sculpture, and you want to capture its shape on a 2D canvas. If you place your camera randomly, the sculpture's features will squash, overlap, and get lost in perspective.

SVD is the process of finding the absolute best angles to position your camera and lighting. It analyzes the sculpture (the matrix AAA) and identifies:

  1. VVV (The Lighting Rig): The natural coordinate directions of the sculpture's structure.
  2. Σ\SigmaΣ (The Zoom Lenses): How prominent or "stretched" the features are along each of those directions.
  3. UUU (The Photo Frame): How those features map onto the final photo canvas.

Instead of a random, distorted projection, SVD systematically aligns the camera with the sculpture's primary axes of variance, capturing the maximum structural detail in the first few shots, and allowing us to discard the rest as "shadows" or noise.

The Math Link

1. The Singular Value Decomposition Theorem

Let A∈Rm×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}A∈Rm×n be a matrix of rank r≤min⁡(m,n)r \le \min(m, n)r≤min(m,n). There exist orthogonal matrices: U=[u1,…,um]∈Rm×ms.t.UTU=ImU = [u_1, \dots, u_m] \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad U^T U = I_mU=[u1​,…,um​]∈Rm×ms.t.UTU=Im​ V=[v1,…,vn]∈Rn×ns.t.VTV=InV = [v_1, \dots, v_n] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad V^T V = I_nV=[v1​,…,vn​]∈Rn×ns.t.VTV=In​ and a diagonal matrix Σ∈Rm×n\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}Σ∈Rm×n with diagonal entries σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥σr>0\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_r > 0σ1​≥σ2​≥⋯≥σr​>0 and σi=0\sigma_{i} = 0σi​=0 for i>ri > ri>r, such that: A=UΣVT=∑i=1rσiuiviTA = U \Sigma V^T = \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i u_i v_i^TA=UΣVT=∑i=1r​σi​ui​viT​ The vectors {ui}\{u_i\}{ui​} are the left-singular vectors, {vi}\{v_i\}{vi​} are the right-singular vectors, and the scalars {σi}\{\sigma_i\}{σi​} are the singular values.

2. Connection to Spectral Theory

For any matrix A∈Rm×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}A∈Rm×n:

  • The matrix ATA∈Rn×nA^T A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}ATA∈Rn×n is symmetric and positive semi-definite. Its eigenvectors are the right-singular vectors viv_ivi​, and its non-zero eigenvalues are λi=σi2\lambda_i = \sigma_i^2λi​=σi2​.
  • The matrix AAT∈Rm×mA A^T \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}AAT∈Rm×m is symmetric and positive semi-definite. Its eigenvectors are the left-singular vectors uiu_iui​, and its non-zero eigenvalues are also λi=σi2\lambda_i = \sigma_i^2λi​=σi2​.

3. Low-Rank Approximation (Eckart-Young-Mirsky Theorem)

Let Ak=∑i=1kσiuiviTA_k = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i u_i v_i^TAk​=∑i=1k​σi​ui​viT​ be the truncated SVD of AAA at rank k<rk < rk<r. The Eckart-Young-Mirsky Theorem states that AkA_kAk​ is the best rank-kkk approximation of AAA under both the spectral norm ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_2∥⋅∥2​ and the Frobenius norm ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_F∥⋅∥F​: min⁡rank(B)≤k∥A−B∥F=∥A−Ak∥F=∑i=k+1rσi2\min_{\text{rank}(B) \le k} \|A - B\|_F = \|A - A_k\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i=k+1}^r \sigma_i^2}minrank(B)≤k​∥A−B∥F​=∥A−Ak​∥F​=∑i=k+1r​σi2​​ min⁡rank(B)≤k∥A−B∥2=∥A−Ak∥2=σk+1\min_{\text{rank}(B) \le k} \|A - B\|_2 = \|A - A_k\|_2 = \sigma_{k+1}minrank(B)≤k​∥A−B∥2​=∥A−Ak​∥2​=σk+1​

Proof-Based Exercises

Exercise 1: Eigenvalues of ATAA^T AATA and AATA A^TAAT

Theorem: Prove that the non-zero eigenvalues of ATAA^T AATA and AATA A^TAAT are identical.

Proof: Let λ≠0\lambda \neq 0λ=0 be an eigenvalue of ATAA^T AATA, and let vvv be its corresponding eigenvector. By definition: (ATA)v=λv(v≠0)(A^T A)v = \lambda v \quad (v \neq 0)(ATA)v=λv(v=0) Multiply both sides of the equation from the left by AAA: A(ATA)v=A(λv)A(A^T A)v = A(\lambda v)A(ATA)v=A(λv) Since matrix multiplication is associative and λ\lambdaλ is a scalar: (AAT)(Av)=λ(Av)(A A^T)(Av) = \lambda (Av)(AAT)(Av)=λ(Av) Let u=Avu = Avu=Av. Since λ≠0\lambda \neq 0λ=0 and v≠0v \neq 0v=0, we have: (ATA)v=λv  ⟹  vTATAv=λvTv  ⟹  ∥Av∥22=λ∥v∥22(A^T A)v = \lambda v \implies v^T A^T A v = \lambda v^T v \implies \|Av\|_2^2 = \lambda \|v\|_2^2(ATA)v=λv⟹vTATAv=λvTv⟹∥Av∥22​=λ∥v∥22​ Since λ>0\lambda > 0λ>0 (as ATAA^T AATA is positive semi-definite and λ≠0\lambda \neq 0λ=0), it must be that Av≠0Av \neq 0Av=0, so u≠0u \neq 0u=0. Thus: (AAT)u=λu(A A^T)u = \lambda u(AAT)u=λu This proves that λ\lambdaλ is also an eigenvalue of AATA A^TAAT with corresponding eigenvector u=Avu = Avu=Av. By symmetry, any non-zero eigenvalue of AATA A^TAAT is also an eigenvalue of ATAA^T AATA. ■\blacksquare■

Exercise 2: Uniqueness of Right-Singular Vectors

Let A=UΣVTA = U \Sigma V^TA=UΣVT be the SVD of AAA. Prove that if all non-zero singular values of AAA are distinct (σ1>σ2>⋯>σr>0\sigma_1 > \sigma_2 > \dots > \sigma_r > 0σ1​>σ2​>⋯>σr​>0), then the right-singular vectors {v1,…,vr}\{v_1, \dots, v_r\}{v1​,…,vr​} are uniquely determined up to a sign change (±1\pm 1±1).

Proof: This is a bit of a headache if you don't use spectral theory, but here is the trick: We know that viv_ivi​ are eigenvectors of the symmetric matrix ATAA^T AATA corresponding to eigenvalues λi=σi2\lambda_i = \sigma_i^2λi​=σi2​. Since the singular values σi\sigma_iσi​ are distinct, their squares λi=σi2\lambda_i = \sigma_i^2λi​=σi2​ are also distinct. For a symmetric matrix, the eigenspace corresponding to any simple (non-repeated) eigenvalue λi\lambda_iλi​ has dimension exactly 111. Thus, any eigenvector www corresponding to λi\lambda_iλi​ must lie in the 1-dimensional subspace spanned by viv_ivi​: w=cvifor some c∈Rw = c v_i \quad \text{for some } c \in \mathbb{R}w=cvi​for some c∈R Since right-singular vectors must be normalized to unit length: ∥w∥2=1  ⟹  ∣c∣∥vi∥2=1  ⟹  ∣c∣=1  ⟹  c=±1\|w\|_2 = 1 \implies |c| \|v_i\|_2 = 1 \implies |c| = 1 \implies c = \pm 1∥w∥2​=1⟹∣c∣∥vi​∥2​=1⟹∣c∣=1⟹c=±1 Thus, w=±viw = \pm v_iw=±vi​. The right-singular vectors are uniquely determined up to their sign. ■\blacksquare■

Let's Run the Numbers

Example: SVD of a 2×12 \times 12×1 Matrix

Let A=(34)A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}A=(34​). Note that m=2,n=1m = 2, n = 1m=2,n=1.

  1. Form ATAA^T AATA: ATA=(34)(34)=[25]∈R1×1A^T A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = [25] \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 1}ATA=(3​4​)(34​)=[25]∈R1×1

  2. Compute Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of ATAA^T AATA: The single eigenvalue is λ1=25\lambda_1 = 25λ1​=25. The singular value is σ1=25=5\sigma_1 = \sqrt{25} = 5σ1​=25​=5. The eigenvector v1v_1v1​ of ATAA^T AATA must satisfy v1Tv1=1v_1^T v_1 = 1v1T​v1​=1, which gives V=[1]V = [1]V=[1]. Thus, Σ=(50)∈R2×1\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 1}Σ=(50​)∈R2×1.

  3. Compute Left-Singular Vectors (UUU): u1=1σ1Av1=15(34)[1]=(0.60.8)u_1 = \frac{1}{\sigma_1} A v_1 = \frac{1}{5} \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} [1] = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 \\ 0.8 \end{pmatrix}u1​=σ1​1​Av1​=51​(34​)[1]=(0.60.8​) We need an orthonormal basis for R2\mathbb{R}^2R2, so we must find a vector u2u_2u2​ that is orthogonal to u1u_1u1​: u2Tu1=0  ⟹  u2=(−0.80.6)u_2^T u_1 = 0 \implies u_2 = \begin{pmatrix} -0.8 \\ 0.6 \end{pmatrix}u2T​u1​=0⟹u2​=(−0.80.6​) Thus, U=(0.6−0.80.80.6)∈R2×2U = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & -0.8 \\ 0.8 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}U=(0.60.8​−0.80.6​)∈R2×2.

  4. Verify Reconstruction: UΣVT=(0.6−0.80.80.6)(50)[1]=(0.6×50.8×5)=(34)=AU \Sigma V^T = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & -0.8 \\ 0.8 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} [1] = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 \times 5 \\ 0.8 \times 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = AUΣVT=(0.60.8​−0.80.6​)(50​)[1]=(0.6×50.8×5​)=(34​)=A The reconstruction is exact. SVD has decomposed the 2×12 \times 12×1 transformation into a scaling of 555 mapping from the 1D input space VVV into the primary output direction u1u_1u1​ of the 2D space.

ML Applications

  1. Low-Rank Matrix Completion (Recommender Systems): In collaborative filtering, we have a partially observed user-item rating matrix R∈Rm×nR \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}R∈Rm×n. We assume RRR can be approximated by a low-rank matrix X=UkΣkVkTX = U_k \Sigma_k V_k^TX=Uk​Σk​VkT​ where k≪min⁡(m,n)k \ll \min(m, n)k≪min(m,n). Algorithms like Alternating Least Squares (ALS) solve this low-rank matrix completion problem, predicting unobserved ratings by learning latent user features (UkU_kUk​) and item features (VkV_kVk​).
  2. Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA): In NLP, a document collection is represented as a term-document matrix X∈Rm×nX \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}X∈Rm×n where XijX_{ij}Xij​ is the frequency of term iii in document jjj. By computing the truncated SVD X≈UkΣkVkTX \approx U_k \Sigma_k V_k^TX≈Uk​Σk​VkT​, we map terms and documents into a low-dimensional "latent semantic space." Words that appear in similar contexts are mapped to nearby vectors, allowing the discovery of latent synonyms and topics.
  3. Principal Component Analysis (PCA): PCA is traditionally implemented via SVD. For a design matrix X∈Rn×dX \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}X∈Rn×d centered to have zero column mean, SVD yields X=UΣVTX = U \Sigma V^TX=UΣVT. The columns of VVV are the principal directions, and the project representation is XV=UΣXV = U\SigmaXV=UΣ. Implementing PCA via SVD is numerically more stable than diagonalizing the covariance matrix XTXX^T XXTX directly.
  4. Image Compression and Denoising: An image represented as a matrix A∈Rm×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}A∈Rm×n is compressed by storing only Uk,Σk,VkTU_k, \Sigma_k, V_k^TUk​,Σk​,VkT​ for k≪min⁡(m,n)k \ll \min(m, n)k≪min(m,n). This reduces storage from O(mn)O(mn)O(mn) to O(k(m+n))O(k(m+n))O(k(m+n)). Similarly, denoising is performed by truncating singular values below a threshold, effectively discarding the low-energy, high-frequency components that represent random noise.

Debugging Tip: When implementing SVD in code, different libraries (e.g., NumPy's np.linalg.svd vs. SciPy's scipy.sparse.linalg.svds) return the matrices in different formats. For example, NumPy returns VTV^TVT directly as the third argument, whereas some packages return VVV. Always check the shape and verify the orthogonality condition UTU=IU^T U = IUTU=I before performing projection operations.

title: Vectors
description: High-dimensional coordinate spaces, vector algebra, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
content:
Chapter 28: Vectors

Prerequisite

  • Scalars: Understanding elements of a field F\mathbb{F}F (e.g., real numbers R\mathbb{R}R).
  • Cartesian Geometry: Familiarity with coordinate axes and plotting points in a plane.

1. Conceptual Hook

In machine learning, data is rarely represented by a single number. An image is a collection of pixels, a document is a sequence of words, and a user profile is a list of preferences and historical interactions. To manipulate these rich entities, we group individual numbers together into a vector.

A vector is not just an arrow in space; in ML, a vector represents a state or a coordinate in a high-dimensional feature landscape. By treating features as coordinates, we can translate abstract concepts into geometry. We can measure the distance between two vectors to see how similar two users are, or compute the angle between word vectors (cosine similarity) to determine semantic relationships. Moving a vector through a network is equivalent to evolving the state of our data.

2. Formal Definition

An nnn-dimensional real column vector v∈Rnv \in \mathbb{R}^nv∈Rn is an ordered list of nnn real numbers, written as: v=[v1v2⋮vn]v = \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ \vdots \\ v_n \end{bmatrix}v=​v1​v2​⋮vn​​​ where vi∈Rv_i \in \mathbb{R}vi​∈R is the iii-th component of the vector. The transpose of vvv, denoted vTv^TvT, is a row vector: vT=[v1,v2,…,vn]v^T = \begin{bmatrix} v_1, & v_2, & \dots, & v_n \end{bmatrix}vT=[v1​,​v2​,​…,​vn​​]

For any two vectors u,v∈Rnu, v \in \mathbb{R}^nu,v∈Rn and a scalar c∈Rc \in \mathbb{R}c∈R, we define two fundamental operations:

  1. Vector Addition: u+v=[u1+v1u2+v2⋮un+vn]u + v = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 + v_1 \\ u_2 + v_2 \\ \vdots \\ u_n + v_n \end{bmatrix}u+v=​u1​+v1​u2​+v2​⋮un​+vn​​​
  2. Scalar Multiplication: c⋅v=[c⋅v1c⋅v2⋮c⋅vn]c \cdot v = \begin{bmatrix} c \cdot v_1 \\ c \cdot v_2 \\ \vdots \\ c \cdot v_n \end{bmatrix}c⋅v=​c⋅v1​c⋅v2​⋮c⋅vn​​​

To measure the length or magnitude of a vector, we define the LpL_pLp​ norm for p≥1p \ge 1p≥1: ∥v∥p=(∑i=1n∣vi∣p)1/p\|v\|_p = \left( \sum_{i=1}^n |v_i|^p \right)^{1/p}∥v∥p​=(∑i=1n​∣vi​∣p)1/p The most common norm in ML is the Euclidean (L2L_2L2​) norm: ∥v∥2=∑i=1nvi2\|v\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n v_i^2}∥v∥2​=∑i=1n​vi2​​

3. Illustrative Derivation

The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality

A foundational result in vector spaces is the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality, which bounds the dot product of two vectors by the product of their Euclidean norms: ∣uTv∣≤∥u∥2∥v∥2∀u,v∈Rn|u^T v| \le \|u\|_2 \|v\|_2 \quad \forall u, v \in \mathbb{R}^n∣uTv∣≤∥u∥2​∥v∥2​∀u,v∈Rn

Proof: For any scalar t∈Rt \in \mathbb{R}t∈R, the norm of the vector u+tvu + t vu+tv must be non-negative: ∥u+tv∥22≥0\|u + t v\|_2^2 \ge 0∥u+tv∥22​≥0 Using the relationship between the norm and the dot product (∥x∥22=xTx\|x\|_2^2 = x^T x∥x∥22​=xTx): (u+tv)T(u+tv)≥0(u + t v)^T (u + t v) \ge 0(u+tv)T(u+tv)≥0 Expanding the transpose and distributing terms: uTu+2tuTv+t2vTv≥0u^T u + 2t u^T v + t^2 v^T v \ge 0uTu+2tuTv+t2vTv≥0 Substituting the norm symbols: ∥u∥22+2t(uTv)+t2∥v∥22≥0\|u\|_2^2 + 2t (u^T v) + t^2 \|v\|_2^2 \ge 0∥u∥22​+2t(uTv)+t2∥v∥22​≥0 This expression is a quadratic polynomial in ttt of the form at2+bt+c≥0a t^2 + b t + c \ge 0at2+bt+c≥0, where: a=∥v∥22,b=2(uTv),c=∥u∥22a = \|v\|_2^2, \quad b = 2(u^T v), \quad c = \|u\|_2^2a=∥v∥22​,b=2(uTv),c=∥u∥22​ For a quadratic polynomial to be non-negative for all real values of ttt, its discriminant (b2−4acb^2 - 4acb2−4ac) must be less than or equal to zero: b2−4ac≤0b^2 - 4ac \le 0b2−4ac≤0 Substitute the values of a,b,a, b,a,b, and ccc: (2(uTv))2−4∥v∥22∥u∥22≤0\left( 2(u^T v) \right)^2 - 4 \|v\|_2^2 \|u\|_2^2 \le 0(2(uTv))2−4∥v∥22​∥u∥22​≤0 4(uTv)2≤4∥u∥22∥v∥224 (u^T v)^2 \le 4 \|u\|_2^2 \|v\|_2^24(uTv)2≤4∥u∥22​∥v∥22​ Divide both sides by 444 and take the square root: ∣uTv∣≤∥u∥2∥v∥2|u^T v| \le \|u\|_2 \|v\|_2∣uTv∣≤∥u∥2​∥v∥2​ This completes the proof. ■\blacksquare■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Vector Addition and the Triangle Inequality

Let u=[34]u = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}u=[34​] and v=[12]v = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}v=[12​].

  1. Vector Addition: w=u+v=[3+14+2]=[46]w = u + v = \begin{bmatrix} 3 + 1 \\ 4 + 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}w=u+v=[3+14+2​]=[46​]
  2. Verify the Triangle Inequality (∥u+v∥2≤∥u∥2+∥v∥2\|u+v\|_2 \le \|u\|_2 + \|v\|_2∥u+v∥2​≤∥u∥2​+∥v∥2​): ∥u∥2=32+42=5\|u\|_2 = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5∥u∥2​=32+42​=5 ∥v∥2=12+22=5≈2.236\|v\|_2 = \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.236∥v∥2​=12+22​=5​≈2.236 ∥u+v∥2=42+62=52≈7.211\|u+v\|_2 = \sqrt{4^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{52} \approx 7.211∥u+v∥2​=42+62​=52​≈7.211 Since 7.211≤5+2.236=7.2367.211 \le 5 + 2.236 = 7.2367.211≤5+2.236=7.236, the triangle inequality holds.

Example 2: Cosine Similarity between Embeddings

Let two vectors representing words in a semantic space be u=[10]u = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}u=[10​] (representing "king") and v=[11]v = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}v=[11​] (representing "queen").

  1. Compute Dot Product: uTv=1⋅1+0⋅1=1u^T v = 1 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 1 = 1uTv=1⋅1+0⋅1=1
  2. Compute Norms: ∥u∥2=12+02=1\|u\|_2 = \sqrt{1^2 + 0^2} = 1∥u∥2​=12+02​=1 ∥v∥2=12+12=2≈1.414\|v\|_2 = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414∥v∥2​=12+12​=2​≈1.414
  3. Compute Cosine Similarity: cos⁡(θ)=uTv∥u∥2∥v∥2=11⋅2=12≈0.707\cos(\theta) = \frac{u^T v}{\|u\|_2 \|v\|_2} = \frac{1}{1 \cdot \sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707cos(θ)=∥u∥2​∥v∥2​uTv​=1⋅2​1​=2​1​≈0.707 This indicates a 45∘45^\circ45∘ angle of separation between the two concept vectors.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Word Embeddings: In natural language processing, words are represented as dense vectors in spaces like R300\mathbb{R}^{300}R300 or R768\mathbb{R}^{768}R768. The similarity between words is measured via the cosine similarity of their embedding vectors.
  2. Feature Representation: In tabular data, each sample is represented as a feature vector x(i)∈Rdx^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^dx(i)∈Rd, where each dimension is a numerical measurement (e.g., age, income, blood pressure) used as input for predictions.
  3. Loss Landscape Gradients: The gradient of a neural network's loss function with respect to its parameters, ∇θL\nabla_\theta L∇θ​L, is a vector pointing in the direction of the steepest ascent on the loss surface. Optimizers scale and invert this vector to update the weights.
  4. Weight Vectors: In linear classifiers (e.g., SVMs, perceptrons), the boundary between classes is a hyperplane defined by a normal weight vector www. The decision boundary is the set of points where wTx+b=0w^T x + b = 0wTx+b=0.
  5. Image Flattening: A grayscale image of size 28×2828 \times 2828×28 is represented as a matrix, but is often flattened into a single vector x∈R784x \in \mathbb{R}^{784}x∈R784 to serve as the input layer of a multi-layer perceptron.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating vector addition and subtraction in a 2D Cartesian plane:

  • Show vector u=[3,4]Tu = [3, 4]^Tu=[3,4]T and v=[1,2]Tv = [1, 2]^Tv=[1,2]T drawn as arrows from the origin.
  • Draw a parallelogram with uuu and vvv as adjacent sides. Plot the diagonal arrow representing u+v=[4,6]Tu+v = [4, 6]^Tu+v=[4,6]T using the Parallelogram Law.
  • Draw a directed line segment from the tip of vvv to the tip of uuu to visualize the vector difference u−v=[2,2]Tu - v = [2, 2]^Tu−v=[2,2]T, illustrating how vector subtraction defines the displacement vector between two states.

Chapter 26: Vector Norms (L1, L2)

Prerequisite

  • Vectors: Understanding coordinate representations of points in space.
  • Calculus basics: Familiarity with derivatives and gradients.

1. Conceptual Hook

In machine learning, we are constantly trying to balance two opposing forces: making our models fit the training data, and keeping them simple enough to generalize to new, unseen data. To control the complexity of a model, we need a mathematical ruler that can measure the "size" or "magnitude" of the model's weight parameters. This ruler is a vector norm.

A vector norm collapses a multi-dimensional vector into a single real number representing its magnitude. Depending on which ruler we choose, we get vastly different learning behaviors. The L1L_1L1​ norm (sum of absolute values) acts like a strict editor, forcing less important weights to become exactly zero, thereby selecting only the most vital features. The L2L_2L2​ norm (Euclidean distance) acts like a stabilizer, shrinking all weights smoothly and preventing any single feature from dominating the network.

2. Formal Definition

Let VVV be a vector space over a field F\mathbb{F}F (where F∈{R,C}\mathbb{F} \in \{\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{C}\}F∈{R,C}). A norm on VVV is a function ∥⋅∥:V→R\|\cdot\|: V \to \mathbb{R}∥⋅∥:V→R that satisfies the following three axioms for all u,v∈Vu, v \in Vu,v∈V and all scalars c∈Fc \in \mathbb{F}c∈F:

  1. Non-negativity and Definiteness: ∥v∥≥0∀v∈V,and∥v∥=0  ⟺  v=0\|v\| \ge 0 \quad \forall v \in V, \quad \text{and} \quad \|v\| = 0 \iff v = 0∥v∥≥0∀v∈V,and∥v∥=0⟺v=0
  2. Absolute Homogeneity: ∥c⋅v∥=∣c∣⋅∥v∥\|c \cdot v\| = |c| \cdot \|v\|∥c⋅v∥=∣c∣⋅∥v∥
  3. Triangle Inequality: ∥u+v∥≤∥u∥+∥v∥\|u + v\| \le \|u\| + \|v\|∥u+v∥≤∥u∥+∥v∥

For a coordinate vector x=[x1,…,xn]T∈Rnx = [x_1, \dots, x_n]^T \in \mathbb{R}^nx=[x1​,…,xn​]T∈Rn, the family of LpL_pLp​ norms for p≥1p \ge 1p≥1 is defined as: ∥x∥p=(∑i=1n∣xi∣p)1/p\|x\|_p = \left( \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|^p \right)^{1/p}∥x∥p​=(∑i=1n​∣xi​∣p)1/p

  • The L1L_1L1​ Norm (Manhattan or Taxicab Norm): Obtained by setting p=1p=1p=1: ∥x∥1=∑i=1n∣xi∣\|x\|_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|∥x∥1​=∑i=1n​∣xi​∣
  • The L2L_2L2​ Norm (Euclidean Norm): Obtained by setting p=2p=2p=2: ∥x∥2=∑i=1nxi2\|x\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}∥x∥2​=∑i=1n​xi2​​

3. Illustrative Derivation

Sparsity of L1L_1L1​ vs. Smoothness of L2L_2L2​

Why does the L1L_1L1​ norm produce sparse solutions (weights exactly zero) while the L2L_2L2​ norm does not? We can understand this by looking at their gradients.

Let w∈Rnw \in \mathbb{R}^nw∈Rn be the weight vector of a model.

  1. Gradient of the squared L2L_2L2​ norm: Let f2(w)=12∥w∥22=12∑i=1nwi2f_2(w) = \frac{1}{2} \|w\|_2^2 = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2f2​(w)=21​∥w∥22​=21​∑i=1n​wi2​. This function is differentiable everywhere: ∂f2∂wi=wi  ⟹  ∇w(12∥w∥22)=w\frac{\partial f_2}{\partial w_i} = w_i \implies \nabla_w \left( \frac{1}{2} \|w\|_2^2 \right) = w∂wi​∂f2​​=wi​⟹∇w​(21​∥w∥22​)=w As the weight wiw_iwi​ gets closer to zero, the gradient wiw_iwi​ also approaches zero. The update step under gradient descent becomes infinitesimally small: wi(t+1)=wi(t)−ηwi(t)=(1−η)wi(t)w_i^{(t+1)} = w_i^{(t)} - \eta w_i^{(t)} = (1 - \eta) w_i^{(t)}wi(t+1)​=wi(t)​−ηwi(t)​=(1−η)wi(t)​ This shrinks the weights exponentially toward zero but never forces them to be exactly zero.

  2. Gradient of the L1L_1L1​ norm: Let f1(w)=∥w∥1=∑i=1n∣wi∣f_1(w) = \|w\|_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n |w_i|f1​(w)=∥w∥1​=∑i=1n​∣wi​∣. This function is non-differentiable at wi=0w_i = 0wi​=0. For wi≠0w_i \neq 0wi​=0: ∂f1∂wi=sign(wi)={1if wi>0−1if wi<0\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial w_i} = \text{sign}(w_i) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } w_i > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } w_i < 0 \end{cases}∂wi​∂f1​​=sign(wi​)={1−1​if wi​>0if wi​<0​ At wi=0w_i = 0wi​=0, we must use the subgradient, which is the interval [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1]. Under gradient descent, the update step for wi≠0w_i \neq 0wi​=0 is: wi(t+1)=wi(t)−η⋅sign(wi(t))w_i^{(t+1)} = w_i^{(t)} - \eta \cdot \text{sign}(w_i^{(t)})wi(t+1)​=wi(t)​−η⋅sign(wi(t)​) Notice that the step size is constant (η\etaη) and does not shrink as wiw_iwi​ approaches zero. This constant force pushes the weight directly to zero. Once a weight hits zero, the subgradient allows it to remain exactly zero if the loss gradient is not strong enough to pull it away. This explains why L1L_1L1​ regularization performs feature selection.

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: L1L_1L1​ and L2L_2L2​ Magnitude Comparison

Let two weight vectors be w1=[304]w_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}w1​=​304​​ (sparse, one feature active) and w2=[2.52.52]w_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2.5 \\ 2.5 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}w2​=​2.52.52​​ (dense, distributed weights).

  1. Compute L1L_1L1​ Norms: ∥w1∥1=∣3∣+∣0∣+∣4∣=7\|w_1\|_1 = |3| + |0| + |4| = 7∥w1​∥1​=∣3∣+∣0∣+∣4∣=7 ∥w2∥1=∣2.5∣+∣2.5∣+∣2∣=7\|w_2\|_1 = |2.5| + |2.5| + |2| = 7∥w2​∥1​=∣2.5∣+∣2.5∣+∣2∣=7 Under L1L_1L1​, both models have the same absolute parameter magnitude.
  2. Compute L2L_2L2​ Norms: ∥w1∥2=32+02+42=25=5\|w_1\|_2 = \sqrt{3^2 + 0^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5∥w1​∥2​=32+02+42​=25​=5 ∥w2∥2=2.52+2.52+22=6.25+6.25+4=16.5≈4.06\|w_2\|_2 = \sqrt{2.5^2 + 2.5^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{6.25 + 6.25 + 4} = \sqrt{16.5} \approx 4.06∥w2​∥2​=2.52+2.52+22​=6.25+6.25+4​=16.5​≈4.06 The L2L_2L2​ norm of w1w_1w1​ is higher than w2w_2w2​. Because L2L_2L2​ squares the coordinates, it heavily penalizes large individual weight values (333 and 444), showing that sparse configurations with larger values carry a higher L2L_2L2​ penalty than distributed configurations.

Example 2: Triangle Inequality Numerical Check

Let u=[1−2]u = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}u=[1−2​] and v=[31]v = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}v=[31​]. Verify ∥u+v∥1≤∥u∥1+∥v∥1\|u+v\|_1 \le \|u\|_1 + \|v\|_1∥u+v∥1​≤∥u∥1​+∥v∥1​.

  1. Compute u+vu+vu+v: u+v=[1+3−2+1]=[4−1]u+v = \begin{bmatrix} 1+3 \\ -2+1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}u+v=[1+3−2+1​]=[4−1​]
  2. Calculate Norms: ∥u∥1=∣1∣+∣−2∣=3\|u\|_1 = |1| + |-2| = 3∥u∥1​=∣1∣+∣−2∣=3 ∥v∥1=∣3∣+∣1∣=4\|v\|_1 = |3| + |1| = 4∥v∥1​=∣3∣+∣1∣=4 ∥u+v∥1=∣4∣+∣−1∣=5\|u+v\|_1 = |4| + |-1| = 5∥u+v∥1​=∣4∣+∣−1∣=5 Since 5≤3+4=75 \le 3 + 4 = 75≤3+4=7, the triangle inequality holds.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. LASSO Regularization (L1L_1L1​ Regularization): Adding the L1L_1L1​ norm of the weights to the loss function (Llasso=Ldata+λ∥w∥1\mathcal{L}_{lasso} = \mathcal{L}_{data} + \lambda \|w\|_1Llasso​=Ldata​+λ∥w∥1​) performs automatic feature selection by forcing the weights of non-essential features to become exactly zero.
  2. Ridge Regularization (L2L_2L2​ Regularization): Adding the squared L2L_2L2​ norm of the weights (Lridge=Ldata+λ∥w∥22\mathcal{L}_{ridge} = \mathcal{L}_{data} + \lambda \|w\|_2^2Lridge​=Ldata​+λ∥w∥22​) prevents overfitting by shrinking the parameter weights towards zero, distributing the importance across features.
  3. Mean Absolute Error (MAE) Loss: A loss function defined by the L1L_1L1​ norm of the prediction error vector (e=y−y^e = y - \hat{y}e=y−y^​): MAE=1n∥e∥1\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n} \|e\|_1MAE=n1​∥e∥1​. MAE is robust to outliers because it does not square the error terms.
  4. Mean Squared Error (MSE) Loss: A loss function defined by the squared L2L_2L2​ norm of the prediction error vector: MSE=1n∥e∥22\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \|e\|_2^2MSE=n1​∥e∥22​. MSE heavily penalizes large errors and is differentiable everywhere, making it highly compatible with standard gradient descent.
  5. Cosine Similarity: The cosine of the angle between two vectors uuu and vvv is computed by dividing their dot product by the product of their L2L_2L2​ norms: Sim(u,v)=uTv∥u∥2∥v∥2\text{Sim}(u, v) = \frac{u^T v}{\|u\|_2 \|v\|_2}Sim(u,v)=∥u∥2​∥v∥2​uTv​. This normalizes the vectors to unit length, evaluating correlation independent of scale.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating the unit spheres (contours of equal norm value) for the L1L_1L1​ and L2L_2L2​ norms in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2:

  • Show a 2D Cartesian coordinate plane (w1,w2w_1, w_2w1​,w2​).
  • Plot the L1L_1L1​ Unit Ball (∣w1∣+∣w2∣=1|w_1| + |w_2| = 1∣w1​∣+∣w2​∣=1), which forms a sharp diamond shape with corners sitting directly on the axes.
  • Plot the L2L_2L2​ Unit Ball (w12+w22=1w_1^2 + w_2^2 = 1w12​+w22​=1), which forms a smooth circle.
  • Draw concentric ellipses representing the contours of a loss function L(w)\mathcal{L}(w)L(w) centered around an optimal point away from the origin.
  • Illustrate how the loss function contour first touches the L1L_1L1​ diamond at a corner (where w1=0w_1 = 0w1​=0 or w2=0w_2 = 0w2​=0), demonstrating why L1L_1L1​ induces sparsity. Contrast this with the L2L_2L2​ circle, where the loss contour touches at a smooth, non-axial point.

title: Vector Spaces
description: Abstract vector spaces, field axioms, subspaces, and closure properties in machine learning.
content:
Chapter 27: Vector Spaces

Prerequisite

  • Fields: Understanding algebraic sets (like R\mathbb{R}R) closed under standard arithmetic operations.
  • Sets and Closure: Conceptual grasp of sets and operations that stay within those sets.

1. Conceptual Hook

In machine learning, we spend our lives designing and training models that handle high-dimensional representations of images, texts, and user profiles. To perform arithmetic on these representations—to combine features, adjust weights, or search for similar items—we need a structured mathematical environment that behaves consistently. This environment is a vector space.

A vector space is a mathematical sandbox. It defines a set of objects (vectors) and a set of rules (axioms) that ensure that no matter how much we add or scale our data, we never "break" the system or escape the boundaries of our space. If we combine two word vectors or scale up a neural network's activations, the results are guaranteed to remain valid coordinates within our representation space. It provides the rigid geometry that allows algorithms like PCA, GAN latent space interpolation, and SVMs to operate safely.

2. Formal Definition

A vector space VVV over a field F\mathbb{F}F (typically R\mathbb{R}R or C\mathbb{C}C) is a set of elements called vectors, equipped with two operations:

  1. Vector Addition (+++): V×V→VV \times V \to VV×V→V mapping (u,v)↦u+v(u, v) \mapsto u + v(u,v)↦u+v.
  2. Scalar Multiplication (⋅\cdot⋅): F×V→V\mathbb{F} \times V \to VF×V→V mapping (c,v)↦c⋅v(c, v) \mapsto c \cdot v(c,v)↦c⋅v.

For VVV to be a vector space, it must satisfy the following eight axioms for all u,v,w∈Vu, v, w \in Vu,v,w∈V and all a,b∈Fa, b \in \mathbb{F}a,b∈F:

  • Axioms for Vector Addition:
    1. Associativity: u+(v+w)=(u+v)+wu + (v + w) = (u + v) + wu+(v+w)=(u+v)+w.
    2. Commutativity: u+v=v+uu + v = v + uu+v=v+u.
    3. Additive Identity: There exists an element 0∈V0 \in V0∈V such that v+0=vv + 0 = vv+0=v for all v∈Vv \in Vv∈V.
    4. Additive Inverse: For every v∈Vv \in Vv∈V, there exists −v∈V-v \in V−v∈V such that v+(−v)=0v + (-v) = 0v+(−v)=0.
  • Axioms for Scalar Multiplication: 5. Compatibility: a(bv)=(ab)va(bv) = (ab)va(bv)=(ab)v. 6. Multiplicative Identity: 1v=v1v = v1v=v, where 111 is the multiplicative identity in F\mathbb{F}F. 7. Distributivity over Scalar Addition: (a+b)v=av+bv(a + b)v = av + bv(a+b)v=av+bv. 8. Distributivity over Vector Addition: a(u+v)=au+ava(u + v) = au + ava(u+v)=au+av.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Subspace Criteria and the Intersection Theorem

A subset U⊆VU \subseteq VU⊆V is a subspace of VVV if UUU is itself a vector space over F\mathbb{F}F under the inherited operations. To prove a subset is a subspace, we use the Subspace Criterion: UUU is a subspace if and only if U≠∅U \neq \emptysetU=∅ (or 0∈U0 \in U0∈U) and UUU is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication: ∀u1,u2∈U,∀c∈F  ⟹  u1+cu2∈U\forall u_1, u_2 \in U, \forall c \in \mathbb{F} \implies u_1 + c u_2 \in U∀u1​,u2​∈U,∀c∈F⟹u1​+cu2​∈U

Theorem: Let U1U_1U1​ and U2U_2U2​ be two subspaces of a vector space VVV. Prove that their intersection U1∩U2U_1 \cap U_2U1​∩U2​ is also a subspace of VVV.

Proof: To prove U1∩U2U_1 \cap U_2U1​∩U2​ is a subspace, we must verify the three Subspace Criterion conditions:

  1. Zero Vector Containment: Since U1U_1U1​ is a subspace of VVV, the zero vector 0∈U10 \in U_10∈U1​. Since U2U_2U2​ is a subspace of VVV, the zero vector 0∈U20 \in U_20∈U2​. Thus, by definition of intersection: 0∈U1∩U20 \in U_1 \cap U_20∈U1​∩U2​
  2. Closure under Addition: Let x,y∈U1∩U2x, y \in U_1 \cap U_2x,y∈U1​∩U2​. This implies:
    • x,y∈U1  ⟹  x+y∈U1x, y \in U_1 \implies x + y \in U_1x,y∈U1​⟹x+y∈U1​ (since U1U_1U1​ is closed under addition).
    • x,y∈U2  ⟹  x+y∈U2x, y \in U_2 \implies x + y \in U_2x,y∈U2​⟹x+y∈U2​ (since U2U_2U2​ is closed under addition). Since x+yx + yx+y belongs to both U1U_1U1​ and U2U_2U2​: x+y∈U1∩U2x + y \in U_1 \cap U_2x+y∈U1​∩U2​
  3. Closure under Scalar Multiplication: Let x∈U1∩U2x \in U_1 \cap U_2x∈U1​∩U2​ and c∈Fc \in \mathbb{F}c∈F. This implies:
    • x∈U1  ⟹  c⋅x∈U1x \in U_1 \implies c \cdot x \in U_1x∈U1​⟹c⋅x∈U1​ (since U1U_1U1​ is closed under scalar multiplication).
    • x∈U2  ⟹  c⋅x∈U2x \in U_2 \implies c \cdot x \in U_2x∈U2​⟹c⋅x∈U2​ (since U2U_2U2​ is closed under scalar multiplication). Since c⋅xc \cdot xc⋅x belongs to both U1U_1U1​ and U2U_2U2​: c⋅x∈U1∩U2c \cdot x \in U_1 \cap U_2c⋅x∈U1​∩U2​ Since all three conditions are satisfied, the intersection U1∩U2U_1 \cap U_2U1​∩U2​ is a subspace of VVV. ■\blacksquare■

Gotcha: The union of two subspaces U1∪U2U_1 \cup U_2U1​∪U2​ is not generally a subspace. For example, if U1U_1U1​ is the x-axis and U2U_2U2​ is the y-axis in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2, both are subspaces. However, their union contains [1,0]T[1, 0]^T[1,0]T and [0,1]T[0, 1]^T[0,1]T, but adding them yields [1,1]T[1, 1]^T[1,1]T, which lies outside the union. Subspaces must be flat and pass through the origin; unions introduce "kinks."

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: The Vector Space Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn

The set of all ordered nnn-tuples of real numbers, Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn, forms a vector space over the field R\mathbb{R}R under coordinate-wise addition and scalar multiplication. Let u,v∈Rnu, v \in \mathbb{R}^nu,v∈Rn and c∈Rc \in \mathbb{R}c∈R.

  1. Addition: u+v=[u1+v1,…,un+vn]T∈Rnu + v = [u_1 + v_1, \dots, u_n + v_n]^T \in \mathbb{R}^nu+v=[u1​+v1​,…,un​+vn​]T∈Rn
  2. Scaling: c⋅v=[cv1,…,cvn]T∈Rnc \cdot v = [c v_1, \dots, c v_n]^T \in \mathbb{R}^nc⋅v=[cv1​,…,cvn​]T∈Rn All 8 axioms follow directly from the properties of real numbers R\mathbb{R}R.

Example 2: Non-Closure of Degree-ddd Polynomials

Let Pd\mathcal{P}_dPd​ be the set of all real polynomials of degree at most ddd. This set forms a vector space. However, the set of polynomials of degree exactly ddd does not.

  • Let f(x)=x2+2xf(x) = x^2 + 2xf(x)=x2+2x and g(x)=−x2+5g(x) = -x^2 + 5g(x)=−x2+5 be two polynomials of degree exactly 2.
  • Adding them: f(x)+g(x)=(x2−x2)+2x+5=2x+5f(x) + g(x) = (x^2 - x^2) + 2x + 5 = 2x + 5f(x)+g(x)=(x2−x2)+2x+5=2x+5
  • The resulting polynomial has degree 1, which is not in the set. The set is not closed under addition, violating the fundamental definition of a vector space.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Latent Vector Space Interpation: In generative models like VAEs or GANs, the latent space is a low-dimensional vector space. We can perform vector addition in this space to blend attributes (e.g., adding a "smiling" vector to a "neutral face" vector generates a smiling face).
  2. Word Semantic Arithmetic: Word embeddings (like Word2Vec) map words to a vector space where semantic relations are modeled as vectors. This allows linear combinations: vec("King")−vec("Man")+vec("Woman")≈vec("Queen")\text{vec("King")} - \text{vec("Man")} + \text{vec("Woman")} \approx \text{vec("Queen")}vec("King")−vec("Man")+vec("Woman")≈vec("Queen").
  3. PCA Subspaces: Principal Component Analysis project high-dimensional data onto a low-dimensional subspace U⊂RdU \subset \mathbb{R}^dU⊂Rd that maximizes variance, reducing noise and dimensions.
  4. Null Space of Linear Layers: In neural networks, the null space of a weight matrix WWW represents the subspace of inputs xxx that are completely blocked (mapped to zero): Wx=0Wx = 0Wx=0. This determines what information the layer discards.
  5. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs): Feature vectors of nodes belong to local vector spaces. The message-passing step aggregates neighbor features using vector addition, staying within the node feature vector space.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating subspaces in 3D Euclidean space R3\mathbb{R}^3R3:

  • Show a 3D coordinate frame representing the full space R3\mathbb{R}^3R3.
  • Plot a 2D flat plane passing through the origin. Label this plane as "Subspace UUU (closed under addition and scaling)."
  • Plot a second 2D flat plane that is shifted up, parallel to the first, but does not pass through the origin. Label this plane as "Not a Subspace (fails zero-vector and closure axioms)."
  • Draw two vectors inside the subspace UUU showing their sum (parallelogram rule) also lying entirely within the plane, illustrating the concept of closure.

title: Convolutional Geometry
description: Spatial transformations, output dimension formulas, cross-correlation equations, and receptive field expansion math.
content:
Chapter 114: Convolutional Geometry

Prerequisite

  • 2D Cross-Correlation: The mathematical operation of sweeping a sliding matrix window (kernel) across a 2D grid, computing the sum of element-wise products.
  • Translation Invariance: The property where a feature detector outputs the same activation regardless of where the target feature resides in the input plane.

1. Conceptual Hook

Images are extremely high-dimensional grids of raw pixel values. Feeding these directly into standard fully connected neural networks is a recipe for parameter explosion and overfitting, as it ignores the spatial structure of visual data. A Convolutional Layer solves this by imposing spatial logic (a strong inductive bias) directly onto the network's architecture.

Instead of looking at the entire image at once, the network sweeps a tiny parameter filter (or kernel) across the input, computing local dot products to extract local features such as edges, textures, and shapes.

The geometry of this operation—defined by kernel size, stride, padding, and dilation—determines how the output feature maps shrink and how the network's "Receptive Field" (its view of the input world) expands. Stacking these simple geometric operations allows deep neural networks to assemble low-level edges into high-level object concepts.

2. Formal Definition

Let X∈RH×W×Cin\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C_{in}}X∈RH×W×Cin​ be the input tensor, where H,WH, WH,W are the height and width, and CinC_{in}Cin​ is the number of input channels. Let K∈RKh×Kw×Cin×Cout\mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{K_h \times K_w \times C_{in} \times C_{out}}K∈RKh​×Kw​×Cin​×Cout​ be the kernel tensor.

2D Cross-Correlation (Convolution in ML)

For a stride of ShS_hSh​ vertically and SwS_wSw​ horizontally, the output tensor Y∈RHout×Wout×Cout\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{H_{out} \times W_{out} \times C_{out}}Y∈RHout​×Wout​×Cout​ at channel ccc and coordinate (i,j)(i, j)(i,j) is: Yi,j,c=bc+∑m=0Kh−1∑n=0Kw−1∑k=0Cin−1Xi⋅Sh+m,j⋅Sw+n,k⋅Km,n,k,c\mathbf{Y}_{i, j, c} = b_c + \sum_{m=0}^{K_h - 1} \sum_{n=0}^{K_w - 1} \sum_{k=0}^{C_{in} - 1} \mathbf{X}_{i \cdot S_h + m, \quad j \cdot S_w + n, \quad k} \cdot \mathbf{K}_{m, n, k, c}Yi,j,c​=bc​+∑m=0Kh​−1​∑n=0Kw​−1​∑k=0Cin​−1​Xi⋅Sh​+m,j⋅Sw​+n,k​⋅Km,n,k,c​ where bcb_cbc​ is the bias term for output channel ccc.

Output Dimension Formula

Given input size III, kernel size KKK, padding PPP, stride SSS, and dilation rate DDD, the output dimension OOO along that axis is: O=⌊I−(K−1)⋅D−1+2PS⌋+1O = \left\lfloor \frac{I - (K - 1) \cdot D - 1 + 2P}{S} \right\rfloor + 1O=⌊SI−(K−1)⋅D−1+2P​⌋+1

Under standard, non-dilated convolution (D=1D = 1D=1), this simplifies to: O=⌊I−K+2PS⌋+1O = \left\lfloor \frac{I - K + 2P}{S} \right\rfloor + 1O=⌊SI−K+2P​⌋+1

3. Illustrative Derivation

Derivation of Receptive Field Growth in Deep Architectures

We derive the recursive formula for the Receptive Field (RFLRF_LRFL​) of layer LLL, proving how strides and kernel sizes interact to scale the network's spatial view.

Proof: The receptive field RFLRF_LRFL​ is the physical coordinate span in the original input image that directly contributes to the value of a single pixel in the feature map of layer LLL. Let KiK_iKi​ be the kernel size and SiS_iSi​ be the stride at layer iii.

  1. Evaluate the base case (Layer 1): A single pixel in the output feature map of Layer 1 is computed directly from a K1×K1K_1 \times K_1K1​×K1​ grid of input pixels: RF1=K1RF_1 = K_1RF1​=K1​

  2. Evaluate Layer 2: A single pixel in Layer 2 is computed from a K2×K2K_2 \times K_2K2​×K2​ grid of pixels in Layer 1. The step size (or jump) between adjacent pixels in Layer 1, measured in input coordinates, is equal to the stride S1S_1S1​. Therefore, the span of K2K_2K2​ pixels in Layer 1 translates to: RF2=RF1+(K2−1)⋅S1=K1+(K2−1)⋅S1RF_2 = RF_1 + (K_2 - 1) \cdot S_1 = K_1 + (K_2 - 1) \cdot S_1RF2​=RF1​+(K2​−1)⋅S1​=K1​+(K2​−1)⋅S1​

  3. Inductive step for Layer LLL: Assume that at layer L−1L-1L−1, the receptive field is RFL−1RF_{L-1}RFL−1​. The cumulative step size (jump) of a single coordinate increment in Layer L−1L-1L−1 features, relative to the input image coordinates, is: JL−1=∏i=1L−1SiJ_{L-1} = \prod_{i=1}^{L-1} S_iJL−1​=∏i=1L−1​Si​ When we apply a kernel of size KLK_LKL​ at layer LLL, the pixels in this kernel are separated by a stride step of JL−1J_{L-1}JL−1​ input pixels. The new receptive field is: RFL=RFL−1+(KL−1)⋅JL−1RF_L = RF_{L-1} + (K_L - 1) \cdot J_{L-1}RFL​=RFL−1​+(KL​−1)⋅JL−1​ Substitute the product form of JL−1J_{L-1}JL−1​: RFL=RFL−1+(KL−1)⋅∏i=1L−1Si■RF_L = RF_{L-1} + (K_L - 1) \cdot \prod_{i=1}^{L-1} S_i \quad \blacksquareRFL​=RFL−1​+(KL​−1)⋅∏i=1L−1​Si​■

This proves that strides in early layers act as multipliers on the receptive field growth of downstream layers, allowing deep networks to rapidly capture global context.

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Output Dimension Calculation

We compute the output size of an ImageNet input image of size I=224I = 224I=224 passing through a kernel of size K=7K = 7K=7 with stride S=2S = 2S=2 and padding P=3P = 3P=3.

  1. Formulate the equation: O=⌊224−7+2(3)2⌋+1O = \left\lfloor \frac{224 - 7 + 2(3)}{2} \right\rfloor + 1O=⌊2224−7+2(3)​⌋+1
  2. Calculate the value: O=⌊217+62⌋+1=⌊2232⌋+1=111+1=112O = \left\lfloor \frac{217 + 6}{2} \right\rfloor + 1 = \left\lfloor \frac{223}{2} \right\rfloor + 1 = 111 + 1 = 112O=⌊2217+6​⌋+1=⌊2223​⌋+1=111+1=112 The resulting feature map has a dimension of 112×112112 \times 112112×112.

Example 2: Receptive Field Calculation

We compute the receptive field of a 3-layer network:

  • Layer 1: K1=3,S1=1K_1 = 3, S_1 = 1K1​=3,S1​=1.
  • Layer 2: K2=3,S2=2K_2 = 3, S_2 = 2K2​=3,S2​=2.
  • Layer 3: K3=3,S3=1K_3 = 3, S_3 = 1K3​=3,S3​=1.
  1. Calculate Layer 1 RF: RF1=K1=3RF_1 = K_1 = 3RF1​=K1​=3
  2. Calculate Layer 2 RF: RF2=RF1+(K2−1)⋅S1=3+(3−1)⋅1=5RF_2 = RF_1 + (K_2 - 1) \cdot S_1 = 3 + (3 - 1) \cdot 1 = 5RF2​=RF1​+(K2​−1)⋅S1​=3+(3−1)⋅1=5
  3. Calculate Layer 3 RF: RF3=RF2+(K3−1)⋅(S1⋅S2)=5+(3−1)⋅(1⋅2)=5+2⋅2=9RF_3 = RF_2 + (K_3 - 1) \cdot (S_1 \cdot S_2) = 5 + (3 - 1) \cdot (1 \cdot 2) = 5 + 2 \cdot 2 = 9RF3​=RF2​+(K3​−1)⋅(S1​⋅S2​)=5+(3−1)⋅(1⋅2)=5+2⋅2=9 Thus, a single pixel in Layer 3 has an effective receptive field of 9×99 \times 99×9 in the input image.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Biometric Face Identification: Deep CNNs extract features hierarchically (edges →\to→ components →\to→ faces) to match faces in datasets.
  2. Clinical MRI Lesion Detection: Convolution filters sweep scans to identify micro-textures indicative of anomalies.
  3. Self-Driving Car Vision (YOLO): Real-time bounding box systems use strided convolutional networks to detect pedestrians.
  4. Satellite Forest Analysis: Dilated convolutions (D>1D > 1D>1) capture macro-scale geological formations without losing local resolution.
  5. Generative Up-scaling (Transposed Convolution): Generator networks reconstruct low-dimensional latent vectors into high-resolution images.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating 2D convolution geometry:

  • Draw a 3D projection comparing the input, kernel, and output grids:
    • Input Map: Draw a 5×55 \times 55×5 grid of blue squares, surrounded by a dashed border of zeros to show Padding (P=1P=1P=1).
    • Kernel Window: Draw a 3×33 \times 33×3 semi-transparent yellow grid hovering over the top-left corner of the input.
    • Output Map: Draw a 3×33 \times 33×3 grid of green squares, with a projection line connecting the 3×33 \times 33×3 input region to a single cell in the output map.
  • Draw a horizontal arrow showing Stride (S=1S=1S=1) moving the kernel window.
  • Add a caption explaining that 2D convolution slides a small weight filter across an input tensor, computing local dot products to project spatial patterns into localized activation maps.
