title: Floating-Point Representation and Machine Epsilon
description: Binary representations, significand-exponent scaling, IEEE 754 precision limits, machine epsilon derivations, and underflow/overflow controls.
content:
Chapter 98: Floating-Point Representation and Machine Epsilon

Prerequisite

  • Binary Floating-Point: Storing real numbers in computers using sign, exponent, and significand (mantissa) bitfields.
  • Underflow and Overflow: Numerical errors occurring when a number is too close to zero to be represented, or exceeds the maximum representable limit.

1. Conceptual Hook

When writing machine learning code, we tend to treat real numbers as if they live on the infinite, continuous real line R\mathbb{R}R. However, computer hardware is physical and finite. It must represent numbers using a fixed set of bits. To do this, computers use floating-point arithmetic—a digital scientific notation in base-2.

This system splits a number into a sign, a significand (the significant digits), and an exponent. To cover a vast range of scales, from subatomic probabilities to astronomical dataset sizes, the spacing between representable numbers is not uniform. Instead, the gap scales with the magnitude of the number. The closer you are to zero, the denser the numbers; the further you go, the wider the gaps.

Machine Epsilon is the mathematical measure of this precision limit. It is the gap between 1.01.01.0 and the next larger representable number.

In deep learning, if your parameter updates (gradients) fall below this relative limit, the hardware rounds them to zero. The model effectively freezes, and learning stops. Understanding these floating-point limits is essential for stable, large-scale model training.

2. Formal Definition

Let F(β,p,emin,emax)\mathcal{F}(\beta, p, e_{min}, e_{max})F(β,p,emin​,emax​) be a normalized floating-point system, where:

  • β∈Z+\beta \in \mathbb{Z}^+β∈Z+ (β≥2\beta \ge 2β≥2): The radix or base of the system (typically β=2\beta = 2β=2 for digital hardware).
  • p∈Z+p \in \mathbb{Z}^+p∈Z+: The precision, representing the number of digits in the significand.
  • e∈[emin,emax]e \in [e_{min}, e_{max}]e∈[emin​,emax​]: The integer exponent range.

Any normalized floating-point number x∈Fx \in \mathcal{F}x∈F is written as: x=±(d0+d1β+d2β2+⋯+dp−1βp−1)×βe=±(∑i=0p−1diβ−i)×βex = \pm \left( d_0 + \frac{d_1}{\beta} + \frac{d_2}{\beta^2} + \dots + \frac{d_{p-1}}{\beta^{p-1}} \right) \times \beta^e = \pm \left( \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} d_i \beta^{-i} \right) \times \beta^ex=±(d0​+βd1​​+β2d2​​+⋯+βp−1dp−1​​)×βe=±(∑i=0p−1​di​β−i)×βe where di∈{0,1,…,β−1}d_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, \beta-1\}di​∈{0,1,…,β−1} and the leading digit is non-zero: d0≠0d_0 \neq 0d0​=0.

Machine Epsilon

Let fl(r):R→F\text{fl}(r): \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{F}fl(r):R→F be the rounding operator that maps a real number rrr to its nearest representable floating-point neighbor in F\mathcal{F}F. Machine Epsilon (ϵmach\epsilon_{mach}ϵmach​) is defined as the distance between 1.01.01.0 and its next larger represent not-equal-to-1.01.01.0 neighbor: ϵmach=min⁡{δ>0∣fl(1.0+δ)>1.0}\epsilon_{mach} = \min \{ \delta > 0 \mid \text{fl}(1.0 + \delta) > 1.0 \}ϵmach​=min{δ>0∣fl(1.0+δ)>1.0}

Depending on the rounding mode, the value is:

  • Rounding-to-nearest: ϵmach=12β1−p\epsilon_{mach} = \frac{1}{2} \beta^{1-p}ϵmach​=21​β1−p (often called unit roundoff uuu).
  • Rounding-by-truncation (chopping): ϵmach=β1−p\epsilon_{mach} = \beta^{1-p}ϵmach​=β1−p.

IEEE 754 Standard Formats

  • Single Precision (FP32): p=24p = 24p=24. Under truncation, ϵmach=2−23≈1.19×10−7\epsilon_{mach} = 2^{-23} \approx 1.19 \times 10^{-7}ϵmach​=2−23≈1.19×10−7.
  • Double Precision (FP64): p=53p = 53p=53. Under truncation, ϵmach=2−52≈2.22×10−16\epsilon_{mach} = 2^{-52} \approx 2.22 \times 10^{-16}ϵmach​=2−52≈2.22×10−16.
  • Half Precision (FP16): p=11p = 11p=11. Under truncation, ϵmach=2−10≈9.77×10−4\epsilon_{mach} = 2^{-10} \approx 9.77 \times 10^{-4}ϵmach​=2−10≈9.77×10−4.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Derivation of Machine Epsilon and Absolute Spacing

We derive the formula for the spacing between adjacent floating-point numbers at a given exponent scale, proving that absolute error scales with magnitude while relative error remains bounded by ϵmach\epsilon_{mach}ϵmach​.

Proof: Let x∈Fx \in \mathcal{F}x∈F be a normalized floating-point number at exponent scale eee: x=(d0.d1d2…dp−1)β×βex = (d_0 . d_1 d_2 \dots d_{p-1})_\beta \times \beta^ex=(d0​.d1​d2​…dp−1​)β​×βe The next larger representable number, xnextx_{next}xnext​, is obtained by incrementing the least significant digit (LSD) of the significand at position p−1p-1p−1 by 111: xnext=[(d0.d1d2…dp−1)β+β−(p−1)]×βex_{next} = \left[ (d_0 . d_1 d_2 \dots d_{p-1})_\beta + \beta^{-(p-1)} \right] \times \beta^exnext​=[(d0​.d1​d2​…dp−1​)β​+β−(p−1)]×βe

  1. Calculate the absolute spacing (Δx\Delta xΔx): Δx=xnext−x=β−(p−1)×βe=βe−p+1\Delta x = x_{next} - x = \beta^{-(p-1)} \times \beta^e = \beta^{e - p + 1}Δx=xnext​−x=β−(p−1)×βe=βe−p+1 This proves that the absolute gap between representable numbers is not constant; it scales exponentially with the exponent eee.

  2. Evaluate at 1.01.01.0 to find Machine Epsilon under truncation: The number 1.01.01.0 is represented as 1.000…0×β01.000\dots0 \times \beta^01.000…0×β0, meaning e=0e = 0e=0. Substituting e=0e = 0e=0 into the spacing formula yields: ϵmach=Δ(1.0)=β0−p+1=β1−p\epsilon_{mach} = \Delta(1.0) = \beta^{0 - p + 1} = \beta^{1 - p}ϵmach​=Δ(1.0)=β0−p+1=β1−p

  3. Evaluate the relative spacing: For any normalized number xxx, its magnitude is bounded below by the minimum significand value (d0=1d_0 = 1d0​=1 and all other digits zero): ∣x∣≥1.000…0×βe=βe|x| \ge 1.000\dots0 \times \beta^e = \beta^e∣x∣≥1.000…0×βe=βe The relative spacing is: Δx∣x∣≤βe−p+1βe=β1−p=ϵmach■\frac{\Delta x}{|x|} \le \frac{\beta^{e - p + 1}}{\beta^e} = \beta^{1 - p} = \epsilon_{mach} \quad \blacksquare∣x∣Δx​≤βeβe−p+1​=β1−p=ϵmach​■

This proves that while the absolute gap grows larger for larger numbers, the relative gap between adjacent numbers remains bounded by Machine Epsilon.

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Toy 4-bit Binary Floating-Point System

We construct a toy system with base β=2\beta = 2β=2 and precision p=4p = 4p=4.

  1. Calculate Machine Epsilon under truncation: ϵmach=21−4=2−3=0.125\epsilon_{mach} = 2^{1 - 4} = 2^{-3} = 0.125ϵmach​=21−4=2−3=0.125
  2. Verify the representable numbers near 1.01.01.0: The representation of 1.01.01.0 is 1.0002×20=11.000_2 \times 2^0 = 11.0002​×20=1. The next larger number is 1.0012×20=1+2−3=1.1251.001_2 \times 2^0 = 1 + 2^{-3} = 1.1251.0012​×20=1+2−3=1.125.
  3. Simulate addition underflow: Suppose we attempt to add δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05 to 1.01.01.0, using round-to-nearest: 1.0+0.05=1.051.0 + 0.05 = 1.051.0+0.05=1.05 Since 1.051.051.05 is closer to 1.01.01.0 than to 1.1251.1251.125, the rounding operator rounds it back to 1.01.01.0: fl(1.0+0.05)=1.0\text{fl}(1.0 + 0.05) = 1.0fl(1.0+0.05)=1.0 The small update is completely lost.

Example 2: FP16 vs. FP32 Machine Epsilon in GPU Calculations

Compare the machine epsilon of Half Precision (FP16) and Single Precision (FP32) under truncation.

  • FP16 (β=2,p=11\beta=2, p=11β=2,p=11): ϵmach=21−11=2−10≈9.77×10−4\epsilon_{mach} = 2^{1-11} = 2^{-10} \approx 9.77 \times 10^{-4}ϵmach​=21−11=2−10≈9.77×10−4
  • FP32 (β=2,p=24\beta=2, p=24β=2,p=24): ϵmach=21−24=2−23≈1.19×10−7\epsilon_{mach} = 2^{1-24} = 2^{-23} \approx 1.19 \times 10^{-7}ϵmach​=21−24=2−23≈1.19×10−7 FP16 has a machine epsilon roughly 800080008000 times larger than FP32. If gradient updates are smaller than ≈10−3\approx 10^{-3}≈10−3, training on FP16 will fail due to underflow, unless a loss scaling factor is applied to shift the gradients into a range with smaller gaps.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Mixed-Precision Training: Accelerating training by running matrix operations in FP16 or BF16. Since FP16 has a high machine epsilon (≈10−3\approx 10^{-3}≈10−3), gradient values can underflow to zero. We apply Loss Scaling (multiplying loss by 2S2^{S}2S) to prevent underflow.
  2. Optimizer Stabilizers: In Adam and RMSprop, the division stabilizer ϵ\epsilonϵ (usually 10−810^{-8}10−8) must be set relative to the precision. If training in FP16, a stabilizer of 10−810^{-8}10−8 is useless because it is below the format's machine epsilon; it must be bumped to 10−410^{-4}10−4 or 10−510^{-5}10−5 to prevent underflow.
  3. Log-Sum-Exp Trick: Computing softmax values (exi/∑exje^{x_i} / \sum e^{x_j}exi​/∑exj​) causes overflow for large xix_ixi​. Subtracting the maximum value (xi−max⁡(x)x_i - \max(\mathbf{x})xi​−max(x)) keeps exponent values negative and in a range where the floating-point spacing is dense.
  4. Gradient Clipping Bounds: Restricting gradient vectors to a maximum norm to prevent activations from scaling to large values where absolute floating-point gaps are huge, which would cause coarse updates.
  5. Glorot/He Weight Initializations: Setting initial weight variances so that activations are normalized around 1.01.01.0, keeping them in the region where the relative resolution of floating-point numbers is maximized.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating floating-point spacing:

  • Draw a horizontal number line representing the real numbers.
  • Place vertical tick marks representing representable floating-point numbers:
    • Make the ticks extremely dense near 000.
    • Show the spacing between ticks widening as you move away from 000.
  • At 1.01.01.0, draw a tick mark and show the gap to the next tick mark. Label this gap as ϵmach\epsilon_{mach}ϵmach​.
  • At a larger number (e.g. 10310^3103), show that the gap between representable numbers is visibly larger than at 1.01.01.0.
  • Add a callout box showing the "dead zone" [1.0,1.0+12ϵmach][1.0, 1.0 + \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_{mach}][1.0,1.0+21​ϵmach​] where any real number added to 1.01.01.0 is rounded back to 1.01.01.0, demonstrating precision loss.
  • Add a caption explaining that floating-point numbers have variable spacing, meaning absolute resolution decreases as numbers grow, though relative precision remains constant.

title: The Digital Forge: Introduction to Numerical Methods
description: Mastering the mathematical foundations of artificial intelligence.
content:
Chapter 95: The Digital Forge: Introduction to Numerical Methods

Roadmap Objective

  • To understand the limits of "Digital Perfection."
  • To outline the tools for hammering complex problems into stable approximations.
  • To bridge the gap between "A Theoretical Formula" and "Working Hardware."

1. Introduction to the Subject: The Digital Forge

Numerical Methods are the study of Computational Reality. While the other subjects gave us the "Perfect Formulas," Numerical Methods tell us how to actually run those formulas on a computer that is limited by bits and memory. It is the science of the "Close Enough."

Think about a Tailor Fixing a Zip. Your favorite jacket is stuck, and there is a "Theoretical Perfect State" where those teeth lock together perfectly. But the tailor doesn't use a laser or a mathematical formula; they use a series of "Quick Fixes"—a pull here, a slight alignment there, a bit of wax. This is the heart of Numerical Methods—it’s the Tools of the Tailor. In the "Digital Forge" of a computer, we rarely solve a problem "Exactly." The real world is too messy for a clean formula. Instead, the computer performs high-speed "Approximations." It makes a guess, checks the alignment, and adjusts until the "Zip" of the model closes with enough precision to be useful. It’s not about being "Perfect"; it’s about being "Stable" and "Fast."

2. What Topics We Will Learn: The Tools of the Forge

In the chapters ahead, we will learn how to work with the "Grit" of digital hardware. We will move from "Infinite Accuracy" to "Practical Stability":

  • Floating Point Reality (Machine Epsilon): We will learn the size of our "Digital Needle." We will see how a computer can "Ignore" tiny changes because its memory isn't infinite.
  • Root-finding (Newton's Guess): We will learn the art of the "Smart Guess." We will see how to find a solution by repeatedly "Aligning the Zip" until the error disappears.
  • Matrix Decomposition (LU and QR): We will learn how to "Break Down" a massive calculation into smaller, safer pieces. This is how a computer solves a system with millions of variables without crashing.
  • Automatic Differentiation (Autograd): We will look at the engine that calculates the "Slope" for us. We will see how the computer "Simulates" calculus by tracking every tiny change in the forge.
  • Numerical Stability (Avoiding NaN): We will learn how to prevent a "Melt-down." We will see why certain calculations lead to "Infinity" and how to add a "Safety Stitch" to prevent our model from exploding.

3. How it is Useful for Machine Learning: The Implementation

Numerical Methods are what turn "Paper Math" into "Production AI." They are the bridge to the real world.

  • Algorithm Stability (Preventing NaN): 90% of model crashes are due to "Numerical Instability." Numerical Methods teach us to use "Tricks" (like the Log-Sum-Exp) to keep our numbers within the safe range of the processor.
  • Scaling to Big Data: Numerical Methods tell us which algorithms are "Linear" and which are "Quadratic." They ensure that our model can process 1 billion data points in an hour instead of 10 years.
  • Model Quantization: We use Numerical Methods to squeeze a massive model (like Llama-3) onto a tiny mobile phone. We learn how to reduce the precision of the "Threads" without ruining the "Fabric" of the intelligence.
  • Forward and Backward Passes: The entire process of training a neural network is a giant numerical approximation. Numerical Methods provide the "Clockwork" that ensures the gradients flow correctly from start to finish.
  • Simulation and Prediction: In areas like Robotics or Weather Prediction, we use Numerical Methods to "Simulate" the future. We solve complex equations of motion step-by-step in the Digital Forge to predict where the car should turn next.

The Core Philosophy: Numerical Methods are the Art of the Smart Guess. A computer is just a very fast guesser. The Digital Forge is the process of making each guess "Smarter" than the last, hammering the solution into a shape that is reliable and computationally efficient.

title: Iterative Solvers (Conjugate Gradient)
description: Large sparse linear systems, quadratic form minimization, Krylov subspaces, A-conjugacy derivations, and preconditioning.
content:
Chapter 99: Iterative Solvers (Conjugate Gradient)

Prerequisite

  • Symmetric Positive-Definite (SPD) Matrix: A symmetric matrix A\mathbf{A}A satisfying vTAv>0\mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} > 0vTAv>0 for all non-zero vectors v\mathbf{v}v.
  • Krylov Subspace: The vector space spanned by the images of a vector under successive powers of a matrix: Kk(A,v)=span{v,Av,…,Ak−1v}\mathcal{K}_k(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{v}) = \text{span}\{\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}, \dots, \mathbf{A}^{k-1}\mathbf{v}\}Kk​(A,v)=span{v,Av,…,Ak−1v}.

1. Conceptual Hook

Solving linear systems of equations Ax=b\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}Ax=b is a core calculation in machine learning. However, when A\mathbf{A}A is a massive, sparse matrix with millions of dimensions, direct solvers (like Gaussian elimination or Cholesky decomposition) become computationally impossible. Inverting the matrix requires O(d3)O(d^3)O(d3) operations and destroys the computational efficiency of sparsity.

Standard gradient descent can approximate the solution iteratively but suffers from a "short-term memory" problem. In narrow, steep valleys, gradient descent takes steps perpendicular to the contours, leading to a slow, zig-zagging trajectory that repeats updates along previously explored directions.

The Conjugate Gradient (CG) method solves this memory problem.

Instead of taking steps along the steepest descent direction, CG generates a sequence of search directions that are mutually orthogonal with respect to the matrix A\mathbf{A}A (called A\mathbf{A}A-conjugate directions). This geometric constraint guarantees that the minimization achieved along one search direction is never undone by subsequent updates. As a result, the algorithm eliminates redundant updates, guaranteeing convergence to the exact solution of a ddd-dimensional linear system in at most ddd steps.

2. Formal Definition

We wish to solve the linear system: Ax=b\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}Ax=b where A∈Rd×d\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}A∈Rd×d is a symmetric, positive-definite (SPD) matrix. Solving this system is mathematically equivalent to locating the unique global minimizer of the strictly convex quadratic function: f(x)=12xTAx−bTxf(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}^T \mathbf{x}f(x)=21​xTAx−bTx

A-Conjugacy

Two non-zero vectors pi,pj∈Rd\mathbf{p}_i, \mathbf{p}_j \in \mathbb{R}^dpi​,pj​∈Rd are defined as A\mathbf{A}A-conjugate (or A\mathbf{A}A-orthogonal) if: piTApj=0∀i≠j\mathbf{p}_i^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}_j = 0 \quad \forall i \neq jpiT​Apj​=0∀i=j

The Conjugate Gradient Algorithm

Starting from an initial guess x(0)\mathbf{x}^{(0)}x(0), we compute the initial residual (which is the negative gradient of fff): r(0)=b−Ax(0)\mathbf{r}^{(0)} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}^{(0)}r(0)=b−Ax(0) and set the initial search direction: p(0)=r(0)\mathbf{p}^{(0)} = \mathbf{r}^{(0)}p(0)=r(0)

For iteration steps k=0,1,2,…k = 0, 1, 2, \dotsk=0,1,2,…:

  1. Calculate Primal Step Size (αk\alpha_kαk​): Minimize f(x(k)+αkp(k))f\left(\mathbf{x}^{(k)} + \alpha_k \mathbf{p}^{(k)}\right)f(x(k)+αk​p(k)) along the direction p(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)}p(k): αk=r(k)Tr(k)p(k)TAp(k)\alpha_k = \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(k)T} \mathbf{r}^{(k)}}{\mathbf{p}^{(k)T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(k)}}αk​=p(k)TAp(k)r(k)Tr(k)​
  2. Update Primal State Vector: x(k+1)=x(k)+αkp(k)\mathbf{x}^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{x}^{(k)} + \alpha_k \mathbf{p}^{(k)}x(k+1)=x(k)+αk​p(k)
  3. Update Residual Vector: r(k+1)=r(k)−αkAp(k)\mathbf{r}^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{r}^{(k)} - \alpha_k \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}r(k+1)=r(k)−αk​Ap(k) If ∥r(k+1)∥2<tolerance\|\mathbf{r}^{(k+1)}\|_2 < \text{tolerance}∥r(k+1)∥2​<tolerance, terminate.
  4. Calculate Conjugacy Coefficient (βk\beta_kβk​): Using the Fletcher-Reeves formula to enforce A\mathbf{A}A-conjugacy: βk=r(k+1)Tr(k+1)r(k)Tr(k)\beta_k = \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(k+1)T} \mathbf{r}^{(k+1)}}{\mathbf{r}^{(k)T} \mathbf{r}^{(k)}}βk​=r(k)Tr(k)r(k+1)Tr(k+1)​
  5. Generate Next Conjugate Search Direction: p(k+1)=r(k+1)+βkp(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{r}^{(k+1)} + \beta_k \mathbf{p}^{(k)}p(k+1)=r(k+1)+βk​p(k)

3. Illustrative Derivation

Derivation of the Conjugate Parameter Updates

Proof: Let p(0)=r(0)=b−Ax(0)\mathbf{p}^{(0)} = \mathbf{r}^{(0)} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}^{(0)}p(0)=r(0)=b−Ax(0).

  1. Prove Residual Orthogonality (r(0)Tr(1)=0\mathbf{r}^{(0)T} \mathbf{r}^{(1)} = 0r(0)Tr(1)=0): The residual update is r(1)=r(0)−α0Ap(0)\mathbf{r}^{(1)} = \mathbf{r}^{(0)} - \alpha_0 \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}^{(0)}r(1)=r(0)−α0​Ap(0). Multiply by r(0)T\mathbf{r}^{(0)T}r(0)T: r(0)Tr(1)=r(0)T(r(0)−α0Ap(0))=r(0)Tr(0)−α0r(0)TAp(0)\mathbf{r}^{(0)T} \mathbf{r}^{(1)} = \mathbf{r}^{(0)T} \left( \mathbf{r}^{(0)} - \alpha_0 \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}^{(0)} \right) = \mathbf{r}^{(0)T} \mathbf{r}^{(0)} - \alpha_0 \mathbf{r}^{(0)T} \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}^{(0)}r(0)Tr(1)=r(0)T(r(0)−α0​Ap(0))=r(0)Tr(0)−α0​r(0)TAp(0) Substitute p(0)=r(0)\mathbf{p}^{(0)} = \mathbf{r}^{(0)}p(0)=r(0) and the step size expression α0=r(0)Tr(0)p(0)TAp(0)\alpha_0 = \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(0)T}\mathbf{r}^{(0)}}{\mathbf{p}^{(0)T}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}^{(0)}}α0​=p(0)TAp(0)r(0)Tr(0)​: r(0)Tr(1)=r(0)Tr(0)−(r(0)Tr(0)r(0)TAr(0))r(0)TAr(0)=r(0)Tr(0)−r(0)Tr(0)=0\mathbf{r}^{(0)T} \mathbf{r}^{(1)} = \mathbf{r}^{(0)T} \mathbf{r}^{(0)} - \left( \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(0)T}\mathbf{r}^{(0)}}{\mathbf{r}^{(0)T}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{r}^{(0)}} \right) \mathbf{r}^{(0)T}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{r}^{(0)} = \mathbf{r}^{(0)T} \mathbf{r}^{(0)} - \mathbf{r}^{(0)T} \mathbf{r}^{(0)} = 0r(0)Tr(1)=r(0)Tr(0)−(r(0)TAr(0)r(0)Tr(0)​)r(0)TAr(0)=r(0)Tr(0)−r(0)Tr(0)=0 The residuals are orthogonal after the first update step.

  3. Simplify the numerator expression: From r(1)=r(0)−α0Ap(0)\mathbf{r}^{(1)} = \mathbf{r}^{(0)} - \alpha_0 \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}^{(0)}r(1)=r(0)−α0​Ap(0), we rearrange terms to isolate Ap(0)\mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}^{(0)}Ap(0): Ap(0)=1α0(r(0)−r(1))\mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}^{(0)} = \frac{1}{\alpha_0} \left( \mathbf{r}^{(0)} - \mathbf{r}^{(1)} \right)Ap(0)=α0​1​(r(0)−r(1)) Substitute this into the numerator of our β0\beta_0β0​ equation: r(1)TAp(0)=1α0r(1)T(r(0)−r(1))=1α0(r(1)Tr(0)−r(1)Tr(1))\mathbf{r}^{(1)T} \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}^{(0)} = \frac{1}{\alpha_0} \mathbf{r}^{(1)T} \left( \mathbf{r}^{(0)} - \mathbf{r}^{(1)} \right) = \frac{1}{\alpha_0} \left( \mathbf{r}^{(1)T}\mathbf{r}^{(0)} - \mathbf{r}^{(1)T}\mathbf{r}^{(1)} \right)r(1)TAp(0)=α0​1​r(1)T(r(0)−r(1))=α0​1​(r(1)Tr(0)−r(1)Tr(1)) Since r(1)Tr(0)=0\mathbf{r}^{(1)T}\mathbf{r}^{(0)} = 0r(1)Tr(0)=0: r(1)TAp(0)=−r(1)Tr(1)α0\mathbf{r}^{(1)T} \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}^{(0)} = -\frac{\mathbf{r}^{(1)T}\mathbf{r}^{(1)}}{\alpha_0}r(1)TAp(0)=−α0​r(1)Tr(1)​

Assemble the final expression for β0\beta_0β0​: β0=−−r(1)Tr(1)/α0p(0)TAp(0)=r(1)Tr(1)α0p(0)TAp(0)\beta_0 = -\frac{-\mathbf{r}^{(1)T}\mathbf{r}^{(1)} / \alpha_0}{\mathbf{p}^{(0)T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(0)}} = \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(1)T}\mathbf{r}^{(1)}}{\alpha_0 \mathbf{p}^{(0)T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(0)}}β0​=−p(0)TAp(0)−r(1)Tr(1)/α0​​=α0​p(0)TAp(0)r(1)Tr(1)​ Substitute α0p(0)TAp(0)=r(0)Tr(0)\alpha_0 \mathbf{p}^{(0)T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(0)} = \mathbf{r}^{(0)T} \mathbf{r}^{(0)}α0​p(0)TAp(0)=r(0)Tr(0) into the denominator: β0=r(1)Tr(1)r(0)Tr(0)■\beta_0 = \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(1)T}\mathbf{r}^{(1)}}{\mathbf{r}^{(0)T}\mathbf{r}^{(0)}} \quad \blacksquareβ0​=r(0)Tr(0)r(1)Tr(1)​■

This unrolls the recursive definition, proving how conjugacy is preserved at each step.

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: 1D Linear System

Solve the system 4x=8  ⟹  A=4,b=84x = 8 \implies A = 4, b = 84x=8⟹A=4,b=8, starting from initial guess x0=0x_0 = 0x0​=0.

  1. Calculate initial residual and search direction: r0=b−Ax0=8−4⋅0=8  ⟹  p0=8r_0 = b - A x_0 = 8 - 4 \cdot 0 = 8 \implies p_0 = 8r0​=b−Ax0​=8−4⋅0=8⟹p0​=8
  2. Calculate step size: α0=r02p0Ap0=828⋅4⋅8=64256=0.25\alpha_0 = \frac{r_0^2}{p_0 A p_0} = \frac{8^2}{8 \cdot 4 \cdot 8} = \frac{64}{256} = 0.25α0​=p0​Ap0​r02​​=8⋅4⋅882​=25664​=0.25
  3. Update parameter state: x1=x0+α0p0=0+0.25⋅8=2x_1 = x_0 + \alpha_0 p_0 = 0 + 0.25 \cdot 8 = 2x1​=x0​+α0​p0​=0+0.25⋅8=2 The algorithm converges to the exact solution x∗=2x^* = 2x∗=2 in a single iteration.

Example 2: 2D Decoupled Linear System

Solve system Ax=b\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}Ax=b where A=[2002]\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}A=[20​02​] and b=[22]\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}b=[22​], starting from x(0)=[00]T\mathbf{x}^{(0)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}^Tx(0)=[00​]T.

  1. Calculate initial residual and search direction: r(0)=[22]−[2002][00]=[22]  ⟹  p(0)=[22]\mathbf{r}^{(0)} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \implies \mathbf{p}^{(0)} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}r(0)=[22​]−[20​02​][00​]=[22​]⟹p(0)=[22​]
  2. Calculate step size: α0=r(0)Tr(0)p(0)TAp(0)=22+22[22][2002][22]=816=0.5\alpha_0 = \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(0)T}\mathbf{r}^{(0)}}{\mathbf{p}^{(0)T}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}^{(0)}} = \frac{2^2 + 2^2}{\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}} = \frac{8}{16} = 0.5α0​=p(0)TAp(0)r(0)Tr(0)​=[2​2​][20​02​][22​]22+22​=168​=0.5
  3. Update parameter state: x(1)=[00]+0.5[22]=[11]\mathbf{x}^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + 0.5 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}x(1)=[00​]+0.5[22​]=[11​] Since Ax(1)=[22]=b\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{b}Ax(1)=[22​]=b, the algorithm converges in a single step.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Hessian-Free Optimization: Deep learning optimization methods use CG to solve the Newton step equation HΔw=−∇f\mathbf{H}\Delta \mathbf{w} = -\nabla fHΔw=−∇f iteratively. This avoids the need to explicitly compute or store the massive Hessian matrix.
  2. Gaussian Process Regressions: Training GPs requires solving covariance systems (K+σ2I)α=y(K + \sigma^2 I)\boldsymbol{\alpha} = \mathbf{y}(K+σ2I)α=y. CG approximates the solution vector α\boldsymbol{\alpha}α in O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) time per iteration, bypassing the expensive O(N3)O(N^3)O(N3) matrix inversion.
  3. Linear Support Vector Machines: The dual optimization objectives of large-scale linear SVM classifiers are solved using CG iterations.
  4. Graph Laplacian Label Propagation: In semi-supervised manifold learning, CG solves the sparse linear equations used to propagate class labels across high-dimensional graph edges.
  5. Collaborative Filtering (ALS): In Alternating Least Squares recommender systems, CG computes user and item latent vector updates quickly when latent factor dimensions are high.

Chapter 100: Matrix Decompositions (LU, QR, Cholesky)

Prerequisite

  • Triangular Systems: Systems of equations where the coefficient matrix is lower or upper triangular, allowing for fast back-solving.
  • Orthonormal Vectors: Vectors of unit length that are mutually perpendicular to one another.

1. Conceptual Hook

In linear algebra, a matrix represents a complex system of linear transformations. However, working with a raw matrix directly is often computationally expensive and numerically unstable. Solving large systems of equations Ax=b\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}Ax=b or inverting massive covariance matrices requires significant processor cycles.

Matrix decomposition (or factorization) is the mathematical practice of breaking a matrix down into a product of simpler, structured matrices—specifically triangular, orthogonal, or diagonal matrices.

Think of a matrix as a complex cabinet of files. If the files are piled in a chaotic heap, finding any document requires searching the entire room. Matrix decompositions organize the heap:

  • LU Decomposition splits the matrix into lower and upper triangular folders.
  • QR Decomposition extracts orthogonal vectors, ensuring no redundant information exists.
  • Cholesky Decomposition takes advantage of symmetry, storing only "half" of the data to solve systems in half the time.

By organizing the matrix structure, we convert complex linear algebra operations into fast, sequential steps.

2. Formal Definition

1. LU Decomposition

Let A∈Rd×d\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}A∈Rd×d be a square matrix. The LU factorization of A\mathbf{A}A is: A=LU\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{U}A=LU where:

  • L∈Rd×d\mathbf{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}L∈Rd×d: A unit lower triangular matrix, meaning Lij=0L_{ij} = 0Lij​=0 for i<ji < ji<j and the diagonal entries are unit values (Lii=1L_{ii} = 1Lii​=1).
  • U∈Rd×d\mathbf{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}U∈Rd×d: An upper triangular matrix, meaning Uij=0U_{ij} = 0Uij​=0 for i>ji > ji>j.

Note on Pivoting: For numerical stability, row swaps are tracked via a permutation matrix P\mathbf{P}P, yielding: PA=LU\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{U}PA=LU

2. QR Decomposition

Let A∈Rm×d\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}A∈Rm×d be a matrix with m≥dm \ge dm≥d. The QR factorization of A\mathbf{A}A is: A=QR\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}A=QR where:

  • Q∈Rm×m\mathbf{Q} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}Q∈Rm×m: An orthogonal matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis for the column space of A\mathbf{A}A, satisfying QTQ=I\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}QTQ=I.
  • R∈Rm×d\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}R∈Rm×d: An upper triangular matrix.

3. Cholesky Decomposition

Let A∈Rd×d\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}A∈Rd×d be a symmetric, positive-definite matrix (A=AT\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}^TA=AT and wTAw>0\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w} > 0wTAw>0 for all w≠0\mathbf{w} \neq \mathbf{0}w=0). The Cholesky factorization of A\mathbf{A}A is: A=LLT\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^TA=LLT where L∈Rd×d\mathbf{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}L∈Rd×d is a lower triangular matrix with strictly positive diagonal entries (Lii>0L_{ii} > 0Lii​>0).

3. Illustrative Derivation

Derivation of Forward and Backward Substitution Algorithms

We derive how solving the linear system Ax=b\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}Ax=b via A=LU\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{U}A=LU is accomplished, proving that triangular systems reduce solving complexity from O(d3)O(d^3)O(d3) to O(d2)O(d^2)O(d2).

Proof: Let Ax=b\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}Ax=b. Substitute A=LU\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{U}A=LU: LUx=b\mathbf{L}\mathbf{U}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}LUx=b Define the intermediate vector y=Ux\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{x}y=Ux. The system splits into two triangular phases:

  1. Solve Ly=b\mathbf{L}\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}Ly=b for y\mathbf{y}y.

  2. Solve Ux=y\mathbf{U}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}Ux=y for x\mathbf{x}x.

  3. Forward Substitution Phase (Ly=b\mathbf{L}\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}Ly=b): Because L\mathbf{L}L is lower triangular:

    L_{11} & 0 & \dots & 0 \\ L_{21} & L_{22} & \dots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ L_{d1} & L_{d2} & \dots & L_{dd} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \\ \vdots \\ b_d \end{bmatrix}$$ We solve sequentially from top to bottom: $$y_1 = \frac{b_1}{L_{11}}$$ $$y_i = \frac{b_i - \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} L_{ij} y_j}{L_{ii}} \quad \text{for } i = 2, 3, \dots, d$$ The number of multiplications and subtractions at step $i$ is $i-1$. Summing operations over all $d$ rows yields: $$\text{Operations}_{Forward} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} (i-1) = \frac{d(d-1)}{2} \approx \frac{1}{2} d^2$$

  4. Backward Substitution Phase (Ux=y\mathbf{U}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}Ux=y): Because U\mathbf{U}U is upper triangular:

    U_{11} & U_{12} & \dots & U_{1d} \\ 0 & U_{22} & \dots & U_{2d} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & U_{dd} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_d \end{bmatrix}$$ We solve sequentially from bottom to top: $$x_d = \frac{y_d}{U_{dd}}$$ $$x_i = \frac{y_i - \sum_{j=i+1}^{d} U_{ij} x_j}{U_{ii}} \quad \text{for } i = d-1, d-2, \dots, 1$$ Summing operations yields: $$\text{Operations}_{Backward} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} (d-i) = \frac{d(d-1)}{2} \approx \frac{1}{2} d^2$$

  5. Calculate Total Complexity: Total Operations≈12d2+12d2=d2=O(d2)■\text{Total Operations} \approx \frac{1}{2} d^2 + \frac{1}{2} d^2 = d^2 = O(d^2) \quad \blacksquareTotal Operations≈21​d2+21​d2=d2=O(d2)■ This proves that solving a factored system takes O(d2)O(d^2)O(d2) operations, which is significantly faster than standard Gaussian elimination or direct matrix inversion, which cost O(d3)O(d^3)O(d3).

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: LU Factorization

We decompose the matrix A=[23821]\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 8 & 21 \end{bmatrix}A=[28​321​]. We set L11=1,L22=1,L12=0L_{11} = 1, L_{22} = 1, L_{12} = 0L11​=1,L22​=1,L12​=0: [23821]=[10L211][U11U120U22]=[U11U12L21U11L21U12+U22]\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 8 & 21 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ L_{21} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} U_{11} & U_{12} \\ 0 & U_{22} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} U_{11} & U_{12} \\ L_{21}U_{11} & L_{21}U_{12} + U_{22} \end{bmatrix}[28​321​]=[1L21​​01​][U11​0​U12​U22​​]=[U11​L21​U11​​U12​L21​U12​+U22​​]

  1. Solve first row: U11=2andU12=3U_{11} = 2 \quad \text{and} \quad U_{12} = 3U11​=2andU12​=3
  2. Solve second row, first column: L21U11=8  ⟹  L21⋅2=8  ⟹  L21=4L_{21} U_{11} = 8 \implies L_{21} \cdot 2 = 8 \implies L_{21} = 4L21​U11​=8⟹L21​⋅2=8⟹L21​=4
  3. Solve second row, second column: L21U12+U22=21  ⟹  4⋅3+U22=21  ⟹  U22=9L_{21} U_{12} + U_{22} = 21 \implies 4 \cdot 3 + U_{22} = 21 \implies U_{22} = 9L21​U12​+U22​=21⟹4⋅3+U22​=21⟹U22​=9 Result: L=[1041]andU=[2309]\mathbf{L} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{U} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 9 \end{bmatrix}L=[14​01​]andU=[20​39​]

Example 2: Cholesky Factorization

We decompose the symmetric, positive-definite matrix A=[4121237]\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 12 \\ 12 & 37 \end{bmatrix}A=[412​1237​]. We solve for L=[L110L21L22]\mathbf{L} = \begin{bmatrix} L_{11} & 0 \\ L_{21} & L_{22} \end{bmatrix}L=[L11​L21​​0L22​​] satisfying A=LLT\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^TA=LLT: [4121237]=[L110L21L22][L11L210L22]=[L112L11L21L21L11L212+L222]\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 12 \\ 12 & 37 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} L_{11} & 0 \\ L_{21} & L_{22} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} L_{11} & L_{21} \\ 0 & L_{22} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} L_{11}^2 & L_{11}L_{21} \\ L_{21}L_{11} & L_{21}^2 + L_{22}^2 \end{bmatrix}[412​1237​]=[L11​L21​​0L22​​][L11​0​L21​L22​​]=[L112​L21​L11​​L11​L21​L212​+L222​​]

  1. Solve first column diagonal: L112=4  ⟹  L11=2L_{11}^2 = 4 \implies L_{11} = 2L112​=4⟹L11​=2
  2. Solve first column off-diagonal: L11L21=12  ⟹  2⋅L21=12  ⟹  L21=6L_{11} L_{21} = 12 \implies 2 \cdot L_{21} = 12 \implies L_{21} = 6L11​L21​=12⟹2⋅L21​=12⟹L21​=6
  3. Solve second column diagonal: L212+L222=37  ⟹  62+L222=37  ⟹  L222=37−36=1  ⟹  L22=1L_{21}^2 + L_{22}^2 = 37 \implies 6^2 + L_{22}^2 = 37 \implies L_{22}^2 = 37 - 36 = 1 \implies L_{22} = 1L212​+L222​=37⟹62+L222​=37⟹L222​=37−36=1⟹L22​=1 Result: L=[2061]\mathbf{L} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 6 & 1 \end{bmatrix}L=[26​01​]

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Stable OLS Solutions via QR: Decomposing the feature matrix X=QR\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}X=QR allows solving for weights via Rβ=QTy\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{y}Rβ=QTy. This avoids computing the Gramian inverse (XTX)−1(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}(XTX)−1, which is numerically unstable.
  2. Gaussian Process Regression: GPs require solving covariance matrix inversions. Cholesky decomposition Σ=LLT\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^TΣ=LLT is used to solve linear systems and compute the covariance log-determinant.
  3. Newton-Raphson Optimization Step: In second-order optimizers, the Hessian matrix is factored using LU or Cholesky to compute the update direction vector Δw=−H−1∇f\Delta \mathbf{w} = -\mathbf{H}^{-1}\nabla fΔw=−H−1∇f.
  4. Latent Semantic Analysis (NLP): QR factorization is used as a preprocessing step to orthogonalize feature spaces before running singular value decompositions.
  5. State-Space Kalman Filtering: In real-time tracking, Cholesky decomposition is performed at each time step to update hidden state covariances under measurement updates.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating matrix factorization geometries:

  • Draw a central square matrix A\mathbf{A}A splitting into three pathways:
    1. LU Split: Show A\mathbf{A}A factorized into lower triangular L\mathbf{L}L (elements shaded bottom-left) and upper triangular U\mathbf{U}U (elements shaded top-right).
    2. QR Split: Show A\mathbf{A}A factorized into orthogonal Q\mathbf{Q}Q (illustrated as mutually perpendicular axis vectors) and upper triangular R\mathbf{R}R.
    3. Cholesky Split: Show symmetric A\mathbf{A}A factorized into lower triangular L\mathbf{L}L and its reflected transpose LT\mathbf{L}^TLT.
  • Add a caption explaining that matrix decompositions factorize a single complex transformation into structured, triangular, or orthogonal components, reducing computational complexity.

Chapter 101: Numerical Stability

Prerequisite

  • Machine Epsilon (ϵmach\epsilon_{mach}ϵmach​): The relative precision limit of a floating-point system.
  • Backward Stability: An algorithm is backward stable if it computes the exact solution to a slightly perturbed version of the original problem.

1. Conceptual Hook

In mathematical theory, equations behave perfectly: functions map inputs to exact outputs, and limits converge smoothly. However, when we implement these formulas on real computer hardware, we are forced to approximate infinite continuous numbers using finite, discrete bits. This introduces tiny rounding errors.

Numerical stability is the study of how these rounding errors propagate through an algorithm.

An algorithm is numerically stable if tiny rounding errors remain small and suppressed; it is unstable if the math amplifies these tiny errors into catastrophic failures—such as division-by-zero, overflows to infinity (NaN), or underflows to zero.

Think of this like negotiating a price for a house. If a one-cent rounding error in the contract causes the bank's transaction system to crash, your process is unstable. In machine learning, where we multiply millions of probabilities and compute long chains of derivatives, maintaining numerical stability is the difference between a successfully trained model and a training loop that collapses into a sea of NaN values.

2. Formal Definition

Let f:R→Rf: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}f:R→R be a mathematical function, and let f^:F→F\hat{f}: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{F}f^​:F→F be its floating-point implementation.

1. Forward Error

The forward error measures the absolute difference between the computed output and the true mathematical value: Δforward=∣f^(x)−f(x)∣\Delta_{\text{forward}} = |\hat{f}(x) - f(x)|Δforward​=∣f^​(x)−f(x)∣

2. Backward Error and Stability

The backward error is the smallest perturbation in the input that yields the computed output: Δbackward=min⁡{∣δ∣∣f(x+δ)=f^(x)}\Delta_{\text{backward}} = \min \{ |\delta| \mid f(x + \delta) = \hat{f}(x) \}Δbackward​=min{∣δ∣∣f(x+δ)=f^​(x)}

An algorithm is defined as backward stable if the relative backward error is bounded by a small multiple of the machine epsilon, independent of the input: ∣δ∣∣x∣≤Cϵmach\frac{|\delta|}{|x|} \le C \epsilon_{mach}∣x∣∣δ∣​≤Cϵmach​ where C>0C > 0C>0 is a constant.

Common Numerical Failures

  • Overflow: A computation yields a value larger than the maximum representable limit (e.g. >3.4×1038> 3.4 \times 10^{38}>3.4×1038 for FP32), causing the system to return ∞\infty∞ or NaN.
  • Underflow: A computation yields a value smaller than the minimum representable positive normal value (e.g. <1.17×10−38< 1.17 \times 10^{-38}<1.17×10−38 for FP32), causing the system to round it to exactly 0.00.00.0.
  • Catastrophic Cancellation: Subtracting two nearly identical large numbers, which cancels out their significant digits and amplifies rounding noise.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Derivation of the Log-Sum-Exp Stability Trick

We derive the mathematical reformulation of the Log-Sum-Exp (LSE) function and prove how it prevents overflow and underflow in softmax evaluations.

We wish to compute the log-sum-exp value: y=ln⁡∑i=1dexiy = \ln \sum_{i=1}^{d} e^{x_i}y=ln∑i=1d​exi​

Proof: Let xmax=max⁡jxjx_{max} = \max_{j} x_jxmax​=maxj​xj​ be the maximum element in the input vector x∈Rd\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^dx∈Rd.

  1. Incorporate xmaxx_{max}xmax​ inside the summation exponent: We multiply and divide each term by exmaxe^{x_{max}}exmax​: ∑i=1dexi=∑i=1dexi−xmax+xmax=∑i=1dexi−xmaxexmax\sum_{i=1}^{d} e^{x_i} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} e^{x_i - x_{max} + x_{max}} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} e^{x_i - x_{max}} e^{x_{max}}∑i=1d​exi​=∑i=1d​exi​−xmax​+xmax​=∑i=1d​exi​−xmax​exmax​

  2. Factor out the constant exponent term: Since exmaxe^{x_{max}}exmax​ is independent of the summation index iii, we pull it outside the sum: ∑i=1dexi=exmax∑i=1dexi−xmax\sum_{i=1}^{d} e^{x_i} = e^{x_{max}} \sum_{i=1}^{d} e^{x_i - x_{max}}∑i=1d​exi​=exmax​∑i=1d​exi​−xmax​

  3. Substitute into the logarithm and simplify: y=ln⁡(exmax∑i=1dexi−xmax)y = \ln \left( e^{x_{max}} \sum_{i=1}^{d} e^{x_i - x_{max}} \right)y=ln(exmax​∑i=1d​exi​−xmax​) Using the log identity ln⁡(ab)=ln⁡(a)+ln⁡(b)\ln(ab) = \ln(a) + \ln(b)ln(ab)=ln(a)+ln(b): y=ln⁡(exmax)+ln⁡(∑i=1dexi−xmax)y = \ln\left(e^{x_{max}}\right) + \ln\left( \sum_{i=1}^{d} e^{x_i - x_{max}} \right)y=ln(exmax​)+ln(∑i=1d​exi​−xmax​) Since ln⁡(eu)=u\ln(e^u) = uln(eu)=u: y=xmax+ln⁡(∑i=1dexi−xmax)■y = x_{max} + \ln\left( \sum_{i=1}^{d} e^{x_i - x_{max}} \right) \quad \blacksquarey=xmax​+ln(∑i=1d​exi​−xmax​)■

Stability Analysis

  1. Overflow Prevention: By definition, xi−xmax≤0x_i - x_{max} \le 0xi​−xmax​≤0 for all iii. Therefore, the exponent term exi−xmaxe^{x_i - x_{max}}exi​−xmax​ is bounded in (0,1](0, 1](0,1]. Since no exponent is positive, overflow is mathematically impossible.
  2. Underflow Prevention: For the index i∗i^*i∗ corresponding to the maximum value (xi∗=xmaxx_{i^*} = x_{max}xi∗​=xmax​), the term is exmax−xmax=e0=1e^{x_{max} - x_{max}} = e^0 = 1exmax​−xmax​=e0=1. The sum is guaranteed to be at least 1.01.01.0, preventing the log input from underflowing to zero.

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Catastrophic Cancellation

Let x=1.0000002x = 1.0000002x=1.0000002 and y=1.0000001y = 1.0000001y=1.0000001. We compute z=x−yz = x - yz=x−y on a machine with 777 decimal digits of significand precision.

  1. Represent the values in floating-point format: x^=1.000000andy^=1.000000\hat{x} = 1.000000 \quad \text{and} \quad \hat{y} = 1.000000x^=1.000000andy^​=1.000000
  2. Perform subtraction: z^=x^−y^=1.000000−1.000000=0.000000\hat{z} = \hat{x} - \hat{y} = 1.000000 - 1.000000 = 0.000000z^=x^−y^​=1.000000−1.000000=0.000000 The true difference is 0.00000010.00000010.0000001. Due to subtraction of large similar values, all significant digits are canceled, leaving zero.

Example 2: Log-Sum-Exp Computation

We evaluate the log-sum-exp value for x=[1000.0,999.0]\mathbf{x} = [1000.0, 999.0]x=[1000.0,999.0] on a system where e1000.0e^{1000.0}e1000.0 overflows.

  1. Identify the maximum value: xmax=1000.0x_{max} = 1000.0xmax​=1000.0
  2. Apply the LSE formula: y=1000.0+ln⁡(e1000.0−1000.0+e999.0−1000.0)y = 1000.0 + \ln\left( e^{1000.0 - 1000.0} + e^{999.0 - 1000.0} \right)y=1000.0+ln(e1000.0−1000.0+e999.0−1000.0) y=1000.0+ln⁡(e0+e−1)y = 1000.0 + \ln\left( e^0 + e^{-1} \right)y=1000.0+ln(e0+e−1) y=1000.0+ln⁡(1+e−1)y = 1000.0 + \ln(1 + e^{-1})y=1000.0+ln(1+e−1) Since e−1≈0.367879e^{-1} \approx 0.367879e−1≈0.367879: y=1000.0+ln⁡(1.367879)≈1000.0+0.31326=1000.31326y = 1000.0 + \ln(1.367879) \approx 1000.0 + 0.31326 = 1000.31326y=1000.0+ln(1.367879)≈1000.0+0.31326=1000.31326 The calculation completes successfully without intermediate overflows.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Softmax Activation Layers: Implementing softmax (σ(x)i=exi−xmax/∑exj−xmax\sigma(\mathbf{x})_i = e^{x_i - x_{max}} / \sum e^{x_j - x_{max}}σ(x)i​=exi​−xmax​/∑exj​−xmax​) with maximum-subtraction to prevent overflow in activations.
  2. Batch Normalization Stabilizers: Adding a small epsilon constant (e.g. ϵ=10−5\epsilon = 10^{-5}ϵ=10−5) to the mini-batch variance in the denominator (1/σ2+ϵ1 / \sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}1/σ2+ϵ​) to prevent division-by-zero.
  3. Naive Bayes Classifiers: Summing log-probabilities (∑ln⁡P(xi∣y)\sum \ln P(x_i \mid y)∑lnP(xi​∣y)) rather than multiplying raw likelihoods (∏P(xi∣y)\prod P(x_i \mid y)∏P(xi​∣y)) to prevent underflow in high-dimensional feature spaces.
  4. Deep Network Gradient Clipping: Enforcing a maximum norm cap on gradients during backpropagation to prevent exploding updates from exceeding floating-point limits.
  5. Mixed-Precision Loss Scaling: Scaling down loss values during mixed-precision training to keep small gradient updates within the representable range of FP16 formats.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating numerical stability paths:

  • Draw a flowchart comparing two calculation paths for Softmax:
    1. Path A (Unstable Path): Shows raw inputs x\mathbf{x}x entering an exponential block (exe^xex). Show a warning sign labeled "Overflow to ∞\infty∞ / Underflow to 000," resulting in NaN outputs.
    2. Path B (Stable Path): Shows a Max-Finder block extracting xmaxx_{max}xmax​. Show x−xmax\mathbf{x} - x_{max}x−xmax​ entering the exponential block, producing values in (0,1](0, 1](0,1]. Show these values dividing cleanly to output a stable probability vector.
  • Add a caption explaining that manual mathematical reformulations (like maximum subtraction) prevent intermediate values from exceeding floating-point limits, preserving precision.

Chapter 84: Adaptive Methods (Adam, RMSProp)

Prerequisite

  • Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA): A recursive statistic that estimates the mean of a sequence by weighting older samples with exponentially decaying coefficients.
  • Hadamard Product (⊙\odot⊙): The element-wise multiplication of two matrices or vectors of identical dimensions.

1. Conceptual Hook

In standard Gradient Descent, we apply a single global learning rate to update all model parameters. However, in deep neural networks, different parameters face vastly different loss landscape geometries. Some parameters are associated with dense features and receive frequent, large gradients; others are associated with sparse features and receive tiny, infrequent updates.

A global learning rate that is small enough to keep volatile parameters from oscillating and diverging will stall the learning of sparse parameters. Conversely, a learning rate large enough to push sparse parameters forward will cause volatile ones to explode.

Adaptive optimization methods (like RMSprop and Adam) solve this by giving each individual parameter its own customized learning rate.

By maintaining running estimates of the historical gradient magnitude, these optimizers automatically throttle back updates for highly volatile parameters and amplify updates for slow, steady ones. This ensures smooth, balanced convergence across all layers of a deep network.

2. Formal Definition

Let wt∈Rd\mathbf{w}_t \in \mathbb{R}^dwt​∈Rd be the parameter vector at iteration step ttt, and let gt=∇f(wt)\mathbf{g}_t = \nabla f(\mathbf{w}_t)gt​=∇f(wt​) be the gradient of the objective function.

1. RMSprop (Root Mean Square Propagation)

RMSprop restricts the accumulation of historical gradients to a recent temporal window using an exponentially decaying average of squared gradients: vt=βvt−1+(1−β)gt2\mathbf{v}_t = \beta \mathbf{v}_{t-1} + (1 - \beta) \mathbf{g}_t^2vt​=βvt−1​+(1−β)gt2​ wt+1=wt−ηvt+ϵ⊙gt\mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \mathbf{w}_t - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{\mathbf{v}_t} + \epsilon} \odot \mathbf{g}_twt+1​=wt​−vt​​+ϵη​⊙gt​ where:

  • β∈[0,1)\beta \in [0, 1)β∈[0,1): The decay rate hyperparameter (typically 0.90.90.9).
  • η>0\eta > 0η>0: The base learning rate.
  • ϵ>0\epsilon > 0ϵ>0: A tiny smoothing term to prevent division by zero (typically 10−810^{-8}10−8).
  • ⊙\odot⊙: The element-wise Hadamard product. All vector square and square-root operations are evaluated element-wise.

2. Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation)

Adam combines the properties of Polyak momentum (the first moment) and RMSprop (the second moment): mt=β1mt−1+(1−β1)gt(First Moment Estimation)\mathbf{m}_t = \beta_1 \mathbf{m}_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_1) \mathbf{g}_t \quad (\text{First Moment Estimation})mt​=β1​mt−1​+(1−β1​)gt​(First Moment Estimation) vt=β2vt−1+(1−β2)gt2(Second Moment Estimation)\mathbf{v}_t = \beta_2 \mathbf{v}_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_2) \mathbf{g}_t^2 \quad (\text{Second Moment Estimation})vt​=β2​vt−1​+(1−β2​)gt2​(Second Moment Estimation)

Bias Correction

Because mt\mathbf{m}_tmt​ and vt\mathbf{v}_tvt​ are typically initialized as zero vectors, they are biased toward zero, especially during early iterations when the decay rates β1\beta_1β1​ and β2\beta_2β2​ are close to 111. To correct this bias, we compute: m^t=mt1−β1tandv^t=vt1−β2t\hat{\mathbf{m}}_t = \frac{\mathbf{m}_t}{1 - \beta_1^t} \quad \text{and} \quad \hat{\mathbf{v}}_t = \frac{\mathbf{v}_t}{1 - \beta_2^t}m^t​=1−β1t​mt​​andv^t​=1−β2t​vt​​ where ttt in βt\beta^tβt represents the iteration step exponent.

Final Parameter Update

wt+1=wt−ηv^t+ϵ⊙m^t\mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \mathbf{w}_t - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_t} + \epsilon} \odot \hat{\mathbf{m}}_twt+1​=wt​−v^t​​+ϵη​⊙m^t​ Common default hyperparameters: β1=0.9\beta_1 = 0.9β1​=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_2 = 0.999β2​=0.999, and ϵ=10−8\epsilon = 10^{-8}ϵ=10−8.

3. Illustrative Derivation

Derivation of the First-Moment Bias Correction Formula

We prove the algebraic correction term m^t=mt1−β1t\hat{\mathbf{m}}_t = \frac{\mathbf{m}_t}{1 - \beta_1^t}m^t​=1−β1t​mt​​ under the assumption of gradient stationarity.

Proof: Let the recursive definition be mt=βmt−1+(1−β)gt\mathbf{m}_t = \beta \mathbf{m}_{t-1} + (1-\beta)\mathbf{g}_tmt​=βmt−1​+(1−β)gt​ with initialization m0=0\mathbf{m}_0 = \mathbf{0}m0​=0.

  1. Unroll the recurrence relation: m1=(1−β)g1m_1 = (1-\beta)g_1m1​=(1−β)g1​ m2=βm1+(1−β)g2=β(1−β)g1+(1−β)g2m_2 = \beta m_1 + (1-\beta)g_2 = \beta(1-\beta)g_1 + (1-\beta)g_2m2​=βm1​+(1−β)g2​=β(1−β)g1​+(1−β)g2​ m3=βm2+(1−β)g3=β2(1−β)g1+β(1−β)g2+(1−β)g3m_3 = \beta m_2 + (1-\beta)g_3 = \beta^2(1-\beta)g_1 + \beta(1-\beta)g_2 + (1-\beta)g_3m3​=βm2​+(1−β)g3​=β2(1−β)g1​+β(1−β)g2​+(1−β)g3​ By mathematical induction, for any step ttt: mt=(1−β)∑i=1tβt−igim_t = (1-\beta) \sum_{i=1}^{t} \beta^{t-i} g_imt​=(1−β)∑i=1t​βt−igi​

  2. Evaluate the expectation of both sides: We assume the true gradient distribution has a stationary mean, so E[gi]=E[gt]\mathbb{E}[g_i] = \mathbb{E}[g_t]E[gi​]=E[gt​] for all i∈{1,…,t}i \in \{1, \dots, t\}i∈{1,…,t}: E[mt]=E[(1−β)∑i=1tβt−igi]\mathbb{E}[m_t] = \mathbb{E}\left[ (1-\beta) \sum_{i=1}^{t} \beta^{t-i} g_i \right]E[mt​]=E[(1−β)∑i=1t​βt−igi​] By linearity of expectation: E[mt]=(1−β)∑i=1tβt−iE[gi]\mathbb{E}[m_t] = (1-\beta) \sum_{i=1}^{t} \beta^{t-i} \mathbb{E}[g_i]E[mt​]=(1−β)∑i=1t​βt−iE[gi​] Since E[gi]=E[gt]\mathbb{E}[g_i] = \mathbb{E}[g_t]E[gi​]=E[gt​]: E[mt]=E[gt](1−β)∑i=1tβt−i\mathbb{E}[m_t] = \mathbb{E}[g_t] (1-\beta) \sum_{i=1}^{t} \beta^{t-i}E[mt​]=E[gt​](1−β)∑i=1t​βt−i

  3. Sum the finite geometric series: Let j=t−ij = t-ij=t−i. As iii ranges from 111 to ttt, the index jjj ranges from t−1t-1t−1 down to 000: ∑i=1tβt−i=∑j=0t−1βj\sum_{i=1}^{t} \beta^{t-i} = \sum_{j=0}^{t-1} \beta^j∑i=1t​βt−i=∑j=0t−1​βj Using the sum formula for a finite geometric series: ∑j=0t−1βj=1−βt1−β\sum_{j=0}^{t-1} \beta^j = \frac{1 - \beta^t}{1 - \beta}∑j=0t−1​βj=1−β1−βt​

  4. Substitute back to isolate the true mean: E[mt]=E[gt](1−β)(1−βt1−β)=E[gt](1−βt)\mathbb{E}[m_t] = \mathbb{E}[g_t] (1-\beta) \left( \frac{1 - \beta^t}{1 - \beta} \right) = \mathbb{E}[g_t] (1 - \beta^t)E[mt​]=E[gt​](1−β)(1−β1−βt​)=E[gt​](1−βt) This shows that the raw running average expectation is biased, scaled by (1−βt)(1-\beta^t)(1−βt). To obtain an unbiased estimator m^t\hat{m}_tm^t​ whose expectation equals the true mean E[gt]\mathbb{E}[g_t]E[gt​], we divide by the scaling factor: m^t=mt1−βt■\hat{m}_t = \frac{m_t}{1 - \beta^t} \quad \blacksquarem^t​=1−βtmt​​■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Volatility Scaling in 2D (RMSprop)

We optimize a function with a steep axis (gt,1=10.0g_{t,1} = 10.0gt,1​=10.0) and a flat axis (gt,2=0.1g_{t,2} = 0.1gt,2​=0.1). Let learning rate η=0.01\eta = 0.01η=0.01, decay rate β=0.9\beta = 0.9β=0.9, and initial second moment vt−1=0v_{t-1} = 0vt−1​=0.

  1. Steep Dimension Update (gt,1=10.0g_{t,1} = 10.0gt,1​=10.0): vt,1=0.9⋅0+0.1⋅(10.0)2=10.0v_{t,1} = 0.9 \cdot 0 + 0.1 \cdot (10.0)^2 = 10.0vt,1​=0.9⋅0+0.1⋅(10.0)2=10.0 Δw1=ηvt,1⋅gt,1=0.0110.0⋅10.0=0.01⋅10.0≈0.0316\Delta w_1 = \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{v_{t,1}}} \cdot g_{t,1} = \frac{0.01}{\sqrt{10.0}} \cdot 10.0 = 0.01 \cdot \sqrt{10.0} \approx 0.0316Δw1​=vt,1​​η​⋅gt,1​=10.0​0.01​⋅10.0=0.01⋅10.0​≈0.0316
  2. Flat Dimension Update (gt,2=0.1g_{t,2} = 0.1gt,2​=0.1): vt,2=0.9⋅0+0.1⋅(0.1)2=0.001v_{t,2} = 0.9 \cdot 0 + 0.1 \cdot (0.1)^2 = 0.001vt,2​=0.9⋅0+0.1⋅(0.1)2=0.001 Δw2=ηvt,2⋅gt,2=0.010.001⋅0.1=0.0010.001=0.001≈0.0316\Delta w_2 = \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{v_{t,2}}} \cdot g_{t,2} = \frac{0.01}{\sqrt{0.001}} \cdot 0.1 = \frac{0.001}{\sqrt{0.001}} = \sqrt{0.001} \approx 0.0316Δw2​=vt,2​​η​⋅gt,2​=0.001​0.01​⋅0.1=0.001​0.001​=0.001​≈0.0316 Even though the steep gradient was 100100100 times larger than the flat gradient, RMSprop scaled their updates to the exact same size, normalizing the optimization step.

Example 2: Early Bias Correction (Adam)

We compute the bias-corrected first moment m^t\hat{m}_tm^t​ at early steps. Let g1=2.0g_1 = 2.0g1​=2.0 and g2=3.0g_2 = 3.0g2​=3.0. Set β1=0.9\beta_1 = 0.9β1​=0.9 and m0=0m_0 = 0m0​=0.

  1. Step 1: m1=0.9⋅0+0.1⋅2.0=0.2m_1 = 0.9 \cdot 0 + 0.1 \cdot 2.0 = 0.2m1​=0.9⋅0+0.1⋅2.0=0.2 m^1=m11−0.91=0.20.1=2.0\hat{m}_1 = \frac{m_1}{1 - 0.9^1} = \frac{0.2}{0.1} = 2.0m^1​=1−0.91m1​​=0.10.2​=2.0
  2. Step 2: m2=0.9⋅0.2+0.1⋅3.0=0.18+0.30=0.48m_2 = 0.9 \cdot 0.2 + 0.1 \cdot 3.0 = 0.18 + 0.30 = 0.48m2​=0.9⋅0.2+0.1⋅3.0=0.18+0.30=0.48 m^2=m21−0.92=0.481−0.81=0.480.19≈2.526\hat{m}_2 = \frac{m_2}{1 - 0.9^2} = \frac{0.48}{1 - 0.81} = \frac{0.48}{0.19} \approx 2.526m^2​=1−0.92m2​​=1−0.810.48​=0.190.48​≈2.526

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Transformer Training (NLP): Adam serves as the default optimizer for models like BERT and GPT. Because word frequencies follow a power law, gradients for rare tokens are sparse; adaptive scaling ensures these parameters receive sufficient updates.
  2. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs): Mini-max optimization in GANs creates a highly non-stationary training landscape. Adam stabilizes learning and prevents mode collapse.
  3. Speech Processing (DeepSpeech): Audio spectrogram features vary widely across frequency bands. RMSprop balances optimization steps across different spectral dimensions.
  4. Sparse Latent Recommendations: In recommendation matrix factorization, adaptive methods adjust steps for user/item parameters that appear infrequently in the dataset.
  5. Volatility Control in Reinforcement Learning: Algorithms like A3C utilize RMSprop to stabilize optimization updates against the high variance of reward signals.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here comparing optimizer paths:

  • Draw a contour plot representing a narrow 2D valley.
  • Trace three optimization paths starting from the same coordinate:
    1. SGD Path: Show it taking tiny, stalled steps along the flat valley axis.
    2. Momentum Path: Show it oscillating back and forth across the steep ravine walls before slowly heading down the floor.
    3. Adam/RMSprop Path: Show it instantly suppressing oscillations on the steep axis and accelerating straight down the flat valley floor toward the minimum.
  • Add a callout diagram illustrating the scaling penalty:
    • Volatile parameters →\to→ large historical second moment →\to→ small step size.
    • Stable parameters →\to→ small historical second moment →\to→ large step size.

content:
Chapter 85: Constrained Optimization (Lagrange, KKT)

Prerequisite

  • Gradient Vector (∇f\nabla f∇f): The vector of partial derivatives pointing along the local direction of maximum ascent.
  • Feasible Region: The set of all parameter coordinate configurations that satisfy all constraints.

1. Conceptual Hook

In machine learning, we rarely optimize in a vacuum. A model that achieves perfect training accuracy by blowing its weights up to infinity is useless. We must locate the best-performing parameter configurations subject to strict physical or regularization limits—such as bounding the norm of weight parameters (regularization), limiting model memory size (pruning), or enforcing strict margins between class boundaries (Support Vector Machines).

Constrained optimization is the mathematical framework that handles these boundaries.

If our parameters are constrained to lie along a specific line or surface, we use the Method of Lagrange Multipliers for equality constraints. When the parameters are restricted to a "fenced-in" region (such as a sphere or box), we use the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions for inequality constraints. These conditions define the math of balancing our desire to minimize loss with the reality of our constraints.

2. Formal Definition

Consider a general constrained optimization problem: min⁡w∈Rdf(w)\min_{\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d} f(\mathbf{w})minw∈Rd​f(w) subject togi(w)=0(i=1,…,m)\text{subject to} \quad g_i(\mathbf{w}) = 0 \quad (i=1, \dots, m)subject togi​(w)=0(i=1,…,m) hj(w)≤0(j=1,…,p)h_j(\mathbf{w}) \le 0 \quad (j=1, \dots, p)hj​(w)≤0(j=1,…,p) where fff is the objective function, gig_igi​ are the equality constraints, and hjh_jhj​ are the inequality constraints.

The Generalized Lagrangian

To solve this system, we define the generalized Lagrangian function L:Rd×Rm×Rp→R\mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}L:Rd×Rm×Rp→R as: L(w,λ,μ)=f(w)+∑i=1mλigi(w)+∑j=1pμjhj(w)\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}, \boldsymbol{\mu}) = f(\mathbf{w}) + \sum_{i=1}^{m} \lambda_i g_i(\mathbf{w}) + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \mu_j h_j(\mathbf{w})L(w,λ,μ)=f(w)+∑i=1m​λi​gi​(w)+∑j=1p​μj​hj​(w) where:

  • λi∈R\lambda_i \in \mathbb{R}λi​∈R: The Lagrange multipliers associated with the equality constraints.
  • μj≥0\mu_j \ge 0μj​≥0: The KKT multipliers associated with the inequality constraints.

The KKT Optimality Conditions

If w∗\mathbf{w}^*w∗ is a local minimum of the primal problem for which the constraint functions satisfy mild regularity conditions (constraint qualifications), there exist multiplier vectors λ∗\boldsymbol{\lambda}^*λ∗ and μ∗\boldsymbol{\mu}^*μ∗ such that the following four conditions hold:

  1. Stationarity (Lagrangian gradient vanishes): ∇wL(w∗,λ∗,μ∗)=∇f(w∗)+∑i=1mλi∗∇gi(w∗)+∑j=1pμj∗∇hj(w∗)=0\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^*, \boldsymbol{\lambda}^*, \boldsymbol{\mu}^*) = \nabla f(\mathbf{w}^*) + \sum_{i=1}^{m} \lambda_i^* \nabla g_i(\mathbf{w}^*) + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \mu_j^* \nabla h_j(\mathbf{w}^*) = \mathbf{0}∇w​L(w∗,λ∗,μ∗)=∇f(w∗)+∑i=1m​λi∗​∇gi​(w∗)+∑j=1p​μj∗​∇hj​(w∗)=0
  2. Primal Feasibility (constraints satisfied): gi(w∗)=0∀i∈{1,…,m}andhj(w∗)≤0∀j∈{1,…,p}g_i(\mathbf{w}^*) = 0 \quad \forall i \in \{1, \dots, m\} \quad \text{and} \quad h_j(\mathbf{w}^*) \le 0 \quad \forall j \in \{1, \dots, p\}gi​(w∗)=0∀i∈{1,…,m}andhj​(w∗)≤0∀j∈{1,…,p}
  3. Dual Feasibility (multipliers non-negative): μj∗≥0∀j∈{1,…,p}\mu_j^* \ge 0 \quad \forall j \in \{1, \dots, p\}μj∗​≥0∀j∈{1,…,p}
  4. Complementary Slackness (active/inactive constraint selector): μj∗hj(w∗)=0∀j∈{1,…,p}\mu_j^* h_j(\mathbf{w}^*) = 0 \quad \forall j \in \{1, \dots, p\}μj∗​hj​(w∗)=0∀j∈{1,…,p}

3. Illustrative Derivation

Geometric Derivation of KKT Complementary Slackness

We derive why the complementary slackness condition μ∗h(w∗)=0\mu^* h(\mathbf{w}^*) = 0μ∗h(w∗)=0 and the non-negativity of μ∗\mu^*μ∗ must hold at an optimal point.

Proof: Consider a single inequality constraint h(w)≤0h(\mathbf{w}) \le 0h(w)≤0. The optimal solution w∗\mathbf{w}^*w∗ must lie in one of two cases:

  • Case 1: The constraint is inactive at the optimum (h(w∗)<0h(\mathbf{w}^*) < 0h(w∗)<0). If h(w∗)<0h(\mathbf{w}^*) < 0h(w∗)<0, the optimum lies strictly in the interior of the feasible region. Small perturbations around w∗\mathbf{w}^*w∗ do not violate the constraint. The local constrained minimum must behave exactly like an unconstrained local minimum, requiring the gradient of the objective to vanish: ∇f(w∗)=0\nabla f(\mathbf{w}^*) = \mathbf{0}∇f(w∗)=0 Substituting this into the stationarity condition ∇f(w∗)+μ∗∇h(w∗)=0\nabla f(\mathbf{w}^*) + \mu^* \nabla h(\mathbf{w}^*) = \mathbf{0}∇f(w∗)+μ∗∇h(w∗)=0 forces: μ∗=0\mu^* = 0μ∗=0 Since h(w∗)<0h(\mathbf{w}^*) < 0h(w∗)<0 and μ∗=0\mu^* = 0μ∗=0, their product is zero: μ∗h(w∗)=0\mu^* h(\mathbf{w}^*) = 0μ∗h(w∗)=0

  • Case 2: The constraint is active at the optimum (h(w∗)=0h(\mathbf{w}^*) = 0h(w∗)=0). If h(w∗)=0h(\mathbf{w}^*) = 0h(w∗)=0, the optimum lies directly on the boundary of the feasible region. To minimize the objective function fff, we want to move along the negative gradient direction −∇f(w∗)-\nabla f(\mathbf{w}^*)−∇f(w∗). However, we cannot step outside the feasible region, which means we cannot step in the direction of increasing hhh (which is ∇h(w∗)\nabla h(\mathbf{w}^*)∇h(w∗)). At the optimal boundary point, the descent force −∇f(w∗)-\nabla f(\mathbf{w}^*)−∇f(w∗) must point directly outward into the infeasible region. Mathematically, it must align with the outward normal vector of the boundary constraint, ∇h(w∗)\nabla h(\mathbf{w}^*)∇h(w∗). Thus, there must exist a positive scalar coefficient μ∗≥0\mu^* \ge 0μ∗≥0 such that: −∇f(w∗)=μ∗∇h(w∗)-\nabla f(\mathbf{w}^*) = \mu^* \nabla h(\mathbf{w}^*)−∇f(w∗)=μ∗∇h(w∗) Rearranging terms yields: ∇f(w∗)+μ∗∇h(w∗)=0withμ∗≥0\nabla f(\mathbf{w}^*) + \mu^* \nabla h(\mathbf{w}^*) = \mathbf{0} \quad \text{with} \quad \mu^* \ge 0∇f(w∗)+μ∗∇h(w∗)=0withμ∗≥0 Since the constraint is active (h(w∗)=0h(\mathbf{w}^*) = 0h(w∗)=0), their product is zero: μ∗h(w∗)=0\mu^* h(\mathbf{w}^*) = 0μ∗h(w∗)=0

Combining both cases, we conclude that μ∗h(w∗)=0\mu^* h(\mathbf{w}^*) = 0μ∗h(w∗)=0 must always hold. This completes the geometric proof. ■\blacksquare■

Example 1: Cylindrical Bottle Volume Maximization (Equality Constraint)

  2.   3. Solve for parameters: Equate the expressions for λ\lambdaλ: rh2r+h=r2  ⟹  2h=2r+h  ⟹  h=2r\frac{r h}{2r + h} = \frac{r}{2} \implies 2h = 2r + h \implies h = 2r2r+hrh​=2r​⟹2h=2r+h⟹h=2r Substitute h=2rh = 2rh=2r into the constraint: 2πr2+2πr(2r)=6π  ⟹  6πr2=6π  ⟹  r=1,h=22\pi r^2 + 2\pi r(2r) = 6\pi \implies 6\pi r^2 = 6\pi \implies r = 1, \quad h = 22πr2+2πr(2r)=6π⟹6πr2=6π⟹r=1,h=2

Example 2: Weight Limit on Insulation Thickness (Inequality Constraint)

We minimize f(x)=(x−10)2f(x) = (x - 10)^2f(x)=(x−10)2 subject to x2≤16x^2 \le 16x2≤16 (which is x2−16≤0x^2 - 16 \le 0x2−16≤0).

  1. Formulate the Lagrangian: L(x,μ)=(x−10)2+μ(x2−16)\mathcal{L}(x, \mu) = (x - 10)^2 + \mu(x^2 - 16)L(x,μ)=(x−10)2+μ(x2−16)
  2. Apply KKT Conditions:
    • Stationarity: 2(x−10)+2μx=0  ⟹  x(1+μ)=10  ⟹  x=101+μ2(x - 10) + 2\mu x = 0 \implies x(1 + \mu) = 10 \implies x = \frac{10}{1 + \mu}2(x−10)+2μx=0⟹x(1+μ)=10⟹x=1+μ10​
    • Complementary Slackness: μ(x2−16)=0\mu(x^2 - 16) = 0μ(x2−16)=0
  3. Solve the system:
    • If μ=0\mu = 0μ=0, then x=10x = 10x=10. This violates primal feasibility since 102=100≰1610^2 = 100 \not\le 16102=100≤16.
    • Thus, we must have μ>0  ⟹  x2−16=0  ⟹  x∗=4\mu > 0 \implies x^2 - 16 = 0 \implies x^* = 4μ>0⟹x2−16=0⟹x∗=4 (excluding negative thickness).
    • Substitute x∗=4x^* = 4x∗=4 into stationarity: 4(1+μ)=10  ⟹  μ∗=1.54(1 + \mu) = 10 \implies \mu^* = 1.54(1+μ)=10⟹μ∗=1.5. Since μ∗=1.5≥0\mu^* = 1.5 \ge 0μ∗=1.5≥0, the KKT conditions are satisfied, yielding the optimal boundary thickness x∗=4x^* = 4x∗=4.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Support Vector Machines (SVM): KKT conditions are used to derive maximum-margin hyperplanes. Complementary slackness guarantees that only support vectors lying directly on the margin boundary determine weight coefficients.
  2. Regularization Bound Equivalences: Lasso and Ridge regressions are constrained optimization problems that minimize training loss subject to norm limits on the weight vectors.
  3. Memory-Constrained Network Pruning: Compressing deep neural networks for deployment on edge devices by optimizing loss subject to bounds on parameter sparsity.
  4. Wasserstein GAN Lipschitz Enforcement: Restricting the discriminator function to be 1-Lipschitz by applying gradient penalties to stabilize adversarial training.
  5. Hard Attention Image Selection: Selecting localized pixel patches in computer vision models using sparsity constraints on spatial attention masks.

Chapter 86: Convex Optimization

Prerequisite

  • Multivariate Calculus: Directional derivatives, gradients ∇f(x)\nabla f(x)∇f(x), and Hessian matrices ∇2f(x)\nabla^2 f(x)∇2f(x).
  • Symmetric Matrices: Understanding positive semi-definite (PSD) operators.
  • Set Theory: Distinguishing between convex and non-convex sets.

1. Conceptual Hook

In machine learning, training a model is essentially an optimization task. We want to find the parameter configuration that minimizes prediction error. However, optimization landscapes are often treacherous—filled with false valleys (local minima), flat plains (saddle points), and steep cliffs. If we start in the wrong spot, gradient descent can easily get stuck. Convex optimization is the gold standard because it deals with a highly cooperative geometry.

Think of convex optimization as finding the absolute lowest spot on a tightly stretched trampoline.

No matter where you place a marble on the trampoline, it will roll smoothly along the slope and settle at the exact spot where the bowling ball rests. There are no ridges or false bottoms to trap it. This trampoline is a convex objective function, and the bowling ball's resting spot is the global minimum.

If we place wooden planks under the trampoline (representing constraints), the marble will roll to the lowest allowed point resting against the planks. The mathematics of locating this constrained optimal point is governed by Lagrange Duality and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions.

2. Formal Definition

Convex Sets and Functions

A set C⊆Rn\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^nC⊆Rn is convex if for all x,y∈Cx, y \in \mathcal{C}x,y∈C and any θ∈[0,1]\theta \in [0, 1]θ∈[0,1]: θx+(1−θ)y∈C\theta x + (1 - \theta)y \in \mathcal{C}θx+(1−θ)y∈C

A function f:C→Rf: \mathcal{C} \to \mathbb{R}f:C→R is convex if its domain C\mathcal{C}C is a convex set and for all x,y∈Cx, y \in \mathcal{C}x,y∈C and θ∈[0,1]\theta \in [0, 1]θ∈[0,1]: f(θx+(1−θ)y)≤θf(x)+(1−θ)f(y)f(\theta x + (1 - \theta)y) \le \theta f(x) + (1 - \theta)f(y)f(θx+(1−θ)y)≤θf(x)+(1−θ)f(y)

If fff is twice continuously differentiable, convexity is equivalent to its Hessian matrix ∇2f(x)\nabla^2 f(x)∇2f(x) being positive semi-definite (PSD) for all x∈Cx \in \mathcal{C}x∈C: vT∇2f(x)v≥0∀v∈Rn\mathbf{v}^T \nabla^2 f(x) \mathbf{v} \ge 0 \quad \forall \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^nvT∇2f(x)v≥0∀v∈Rn

General Constrained Optimization

Consider the primal optimization problem: min⁡x∈Rnf0(x)subject tofi(x)≤0(i=1,…,m),hj(x)=0(j=1,…,r)\min_{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} f_0(x) \quad \text{subject to} \quad f_i(x) \le 0 \quad (i=1, \dots, m), \quad h_j(x) = 0 \quad (j=1, \dots, r)minx∈Rn​f0​(x)subject tofi​(x)≤0(i=1,…,m),hj​(x)=0(j=1,…,r)

We define the Lagrangian L:Rn×Rm×Rr→R\mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^r \to \mathbb{R}L:Rn×Rm×Rr→R as: L(x,λ,ν)=f0(x)+∑i=1mλifi(x)+∑j=1rνjhj(x)\mathcal{L}(x, \lambda, \nu) = f_0(x) + \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i f_i(x) + \sum_{j=1}^r \nu_j h_j(x)L(x,λ,ν)=f0​(x)+∑i=1m​λi​fi​(x)+∑j=1r​νj​hj​(x) where λi≥0\lambda_i \ge 0λi​≥0 are the Lagrange multipliers for the inequality constraints, and νj∈R\nu_j \in \mathbb{R}νj​∈R are the multipliers for the equality constraints.

The Lagrange Dual Function g:Rm×Rr→Rg: \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^r \to \mathbb{R}g:Rm×Rr→R is: g(λ,ν)=inf⁡x∈RnL(x,λ,ν)g(\lambda, \nu) = \inf_{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \mathcal{L}(x, \lambda, \nu)g(λ,ν)=infx∈Rn​L(x,λ,ν)

The dual optimization problem is: max⁡λ,νg(λ,ν)subject toλ≥0\max_{\lambda, \nu} g(\lambda, \nu) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \lambda \ge 0maxλ,ν​g(λ,ν)subject toλ≥0

Weak and Strong Duality

Let p∗p^*p∗ be the primal optimal value, and d∗d^*d∗ be the dual optimal value. Weak duality always holds: d∗≤p∗d^* \le p^*d∗≤p∗. Under Slater's Constraint Qualification (if the primal is convex and there exists a strictly feasible point), strong duality holds: d∗=p∗d^* = p^*d∗=p∗.

Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) Conditions

For any optimization problem where strong duality holds, any primal-dual optimal pair (x∗,λ∗,ν∗)(x^*, \lambda^*, \nu^*)(x∗,λ∗,ν∗) must satisfy the KKT conditions:

  1. Primal Feasibility: fi(x∗)≤0  ∀if_i(x^*) \le 0 \; \forall ifi​(x∗)≤0∀i, and hj(x∗)=0  ∀jh_j(x^*) = 0 \; \forall jhj​(x∗)=0∀j.
  2. Dual Feasibility: λi∗≥0  ∀i\lambda_i^* \ge 0 \; \forall iλi∗​≥0∀i.
  3. Complementary Slackness: λi∗fi(x∗)=0  ∀i\lambda_i^* f_i(x^*) = 0 \; \forall iλi∗​fi​(x∗)=0∀i.
  4. Stationarity: ∇xL(x∗,λ∗,ν∗)=∇f0(x∗)+∑i=1mλi∗∇fi(x∗)+∑j=1rνj∗∇hj(x∗)=0\nabla_x \mathcal{L}(x^*, \lambda^*, \nu^*) = \nabla f_0(x^*) + \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i^* \nabla f_i(x^*) + \sum_{j=1}^r \nu_j^* \nabla h_j(x^*) = \mathbf{0}∇x​L(x∗,λ∗,ν∗)=∇f0​(x∗)+∑i=1m​λi∗​∇fi​(x∗)+∑j=1r​νj∗​∇hj​(x∗)=0

3. Illustrative Derivation

Dual Formulation of Soft-Margin SVM

We derive the dual optimization problem for the soft-margin Support Vector Machine classifier.

Primal problem: min⁡w,b,ξ12∥w∥22+C∑i=1Nξi\min_{w, b, \xi} \frac{1}{2} \|w\|_2^2 + C \sum_{i=1}^N \xi_iminw,b,ξ​21​∥w∥22​+C∑i=1N​ξi​ subject to1−ξi−yi(wTϕ(xi)+b)≤0and−ξi≤0(i=1,…,N)\text{subject to} \quad 1 - \xi_i - y_i (w^T \phi(x_i) + b) \le 0 \quad \text{and} \quad -\xi_i \le 0 \quad (i=1, \dots, N)subject to1−ξi​−yi​(wTϕ(xi​)+b)≤0and−ξi​≤0(i=1,…,N)

Proof:

  1. Formulate the Lagrangian: Introduce Lagrange multipliers αi≥0\alpha_i \ge 0αi​≥0 and ri≥0r_i \ge 0ri​≥0: L(w,b,ξ,α,r)=12wTw+C∑i=1Nξi+∑i=1Nαi(1−ξi−yi(wTϕ(xi)+b))−∑i=1Nriξi\mathcal{L}(w, b, \xi, \alpha, r) = \frac{1}{2} w^T w + C \sum_{i=1}^N \xi_i + \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i \left( 1 - \xi_i - y_i (w^T \phi(x_i) + b) \right) - \sum_{i=1}^N r_i \xi_iL(w,b,ξ,α,r)=21​wTw+C∑i=1N​ξi​+∑i=1N​αi​(1−ξi​−yi​(wTϕ(xi​)+b))−∑i=1N​ri​ξi​

  2. Apply Stationarity (minimize over primal variables):

    • With respect to www: ∇wL=w−∑i=1Nαiyiϕ(xi)=0  ⟹  w∗=∑i=1Nαiyiϕ(xi)\nabla_w \mathcal{L} = w - \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i y_i \phi(x_i) = \mathbf{0} \implies w^* = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i y_i \phi(x_i)∇w​L=w−∑i=1N​αi​yi​ϕ(xi​)=0⟹w∗=∑i=1N​αi​yi​ϕ(xi​)
    • With respect to bbb: ∂L∂b=−∑i=1Nαiyi=0  ⟹  ∑i=1Nαiyi=0\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b} = -\sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i y_i = 0 \implies \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i y_i = 0∂b∂L​=−∑i=1N​αi​yi​=0⟹∑i=1N​αi​yi​=0
    • With respect to slack variables ξi\xi_iξi​: ∂L∂ξi=C−αi−ri=0  ⟹  αi+ri=C\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \xi_i} = C - \alpha_i - r_i = 0 \implies \alpha_i + r_i = C∂ξi​∂L​=C−αi​−ri​=0⟹αi​+ri​=C Since ri≥0r_i \ge 0ri​≥0, this implies 0≤αi≤C0 \le \alpha_i \le C0≤αi​≤C.

  3. Substitute back to form the Dual Objective: Substitute w∗w^*w∗ and the relations into the Lagrangian. The bbb term vanishes because ∑αiyi=0\sum \alpha_i y_i = 0∑αi​yi​=0. The slack terms cancel because (C−αi−ri)ξi=0(C - \alpha_i - r_i)\xi_i = 0(C−αi​−ri​)ξi​=0: L=12(∑i=1Nαiyiϕ(xi))T(∑j=1Nαjyjϕ(xj))+∑i=1Nαi−∑i=1Nαiyi(∑j=1Nαjyjϕ(xj))Tϕ(xi)\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i y_i \phi(x_i) \right)^T \left( \sum_{j=1}^N \alpha_j y_j \phi(x_j) \right) + \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i - \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i y_i \left( \sum_{j=1}^N \alpha_j y_j \phi(x_j) \right)^T \phi(x_i)L=21​(∑i=1N​αi​yi​ϕ(xi​))T(∑j=1N​αj​yj​ϕ(xj​))+∑i=1N​αi​−∑i=1N​αi​yi​(∑j=1N​αj​yj​ϕ(xj​))Tϕ(xi​) L=∑i=1Nαi−12∑i=1N∑j=1NαiαjyiyjK(xi,xj)\mathcal{L} = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^N \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j K(x_i, x_j)L=∑i=1N​αi​−21​∑i=1N​∑j=1N​αi​αj​yi​yj​K(xi​,xj​) where K(xi,xj)=ϕ(xi)Tϕ(xj)K(x_i, x_j) = \phi(x_i)^T \phi(x_j)K(xi​,xj​)=ϕ(xi​)Tϕ(xj​) is the kernel function.

  4. Formulate the final Dual problem: max⁡α∑i=1Nαi−12∑i=1N∑j=1NαiαjyiyjK(xi,xj)\max_{\alpha} \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^N \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j K(x_i, x_j)maxα​∑i=1N​αi​−21​∑i=1N​∑j=1N​αi​αj​yi​yj​K(xi​,xj​) subject to0≤αi≤C(i=1,…,N)and∑i=1Nαiyi=0■\text{subject to} \quad 0 \le \alpha_i \le C \quad (i=1, \dots, N) \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i y_i = 0 \quad \blacksquaresubject to0≤αi​≤C(i=1,…,N)and∑i=1N​αi​yi​=0■

4. Concrete Examples

Example 1: Convex Equality-Constrained Optimization

Minimize f(x,y)=x2+y2f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2f(x,y)=x2+y2 subject to x+y=10x + y = 10x+y=10.

  1. Formulate the Lagrangian: L(x,y,ν)=x2+y2+ν(x+y−10)\mathcal{L}(x, y, \nu) = x^2 + y^2 + \nu(x + y - 10)L(x,y,ν)=x2+y2+ν(x+y−10)
  2. Calculate gradients (Stationarity): ∂L∂x=2x+ν=0  ⟹  x=−ν2\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = 2x + \nu = 0 \implies x = -\frac{\nu}{2}∂x∂L​=2x+ν=0⟹x=−2ν​ ∂L∂y=2y+ν=0  ⟹  y=−ν2\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y} = 2y + \nu = 0 \implies y = -\frac{\nu}{2}∂y∂L​=2y+ν=0⟹y=−2ν​
  3. Enforce Primal Feasibility: x+y=10  ⟹  −ν2−ν2=10  ⟹  ν∗=−10x + y = 10 \implies -\frac{\nu}{2} - \frac{\nu}{2} = 10 \implies \nu^* = -10x+y=10⟹−2ν​−2ν​=10⟹ν∗=−10 Substituting back yields the unique global minimum: x∗=5,y∗=5x^* = 5, \quad y^* = 5x∗=5,y∗=5

Example 2: Inequality-Constrained KKT Verification

Minimize f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2 subject to x≥2x \ge 2x≥2 (which is 2−x≤02 - x \le 02−x≤0).

  1. Formulate the Lagrangian: L(x,λ)=x2+λ(2−x)\mathcal{L}(x, \lambda) = x^2 + \lambda(2 - x)L(x,λ)=x2+λ(2−x)
  2. Apply KKT Conditions:
    • Stationarity: 2x−λ=0  ⟹  λ=2x2x - \lambda = 0 \implies \lambda = 2x2x−λ=0⟹λ=2x
    • Complementary Slackness: λ(2−x)=0\lambda(2 - x) = 0λ(2−x)=0
  3. Solve the system:
    • If λ=0\lambda = 0λ=0, then x=0x = 0x=0. However, this violates primal feasibility (x≥2x \ge 2x≥2).
    • Therefore, we must have λ>0\lambda > 0λ>0, which implies 2−x=0  ⟹  x∗=22 - x = 0 \implies x^* = 22−x=0⟹x∗=2.
    • Substituting x∗=2x^* = 2x∗=2 into stationarity: λ∗=2(2)=4\lambda^* = 2(2) = 4λ∗=2(2)=4. Since λ∗=4≥0\lambda^* = 4 \ge 0λ∗=4≥0, dual feasibility is satisfied. The optimal constrained solution is x∗=2x^* = 2x∗=2.

5. Applied ML Context

  1. Support Vector Machines (SVM): The dual representation allows classifying non-linear boundaries via kernels. Complementary slackness guarantees that only points lying on or violating margins (support vectors) have non-zero weights αi∗>0\alpha_i^* > 0αi∗​>0.
  2. LASSO Sparsity (L1 Regularization): The L1 weight penalty is convex but non-differentiable at zero. Convex analysis and proximal operators are used to solve this, yielding sparse feature selections.
  3. Logistic Regression Duality: Minimizing binary cross-entropy loss is the direct dual problem of maximizing entropy under expectation constraints, ensuring both models converge to the same distribution.
  4. Manifold Learning Semidefinite Programming: Algorithms like Maximum Variance Unfolding (MVU) flatten high-dimensional manifolds while preserving local distances by solving semidefinite convex constraints.
  5. Matrix Completion (Collaborative Filtering): Reconstructing sparse ratings matrices is solved via convex relaxations that minimize the nuclear norm (sum of singular values) of the matrix.

6. Visual/Intuitive Summary

A diagram should be placed here illustrating constrained convex optimization geometry:

  • Draw a 2D contour plot of a convex paraboloid bowl f(x,y)=x2+y2f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2f(x,y)=x2+y2 represented by concentric circles.
  • Draw a straight line representing the boundary constraint x+y=10x + y = 10x+y=10. Shade the disallowed region (x+y<10x+y < 10x+y<10 or similar depending on boundary).
  • Show that the unconstrained minimum lies at (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) (the center of the circles).
  • Show that the constrained minimum lies at (5,5)(5, 5)(5,5), which is the tangent point where the circular contour line touches the straight constraint boundary.
  • Draw gradient vectors ∇f(x∗,y∗)\nabla f(x^*, y^*)∇f(x∗,y∗) and the constraint normal ∇h(x∗,y∗)\nabla h(x^*, y^*)∇h(x∗,y∗) at the tangent point. Show that they point in opposite directions along the same line, visually proving the stationarity KKT condition: ∇f+ν∇h=0\nabla f + \nu \nabla h = \mathbf{0}∇f+ν∇h=0.
  • Add a caption explaining that the constrained minimum always occurs where the objective contour lines are perfectly parallel (tangent) to the active constraint boundaries, aligning their gradient vectors.
